name: 1,4-butanediol

binding.assay_buffer_notes: 1,4-BD is converted in two steps: alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) → γ-hydroxybutyraldehyde → aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) → GHB. Both enzymes are the same as for ethanol metabolism.
binding.notes: Onset slower than GHB or GBL (~20-40 min) because of two-step enzymatic conversion. Co-administration with ethanol drastically slows conversion (ADH competitive substrate) → unpredictable, delayed, prolonged effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pure prodrug. All effects are GHB-mediated after conversion via ADH/ALDH.

routes.notes: Pharmacokinetics governed by ADH Km (saturable) — like ethanol, exhibits zero-order conversion at high doses. Equimolar potency to GHB. Ethanol co-ingestion → ADH competition → delayed and unpredictable onset, can cause stacking overdoses.

metabolism.notes: Competition with ethanol at ADH explains the well-documented danger of mixing BD with alcohol.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Competitive ADH inhibition → delayed conversion to GHB; ethanol metabolism wins, BD pools
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Delayed/prolonged sedation, re-dosing risk, increased overdose deaths.
Blocks BD → GHB conversion; theoretical antidote for BD overdose although clinical evidence sparse.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: ALDH2*2 variant would cause aldehyde intermediate accumulation; potentially severe flush-like reaction.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Same as GHB.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Aldehyde intermediate may contribute to hepatotoxicity with repeated use; less well characterised than GHB.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment slows conversion; renal impairment slows GHB excretion.

notes: Slowest-onset GHB prodrug due to two enzymatic conversion steps. Co-ingestion with ethanol is uniquely dangerous because the ADH bottleneck causes BD to accumulate then release as ethanol clears.

biased_agonism.interpretation: G-protein biased (opposite of LSD) — much weaker β-arrestin recruitment relative to Gq. May explain low/absent tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing

Reduces bufotenin formation; net effect depends on bufotenin contribution to subjective effects (debated)

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PM: less bufotenin formed; may experience purer 5-HT1A-driven effects. UM: more bufotenin → stronger 5-HT2A effects.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Mild
Brief exposure makes hERG concern minimal even if present

demographic_differences.weight: Inhalation dosing inherently fixed-quantity; vapour delivery variability dominates
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment likely increases AUC via MAO-A and CYP2D6 reductions

notes: 5-MeO-DMT is the canonical G-protein-biased 5-HT2A agonist among classical psychedelics — opposite end of the bias spectrum from LSD. This is mechanistically tied to its lack of tachyphylaxis and the qualitative difference in phenomenology (ego-loss with minimal imagery).

name: Alcohol

primary_targets: nAChR (α7, α4β2 inhibition at intox conc.)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Whole-cell patch; ~50 mM ethanol gives ~50% inhibition of NMDA-evoked current; effect is NOT voltage-dependent (so not Mg2+ pore-block-like).
binding.notes: Lovinger, White, Weight 1989, Science 243:1721 — landmark paper. ~50 mM corresponds to ~0.23 g/dL BAC, achievable in heavy drinkers.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Potentiation observed at concentrations as low as 1–3 mM (~5–15 mg/dL BAC) at δ-containing extrasynaptic receptors — controversial; many labs failed to replicate.
binding.notes: Wallner, Hanchar, Olsen 2003. Sensitivity at δ-subunit receptors is disputed; later studies (Borghese et al. 2006, pmid:16921002) failed to replicate the effect, suggesting it requires specific assay conditions.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Ethanol potentiates glycine-evoked Cl- current; effect mapped to residues in TM2/TM3 (S267, A52). Mihic, Whiting, Harris 1997 Nature 389:385.
binding.notes: Mihic-Harris site — alcohol pocket in TM2/3 confirmed by mutagenesis.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Lovinger, White 1991 — ethanol 25-200 mM potentiates 5-HT-evoked cation current 2-3x.
binding.notes: Underlies emetic and reinforcing effects; ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) reduces alcohol craving in early-onset alcoholics.

functional.notes: Synaptic α1β2γ2 receptors are RELATIVELY ethanol-insensitive (require >60 mM, supra-lethal); the behaviourally relevant GABA-A potentiation appears mediated by extrasynaptic δ-subunit receptors AND by indirect mechanisms (allopregnanolone release, GABA release from interneurons via 5-HT3).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Multi-target depressant. Direct effects: NMDA antagonism (50 mM IC50), glycine PAM, GABA-A δ-subunit PAM at low conc, 5-HT3 PAM. Indirect: ethanol induces neurosteroid (allopregnanolone) synthesis via HPA axis activation, and allopregnanolone is a much more potent GABA-A PAM (nM) than ethanol itself — this neurosteroid loop explains why GABA-A involvement persists at conc where direct ethanol PAM is undetectable. Chronic exposure → adaptive NMDA upregulation (NR2B subunit), GABA-A α4/γ2 switching, and cAMP/PKA signalling rearrangement, all of which underlie tolerance and the withdrawal/seizure phenotype.

neuroimaging.finding: Acute alcohol (0.75 g/kg) increases [11C]raclopride displacement in ventral striatum, indicating ~5-15% dopamine release — much smaller than psychostimulants.
Increased low-frequency (delta/theta) power and reduced alpha at BAC ~0.05-0.10 g/dL. Chronic alcoholics show reduced P300 amplitude (endophenotype for AUD risk).

routes.subject_demographics: Mixed populations; Vd ~0.55 L/kg males, ~0.50 L/kg females (less body water).
routes.notes: Zero-order elimination via ADH (Km ~0.1 g/L = ~2 mM; saturated above ~0.02 g/dL BAC). Elimination rate ~0.015 g/dL/h (range 0.010-0.025); 4-5x higher when CYP2E1 is induced in chronic heavy drinkers. F% reduced by first-pass gastric ADH (~10-25%). Tmax 30-90 min on empty stomach, 60-180 min with food.

concentration_effect.notes: 0.02 BAC = subtle effects; 0.05 = impairment; 0.08 = legal intoxication; 0.30 = stupor; 0.40 = LD50 (untreated); >0.50 typically fatal but tolerance changes this.

metabolism.notes: ADH1B*2 (Arg47His) variant common in East Asians — ~40x faster Vmax → acetaldehyde flush; ADH1B*3 (Arg369Cys) in African ancestry. Acetaldehyde is the toxic intermediate responsible for the disulfiram-like reaction, mutagenicity, and hangover.
ALDH2*2 (Glu487Lys) — homozygotes have <10% enzyme activity, severe acetaldehyde accumulation; ~30-50% of East Asians carry at least one *2 allele. Strong protection against alcoholism.

Low-affinity (Km ~10 mM) but inducible up to 10x by chronic ethanol — explains accelerated clearance in heavy drinkers and increased hepatotoxicity (CYP2E1 generates ROS). Disulfiram is a mechanism-based CYP2E1 inactivator (its metabolite DDC).
Brain catalase pathway contributes to central ethanol metabolism and may be relevant to behavioural effects (acetaldehyde in CNS is rewarding).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Acetaldehyde accumulates 5-10x → flushing, tachycardia, vomiting, hypotension. Onset within 10 min, lasts hours. Inhibition irreversible — effect persists ~1-2 wks after last disulfiram dose.
Disulfiram-like flushing reaction with ethanol co-ingestion.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: CYP2E1 induction shifts paracetamol metabolism toward toxic NAPQI metabolite; glutathione depletion in chronic drinkers
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased hepatotoxicity risk at supratherapeutic paracetamol doses in chronic alcohol users.
Marked respiratory depression risk; common cause of accidental overdose death.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: ADH1B*2 (rs1229984, Arg47His) — ~40x increased Vmax, common in East Asians, protective against AUD. ALDH2*2 (rs671, Glu487Lys) — heterozygotes ~30% activity, homozygotes ~0%; strong AUD protection via flush. CYP2E1*5B (c1/c2) — moderately inducible variant, weak AUD association.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-A α1 downregulation and α4/γ2 upregulation in chronic exposure (rats, weeks); NMDA NR2B upregulation drives kindling and withdrawal seizures.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 6-24 h after last drink. Mild: tremor, anxiety, autonomic hyperactivity (peak 24-48 h). Severe: seizures (peak 24-48 h, occur in 5-15% of dependent withdrawers without prophylaxis), delirium tremens (onset 48-96 h, mortality 5% treated / 35% untreated). Driven by NMDA upregulation + GABA-A downregulation. Benzodiazepine cover (CIWA-Ar protocol) is the standard of care.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Direct GIRK potentiation contributes to GABA-B-like analgesia and sedation at high doses.
Cross-talk with nicotine reward circuitry; partly underlies the alcohol-tobacco co-use epidemiology.

demographic_differences.sex: Women reach ~30-40% higher peak BAC for same dose/kg due to lower body water (Vd ~0.49 vs 0.55 L/kg) and lower gastric ADH activity (~40% lower first-pass).
demographic_differences.age: Elderly have ~10-20% lower Vd and slower elimination; teens have higher tolerance to motor effects but equal or greater impairment of memory.
demographic_differences.weight: Standard dose calc uses Widmark formula: BAC = dose(g) / (Vd(L/kg) × body weight(kg)).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Cirrhosis prolongs elimination by ~50% and disrupts the ADH/ALDH ratio toward acetaldehyde accumulation.

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative cross-talk between ethanol PAM and neurosteroid pathway in humans
notes: The 'GABA-A potentiator' label is correct but misleading — ethanol's direct GABA-A effects require >>10 mM at synaptic receptors; the behaviourally relevant GABA enhancement is mostly via neurosteroid (allopregnanolone) induction. NMDA antagonism dominates at typical intoxicating BACs.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced metabolism to active ethcathinone → potentially reduced anorectic effect AND elevated parent drug accumulation; clinical impact not well studied

name: Amphetamine

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 transiently expressing hTAAR1, cAMP readout
binding.notes: Bunzow et al. 2001 — original TAAR1 (then TA1) cloning paper; racemic amphetamine listed as full agonist with EC50 ~1.8 µM

functional.notes: Rothman 2001 Synapse — d-amphetamine, EC50 24.8 nM DA release
Rothman 2001 — d-amphetamine, EC50 7.07 nM NE release; ~3.5× more potent at NET than DAT
Rothman 2001 — d-amphetamine, very weak SERT releaser (~250× weaker than at DAT)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Amphetamine enters DA terminals as a DAT substrate, activates cytosolic TAAR1, which signals through Gαs to elevate cAMP/PKA and through Gαq/Ca²+, both of which phosphorylate DAT at N-terminal serines (Ser7, Ser12, Ser53), promoting reverse transport. PKC activation also internalises DAT. Inside terminals, amphetamine collapses VMAT2 proton gradient (it is a weak base, accumulates in vesicles) and as α-MPT inhibitor / direct vesicle disruptor, dumps DA into cytosol which is then reverse-transported.

neuroimaging.finding: 0.3 mg/kg oral d-amphetamine reduces striatal [11C]raclopride binding by ~5–15%, corresponding to ~50–150% increase in extracellular DA; magnitude correlates with novelty-seeking scores and subjective 'wanting'

routes.notes: Markowitz & Patrick 2017 — d-amphetamine t1/2 9–11 h, l-amphetamine 11–14 h, Tmax IR 2.5–3.5 h, XR 5.3–8.2 h; protein binding 16–20%

metabolism.notes: Highly pH-dependent: 1–75% urinary recovery of unchanged drug; acidic urine clears faster

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers show modestly reduced 4-hydroxylation but main clearance is renal — clinical impact is small. CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion, quinidine) prolong amphetamine effects.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Negligible direct binding; serotonergic effects are via SERT release

data_gaps_remaining: Direct human σ1 binding data for racemic amphetamine
notes: The 'amphetamine' record in the user database is racemic. In clinical formulations the salt is usually d-isomer (Dexedrine) or 3:1 d/l mixture (Adderall). Pharmacological data above are for d-amphetamine — l-amphetamine has a separate record and is dramatically weaker at DAT but only slightly weaker at NET.

name: Baclofen

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Classical value from Bowery 1980s. Recombinant hR1a/R1b receptors give higher EC50s (~30 μM) — discrepancy attributed to lack of native receptor accessory proteins (KCTD subunits) in recombinant systems.
binding.notes: R-baclofen is the active enantiomer (~50-200x more potent than S).

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO cells expressing human GABA-B R1a/R2 coupled to Kir3.1/3.2
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Liu et al. 2004 — EC50 11.3 μM at hR1a/R2 + Kir3.1/3.2 channels. Differs from native receptor EC50 by ~100x, illustrating the role of accessory subunits.
binding.notes: Reference agonist for the GABA-B receptor.

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: Functional receptor requires both R1 (orthosteric site) and R2 (Gi/o coupling). KCTD8/12/16 cytoplasmic accessory proteins shape kinetics and desensitisation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Gi/o → ↓adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP) + βγ → Kir3 (GIRK) opening (hyperpolarisation) and Cav2.x inhibition (↓presynaptic Ca2+ → ↓transmitter release). Both pre- and postsynaptic actions contribute. Baclofen is the prototype selective GABA-B agonist and the reference for all GABA-B pharmacology.

routes.notes: t1/2 2-6 h. 70-85% renally excreted unchanged. ~15% hepatic deamination.
Intrathecal dosing 1000x lower than oral (~50-800 μg/day vs 30-80 mg/day PO). Bypasses limited BBB penetration.

metabolism.notes: Most clearance is renal of unchanged drug.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Profound CNS / respiratory depression. Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal is a medical emergency (rebound spasticity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis).

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-B desensitisation via KCTD-dependent kinetics; chronic baclofen → tolerance and rebound on abrupt withdrawal.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 24-72 h after oral discontinuation; faster after pump failure (intrathecal). Severe rebound spasticity, hallucinations, seizures, autonomic instability, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis. Intrathecal withdrawal can be fatal — requires emergency intrathecal restart or oral high-dose substitution.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: increased CNS sensitivity, reduce dose.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: CrCl <60: reduce dose; CrCl <30: marked accumulation, prolonged t1/2 → encephalopathy risk at standard doses.

notes: Reference selective GABA-B agonist. The R1/R2 obligate heterodimer architecture (Marshall & Foord 1998; Pin & Bettler crystal structures) and KCTD accessory subunits are essential for understanding why recombinant Ki values diverge from native-tissue Ki values by 100-1000x.

name: Brivaracetam

binding.tissue_or_cell: human brain homogenate (cortex) and CHO cells expressing human recombinant SV2A
binding.assay_buffer_notes: 37 C; standard binding buffer
binding.notes: Reported ~15-20x higher affinity for SV2A than levetiracetam in same assay system; pIC50 ~7.4. Brivaracetam shows no measurable affinity for AMPA receptors despite the racetam scaffold — the SV2A site is the entire mechanism.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Binds SV2A on synaptic vesicles. SV2A is required for normal neurotransmitter release and is hypothesized to act as a positive modulator of vesicle priming / Ca2+-dependent exocytosis; brivaracetam binding appears to dampen excessive release in epileptic conditions through allosteric modulation rather than block. Sodium channel blockade is a secondary, weaker activity (IC50 in the low-micromolar range) but is not believed to drive clinical efficacy at therapeutic plasma concentrations.

neuroimaging.finding: SV2A occupancy in human brain measured with [11C]UCB-J: brivaracetam ~80% occupancy at therapeutic doses (50-200 mg), confirming the SV2A target engagement at clinically used exposures.

routes.subject_demographics: healthy adult males, multiple ascending dose, ages 18-55

metabolism.metabolite_name: BRV acid (hydroxy-acid metabolite from acetamide hydrolysis)

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: AUC of brivaracetam decreased ~45%; dose increase may be needed
modest decrease in brivaracetam exposure; brivaracetam itself increases carbamazepine-epoxide AUC ~37%

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers (PMs, ~2-4% of Europeans, ~13-23% of East Asians) show ~50% higher steady-state brivaracetam plasma concentrations; CYP2C19 ultrarapid metabolizers (UMs) show modestly lower exposure. FDA label notes that dose reduction may be considered in known PMs.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: no SV2A downregulation reported in chronic dosing studies
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: abrupt discontinuation can precipitate breakthrough seizures (rebound); taper recommended over weeks. No characterized somatic withdrawal syndrome distinct from levetiracetam.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: secondary mechanism; not relevant at therapeutic free plasma concentrations (~2-10 µM)

demographic_differences.sex: no clinically meaningful sex differences in PK
demographic_differences.age: elderly: ~20% higher exposure due to declining renal/hepatic function; pediatric dosing weight-based
demographic_differences.weight: weight-based dosing in children <50 kg
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: hepatic impairment: ~50-60% AUC increase; reduce dose. Mild-moderate renal impairment: no adjustment. Severe renal impairment without dialysis: limited data.

data_gaps_remaining: No direct AMPA receptor binding data — confirmed absent rather than missing
notes: Despite the 'racetam' name, brivaracetam has no AMPA activity; it is an SV2A ligand and structurally a 4-propyl derivative of levetiracetam. Higher SV2A affinity and better brain penetration than levetiracetam translate to faster onset of seizure protection. The behavioral/psychiatric adverse-event profile (irritability, depression) is qualitatively similar to but milder than levetiracetam.

binding.notes: In vivo potency originally reported as 10,000× morphine; modern hot-plate work gives ~500× morphine, 2.9× fentanyl. trans-isomer >> cis. Direct Ki at recombinant hMOR not published.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR full agonist; ultra-high potency means microgram doses are active and unintentional overdose risk extreme.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Microgram-active → extreme overdose risk; naloxone reversible but may require multiple doses.

notes: Cyclohexanol scaffold (not morphinan, not fentanyl). Trans-isomer is the active form. Microgram potency means extreme overdose risk.

name: Bromantane

primary_targets: aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC, genomic upregulation)

functional.readout: qPCR + Western blot in striatum, hypothalamus, VTA
functional.notes: Bromantane upregulates TH and AADC mRNA/protein in dopaminergic regions over 1-2 h post-dose, increasing newly-synthesized dopamine stores without releasing pre-formed pools. This is the basis for its 'actoprotector' / atypical psychostimulant profile.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Genomic mechanism — bromantane elevates CREB phosphorylation, disinhibiting TH transcription that is normally suppressed by dopamine autoregulation. Effect is slow-onset (hours) and long-lasting (weeks of chronic use) compared to classical psychostimulants. σ1 receptor involvement is inferred from amantadine/memantine analogy but not directly demonstrated for bromantane.

routes.notes: Russian-language PK literature reports oral t½ ~11 h; lipophilic adamantane scaffold gives high BBB penetrance. Cmax data poorly reported in English-language sources.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Bromantane is uniquely described as resistant to classical stimulant tolerance — repeated dosing maintains efficacy over weeks in Russian clinical trials. Rationale: the mechanism does not deplete catecholamine stores or chronically over-stimulate post-synaptic dopamine receptors.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No documented opioid- or amphetamine-type withdrawal in published Russian trials; possible rebound fatigue.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Inferred from amantadine analogy; not directly measured for bromantane.

data_gaps_remaining: controlled long-term safety data outside Russian Federation
notes: Atypical psychostimulant approved in Russia (Ladasten) for asthenia. Mechanism is genomic upregulation of dopamine synthesis enzymes rather than classical monoamine release or reuptake inhibition. Most clinical and PK literature is in Russian and not independently validated. WADA-banned for athletic competition (2002 Salt Lake City Olympics doping case).

name: Bromazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM with pyridyl ring substituting phenyl. Metabolism is unusual for a benzo — mainly CYP1A2 (not CYP3A4).

metabolism.notes: Fluvoxamine (CYP1A2 inhibitor) ↑ AUC 2.4-fold. Itraconazole (CYP3A4 inhibitor) has no effect → CYP3A4 not involved.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP1A2 inducers (smoking, char-grilled meat) may reduce bromazepam exposure.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: t1/2 prolonged.

data_gaps_remaining: Specific GABA-A subunit Ki values not separately determined
notes: Unusual among benzos in being metabolized predominantly by CYP1A2 rather than CYP3A4. Marketed primarily outside US (Lexotan/Lexotanil).

name: Bromazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Alprazolam's 8-bromo analogue (vs 8-chloro). Synthesized 1976 (Hester) but never marketed. Late-2010s/2020s NPS — increasingly common in North American post-mortem case series, often as a fentanyl adulterant.

notes: Emerged as a major opioid adulterant in 2022–2024 North American drug supply. Increasingly detected in overdose deaths. CFSRE NPS Discovery monitoring shows >300% increase 2022–2023.

name: Bromo-dragonfly

binding.notes: Among the most potent 5-HT2A agonists known; Nichols 1998 original report
Subnanomolar at 2B — strong valvulopathy concern
Potent MAO-A inhibition contributes to serotonin syndrome risk

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Picomolar-range 5-HT2A agonist with α1 adrenergic vasoconstrictor activity; resistant to hepatic metabolism → extended duration.

routes.notes: Typical dose 100–1000 µg; onset delayed up to 6 h; duration 12–24 h, sometimes 2–3 days. Fatal at ~700 µg.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome risk

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Severe peripheral vasoconstriction — limb necrosis and amputation cases (Sweden 2007)
Picomolar 5-HT2B — valvulopathy with chronic use

notes: ≥5 deaths documented (Scandinavia + US). Mislabelling as 2C-B-FLY (20× less potent) has caused mass overdoses. Resistant to MAO/CYP → very long duration.

name: Bromoketamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 2-Bromodeschloroketamine.

notes: Same compound as 2-Bromodeschloroketamine.

name: Brorphine

binding.tissue_or_cell: FLP-FRT-HEK hMOR; HTRF cAMP / Gi pathway
binding.notes: Less potent than fentanyl at binding (Ki ~17× higher than fentanyl 1.4 nM in same assay), but comparable in-vivo potency (rat antinociception ED50 0.0858 mg/kg)

functional.notes: Brorphine analogues do NOT show significant bias vs hydromorphone (Connors 2024 — Neuropharmacology); Emax above reference compound (so-called 'superagonist' for arrestin)

biased_agonism.interpretation: Not significantly biased relative to reference. Brorphine and halogenated analogues recruit β-arrestin2 with high efficacy — at odds with the idea that 'designer opioids are uniformly β-arrestin-biased'.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist via Gαi/o; high β-arrestin2 recruitment with Emax 209% of hydromorphone but unbiased relative to reference (i.e., both pathways activated proportionally).

metabolism.notes: Hepatocyte studies show oxidative metabolism; primary metabolites are hydroxy-brorphine and the descyclized piperidine ring-opened products.

notes: Piperidine-benzimidazolone scaffold — a bridge between nitazenes (benzimidazole) and fentanyl-like piperidines. Found in supply since 2019; mostly displaced by nitazenes by 2022 but resurfaced 2023.

name: Brotizolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienotriazolodiazepine — like etizolam structurally. Very potent hypnotic.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: prolonged.

notes: Marketed in Japan/Europe (Lendormin); not US.

name: BTCP

binding.notes: Vignon 1988; IC50 7-8 nM for DA uptake. ~50× selectivity over SERT/NET.
Essentially inactive at NMDA — BTCP is a 'PCP without NMDA activity'

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pure DAT inhibitor with cocaine-like behavioral profile (Le Foll 2000 Neuropsychopharmacology) but binds at a DAT site allosterically distinct from cocaine.

metabolism.notes: Two active hydroxylated metabolites bind DAT with Ki within 2× of parent

notes: Atypical arylcyclohexylamine — replacing the phenyl with benzothiophene shifts pharmacology entirely from NMDA blockade to DAT inhibition. Behaviorally cocaine-like, not PCP-like. Tag 'NMDA-antagonist' is wrong.

name: Bufotenin

binding.notes: ~10× higher 5-HT2A affinity than 5-MeO-DMT
High 5-HT3 activity — drives nausea/vomiting

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Strong 5-HT2A and 5-HT3 — combination yields intense somatic load (vasoconstriction, vomiting) limiting recreational use; CNS entry limited by 5-OH polarity (cf. norpsilocin)

routes.notes: Severe somatic effects at IV doses ≥4 mg — facial cyanosis, hypertension

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: PM may have higher endogenous bufotenin levels; relevance debated

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Vomiting, nausea, severe somatic discomfort
Chronic exposure cardiac valvulopathy theoretical

notes: 5-hydroxy substitution gives higher 5-HT2A affinity but BBB-limited like other peripherally polar 5-OH tryptamines — most psychoactivity may occur via central conversion or paradox. Anu Anaipakkam Bufo Alvarius venom = 5-MeO-DMT, not bufotenin.

name: bufotenine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Bufotenin entry — same compound

notes: Duplicate of Bufotenin in input list.

name: bufoviridine
data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor
notes: Novel or obscure tryptamine without published controlled pharmacology. Effects unknown in humans.

name: Buphedrone

binding.notes: Simmler 2014 — buphedrone preferentially inhibits NET and DAT and also releases NE; transitional between methcathinone (pure releaser) and pentedrone (pure blocker) due to intermediate α-ethyl chain length

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hybrid mechanism: NE releaser + DAT/NET blocker. The α-ethyl chain is the SAR transition point — methyl (methcathinone) is pure releaser, propyl (pentedrone) is pure blocker, ethyl (buphedrone) is hybrid.

notes: Buphedrone is the α-ethyl analogue of methcathinone — pivotal SAR position where substrate behavior gradually transitions to blocker behavior.

name: Buprenorphine

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO membranes expressing recombinant human MOR
binding.notes: Sub-nanomolar MOR Ki; very slow off-rate explains long clinical duration and difficulty in displacement during overdose.
Functional KOR antagonism contributes to mood-elevating effects and is the basis for buprenorphine's antidepressant signal.
Weak NOP partial agonism — proposed to modulate reward and may contribute to reduced abuse liability.

functional.notes: Virk & Williams 2009 / J. Neurosci. — buprenorphine Emax ~25-40% of full agonists; intrinsic efficacy at MOR is low.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Partial Gαi activation, very slow MOR dissociation (>2 h), poor internalisation. Norbuprenorphine metabolite is a FULL agonist at MOR, DOR, NOP — and 10× more respiratory-depressant than parent in rats (Brown 2011, doi:10.1016/j.taap.2011.02.014) — BUT does not cross the human BBB efficiently, which is why buprenorphine's clinical respiratory ceiling holds. Buprenorphine itself competitively blocks norbuprenorphine from CNS MOR (Brown 2011).

neuroimaging.finding: 16 mg sublingual buprenorphine produces ~80-95% MOR occupancy that persists 24-76 h; this is the basis for once-daily and depot dosing.

routes.notes: Oral F% <10% due to first-pass; sublingual ≈30%. Effective elimination half-life 24-42 h.

concentration_effect.notes: Dahan 2006 — respiratory depression plateaus at ≈50% of baseline minute ventilation, the famous ceiling effect.

metabolism.notes: Picard 2005 — CYP3A4 dominant, CYP2C8 minor contributor. Norbup is a full MOR/DOR/NOP agonist but has poor BBB penetration in humans.
Brown 2011 — both glucuronides are biologically active at opioid receptors.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: ↑ buprenorphine AUC 1.5-3x
↓ buprenorphine AUC ≥50%, possible withdrawal

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP3A4 polymorphisms and inducers/inhibitors meaningfully alter buprenorphine and norbuprenorphine AUC. OPRM1 118G carriers may need higher maintenance doses.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Very slow MOR off-rate (>2 h dissociation) means antagonist effects persist; withdrawal symptoms milder and slower-onset than full agonists.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 24-72 h after last dose; peak 5-7 d; milder but more protracted than morphine; insomnia and dysphoria last weeks.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Clinically meaningful QT prolongation rare; no torsades signal in routine use.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: reduce initial dose; longer half-life.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: large F% changes; avoid in severe liver disease. Renal failure: no major dose change needed.

notes: The respiratory ceiling effect — partial agonism at MOR limits maximal respiratory depression — is the safety feature that makes bup viable for opioid use disorder maintenance. Naloxone reversal of buprenorphine overdose requires HIGH doses (≥2-4 mg) and may not fully overcome the slow off-rate.

name: Bupropion

binding.notes: Stahl review — bupropion is a weak NET/DAT inhibitor at parent level; hydroxybupropion metabolite contributes substantially.
Negligible serotonin activity.
Non-competitive nicotinic antagonism — basis for Zyban smoking-cessation indication.

functional.notes: Bupropion at clinical doses (150-300 mg/day) achieves only ~25% striatal DAT occupancy — weaker than methylphenidate.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Weak parent + active hydroxybupropion metabolite (NET-selective) drives clinical NE/DA enhancement. Nicotinic antagonism is mechanistically separate and drives smoking cessation.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~21 h for parent; hydroxybupropion t1/2 ~20 h and reaches 4-7x higher plasma than parent.

metabolism.notes: Active NET-selective metabolite; reaches 4-7x higher steady-state plasma than parent.
Carbonyl reduction; threohydro responsible for dry mouth.
Erythrohydro plasma levels correlate with insomnia.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 5-fold increase in desipramine AUC; bupropion is clinically a strong CYP2D6 inhibitor

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2B6*6 and *18 reduce hydroxybupropion formation by ~33% without altering parent or other metabolites — implications for smoking cessation efficacy.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No physical withdrawal; dose tapering recommended to avoid rebound depression

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Dose-dependent seizure risk — 0.4% at ≤450 mg/day; markedly higher in eating-disorder patients, bulimia, or with concurrent stimulants

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: 35% reduction in CL; reduced doses recommended
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment: doses ≤150 mg every other day

notes: Weak NDRI at parent + strong nAChR antagonism; clinical activity driven substantially by hydroxybupropion (NET-selective active metabolite). NDRI profile gives less euphoria than pure DRIs because NET inhibition normalises PFC DA without striatal DA spike.

name: buserelin
data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor
notes: Not a recreational psychedelic. Peptide hormone analogue, oncology probe, neuropeptide ligand, or unrelated approved drug; included in parent dataset due to indole or tryptophan substructure. No psychedelic pharmacology relevant.

notes: Alkoxy chain SAR: methoxy < butoxy < propoxy < ethoxy ≈ isopropoxy at MOR (Vandeputte 2023).

name: Butorphanol

binding.notes: Gharagozlou 2003 — high-affinity KOR partial agonist.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: KOR-dominant analgesia + MOR partial agonism. Ceiling for respiratory depression.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mixed opioid/dysphoric; less severe than morphine.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Weak σ binding (Ki > 1 μM); minimal contribution to clinical effects.

demographic_differences.sex: Women show greater KOR-mediated analgesia.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: ~25% reduced clearance.

notes: Like pentazocine but with stronger KOR affinity and weaker σ component → less dysphoria.

name: Butylcathinone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Predicted weak DAT/NET blocker; N-butyl is the boundary at which N-substitution begins to mimic pyrrolidine's steric bulk, switching to blocker. Limited direct data.

notes: Minimal published data; predicted from N-substituent SAR.

name: Butylone

binding.notes: Saha 2018 — butylone is a DAT BLOCKER but SERT SUBSTRATE (hybrid mechanism, different from methylone's pure substrate profile)
Substrate-type releaser at SERT (monensin-confirmed); blocker at DAT — α-ethyl extension prevents DAT translocation but not SERT

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hybrid mechanism: DAT blocker + SERT substrate. The α-ethyl group (vs methyl in methylone) creates steric hindrance for DAT translocation but permits SERT.

notes: Butylone is the methylone homologue with α-ethyl (vs α-methyl). Critically — α-ethyl extension is sufficient to switch from substrate to blocker at DAT while preserving SERT substrate behavior. Same hybrid pattern as pentylone.

name: Butyrfentanyl

binding.tissue_or_cell: rat brain membrane or CHO hMOR depending on source
binding.notes: Ki 32 nM at MOR (~32× weaker than fentanyl). Metabolised by CYP2D6 AND CYP3A4 (notable — most fentalogs are CYP3A4-dominant). Active metabolites include hydroxybutyrfentanyl and carboxybutyrfentanyl.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist via Gαi/o. β-arrestin bias not reliably established for most fentalogs — fentanyl class is broadly unbiased per Ramos-González 2023.

metabolism.notes: Class-default CYP3A4 N-dealkylation pathway shared with fentanyl. Also 4-ANPP (4-anilino-N-phenethylpiperidine) from amide hydrolysis is a marker of synthesis.
Steuer 2017 — CYP2D6 contribution makes PM/UM polymorphisms potentially relevant.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased AUC, overdose risk.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inferred from fentanyl-class — no analogue-specific human data.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Classical opioid; typically shorter than morphine due to higher lipophilicity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Wooden chest syndrome — class-shared; rapid IV / smoked / IV illicit exposure.

notes: Ki 32 nM at MOR (~32× weaker than fentanyl). Metabolised by CYP2D6 AND CYP3A4 (notable — most fentalogs are CYP3A4-dominant). Active metabolites include hydroxybutyrfentanyl and carboxybutyrfentanyl.

name: C-Glycosyltryptophan
data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor
notes: Tryptophan metabolic derivative or peptide. Not directly psychoactive. Either upstream of serotonin synthesis or a chemical intermediate / analytical reference compound.

name: C30-nbome

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Reported inactive — no functional 5-HT2A engagement.

notes: Identifier not recovered in literature search; existing 'inactive' tag retained.

name: Camazepam

binding.notes: Low intrinsic BZD affinity; effects mostly via temazepam metabolite

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug to temazepam via carbamate hydrolysis.

routes.notes: Terminal t1/2 6.4–10.5 h

name: Canket

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 2-fluoro analogue of O-PCE / N-ethyl-2F-DCK. Expected NMDA affinity similar to or higher than ketamine, by analogy to 2F-DCK.

notes: 2'-Fluoro-2-Oxo-PCE. Marketplace identity ambiguous — sometimes called 'Canberra ketamine'. The name 'Fluorexetamine' overlaps with this and with 3-F-2-oxo-PCE.

name: Cannabichromene

binding.notes: Weak CB1 binding (~20× weaker than THC) — not the primary mechanism.
CB2 activity resides exclusively in (−) isomer; (+) isomer inactive at CB2.
Both enantiomers active at TRPA1 (stereo-non-selective).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Primary actions via TRP channel activation (TRPA1>>TRPV1) producing calcium influx; weak partial CB2 agonism contributes to anti-inflammatory effects.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Increases endogenous anandamide tone — may contribute to indirect endocannabinoid effects

data_gaps_remaining: in vivo TRPA1 contribution to subjective effects
notes: No clinical human PK data; classified as non-intoxicating because CB1 affinity is too weak for psychoactive effect at achievable doses.

name: Cannabidiolic acid

binding.notes: Bolognini 2013: CBDA is more potent than CBD at 5-HT1A in vitro and in vivo anti-nausea models.
Takeda 2008: CBDA IC50 ~2 µM at COX-2 with 9× selectivity over COX-1; methylation of carboxyl group abolishes selectivity — carboxylate is the pharmacophore.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 5-HT1A activation → Gi → decreased cAMP and neuronal hyperpolarisation (anti-nausea, anti-anxiety); COX-2 selective inhibition.

metabolism.notes: Decarboxylates to CBD on heating (smoking/vaping) or storage; in body, CBDA mostly stable but slowly converts.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Antagonist; potential anti-inflammatory mechanism

notes: Raw cannabinoid acid in fresh plant material — converted to CBD by heat/UV/time. Mechanism differs from CBD: more potent 5-HT1A agonist, has selective COX-2 inhibition (CBD does not). Has been formulated as a metallic salt 'EPM301' for stability.

name: Cannabigerol

binding.notes: Cascio 2010: CBG is potent (sub-nM) α2-adrenoceptor agonist — likely dominant mechanism for in vivo effects (sedation, hypotension, anti-anxiety).
Cascio 2010: Moderate potency 5-HT1A antagonist; opposite direction from CBD.
Weak partial agonist / very weak antagonist.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: α2-adrenergic Gi signalling → decreased cAMP → reduced noradrenergic outflow (sedation, hypotension).

data_gaps_remaining: clinical CV monitoring data for high-dose CBG
notes: Often marketed as 'mother of all cannabinoids' (biosynthetic precursor). Importantly, primary pharmacology is NOT cannabinoid — sub-nM α2-adrenoceptor agonism is much more potent than CB1/CB2 activity. Safety concern: potential additive hypotension/bradycardia with clonidine or β-blockers.

name: Cannabis

binding.notes: Original Felder/Showalter measurement; commonly reported 40 nM range. Partial agonist with low intrinsic activity (15-30%) vs full agonists like CP55,940 or WIN55,212-2.
Felder et al 1995. Partial agonist at CB2 as well; immune-cell modulation context.
Ryberg 2007. CBD is GPR55 antagonist (opposite direction).

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: Switches CB1 Gi coupling to Gs; implicated in addiction-related signalling

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Δ9-THC, as a partial CB1 agonist, inhibits adenylyl cyclase via Gαi/o (lower Emax than full agonists like JWH-018 or CP55,940), recruits β-arrestin-2 weakly, activates ERK1/2. CB1 partial agonism = ceiling on intoxication and key reason THC does not cause the seizures/AKI/MI seen with full synthetic agonists.

neuroimaging.finding: Acute Δ9-THC reduces [11C]OMAR (CB1 antagonist) binding by ~30% in cortex, confirming target engagement at recreational doses
Increased BOLD in striatum/ACC during reward and salience tasks; decreased in DLPFC during working memory

routes.notes: Smoking bioavailability 18-50% depending on smoking topography; terminal half-life is long (1-3 days) due to deep adipose redistribution.
First-pass metabolism produces ~equipotent 11-OH-THC, contributing to delayed/more intense effects of edibles.

metabolism.notes: 11-OH-THC is equipotent or slightly more potent at CB1 than parent; major active metabolite especially after oral dosing.
Inactive carboxylic acid; primary urinary marker (as glucuronide).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: ≈1.8× THC AUC, 3× 11-OH-THC AUC
≈40% reduction THC AUC

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C9*3/*3 carriers show ~3× higher THC AUC than *1/*1; clinically relevant for medical cannabis dosing.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: CB1 receptors downregulate within 4 weeks of daily heavy use (~20% reduction in cortical [18F]MK-9470 binding); recovery within 4 weeks of abstinence (D'Souza 2016).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 24-48h, peak 2-6 days, resolves 1-2 weeks. Irritability, anxiety, sleep disturbance with vivid dreams, decreased appetite, sweating.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Putative role in pain processing; clinical significance unclear
May contribute to metabolic effects and anti-inflammatory action

demographic_differences.sex: Women show 1.7× higher peak plasma Δ9-THC than men at same per-kg dose; possibly due to higher adipose redistribution.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly show slower clearance and greater sensitivity to cognitive/cardiovascular effects.
demographic_differences.weight: Higher BMI → larger Vd → longer detection window but delayed Cmax
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment significantly prolongs half-life; renal clearance minimal.

data_gaps_remaining: definitive Bmax data in human living brain for CB1 downregulation
notes: Δ9-THC's PARTIAL agonism at CB1 (~15-30% intrinsic activity vs CP55,940) is the single most important pharmacological fact distinguishing natural cannabis from synthetic cannabinoid full agonists. This ceiling effect is why THC has never produced confirmed lethal overdose: maximum CB1 activation is intrinsically limited regardless of dose.

name: Carfentanil

binding.tissue_or_cell: Multiple — rat brain (Filizola 2019 IC50 0.19 nM) and human cloned MOR; carfentanil itself used as PET radioligand ([11C]carfentanil)
binding.radioligand_or_probe: [3H]DAMGO; carfentanil also serves as MOR PET tracer
binding.notes: Among the most potent MOR ligands known. Kd 0.024 nM at human MOR (Ramos-Gonzalez 2023). ~10,000× morphine in-vivo.

functional.notes: log(EC50) -8.11; 130× more potent than fentanyl at G-protein activation.
log(EC50) -8.50; 625× more potent than DAMGO at β-arrestin2.

biased_agonism.interpretation: Carfentanil is β-arrestin–BIASED relative to DAMGO (Ramos-González 2023) — opposite of fentanyl. Bias may contribute to apnea / respiratory depression at sub-analgesic doses. Carfentanil also stabilises MOR conformations resistant to naloxone reversal (Faouzi 2024 — see notes).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ultra-efficient MOR agonist — full Emax at picomolar concentrations. Carfentanil-bound MOR is sensitive to naltrexone but partially resistant to naloxone and nalmefene (Faouzi et al., bioRxiv 2024 — PMC12198324); has clinical implications for overdose reversal.

neuroimaging.finding: [11C]carfentanil is the standard PET radioligand for quantifying brain MOR occupancy in humans (Bencherif 2002).

routes.notes: Case-report-derived t½ 5.7h for carfentanil and 11.8h for norcarfentanyl (one-compartment model).

metabolism.notes: N-dealkylation to norcarfentanyl (inactive) is dominant pathway; also monohydroxylation of piperidine ring.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Classical opioid; potentially severe due to extreme MOR engagement.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Wooden chest syndrome more frequent and severe than with fentanyl due to extreme potency and rapid onset.

notes: Veterinary use only (Wildnil). ~10,000× morphine in-vivo. Detection in illicit supply since 2016. The β-arrestin bias + naloxone-resistant receptor conformation is a CRITICAL safety message — may need nalmefene or naltrexone instead of naloxone in pure carfentanil exposures.

name: Carisoprodol

primary_targets: GABA-A (barbiturate-like PAM, partly via meprobamate metabolite)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Gonzalez et al. 2009: carisoprodol potentiates and directly gates GABA-A in a barbiturate-like manner (EC50 ~480 μM PAM; ~3 mM direct activation). Meprobamate metabolite contributes substantially to abuse liability.
binding.notes: PMC2858432 — 'Abuse Potential of Soma: the GABA-A Receptor as a Target' is the modern definitive characterisation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Direct GABA-A PAM (and at high conc, direct gating) + meprobamate (an active anxiolytic metabolite at GABA-A). Combined pharmacology underlies muscle relaxation, anxiolysis, and abuse potential.

routes.subject_demographics: Adults. t1/2 carisoprodol 1-2 h; meprobamate metabolite t1/2 6-17 h.
routes.notes: CYP2C19 PMs: 4x parent exposure, 50% less meprobamate — abuse pattern differs by genotype.

metabolism.notes: Meprobamate is the major anxiolytic metabolite; itself was a marketed drug (Miltown, withdrawn for abuse).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased sedation from parent; reduced anxiolytic efficacy.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CPIC-grade pharmacogenetic effect: PMs have 4x carisoprodol exposure and 50% reduced meprobamate.

notes: The CYP2C19 pharmacogenetic dimension is unusual and clinically meaningful — PMs get more direct sedation, EMs get more meprobamate-mediated anxiolysis.

name: CBDV

notes: Propyl analogue of CBD. Studied as anticonvulsant (GWP42006), but Phase 2 trial in focal epilepsy was negative. Continues to be studied for autism (Rett, Fragile X).

name: CBN

name: CE-123

binding.notes: (S)-CE-123 — Sitte/Hutchinson groups; atypical, non-substrate DAT inhibitor.

name: Centrophenoxine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hepatic esterase hydrolysis releases DMAE (deanol) and p-chlorophenoxyacetic acid (pCPA). DMAE → choline → acetylcholine in CNS. pCPA itself crosses BBB and may have direct effects (this is the pharmacological rationale for the ester being more effective than DMAE alone).

notes: 1960s pharmaceutical (Lucidril). Mechanism is DMAE release + (possibly) pCPA. DMAE itself has limited evidence for cognitive enhancement; pregnant-rat teratogenicity has been reported (avoid in pregnancy).

name: Cerebrolysin

primary_targets: multiple — porcine brain hydrolysate of peptides <10 kDa
pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Mixture of low-molecular-weight peptides (15%) and free amino acids (85%) prepared by enzymatic hydrolysis of pig brain. Claimed to mimic endogenous neurotrophic factors (NGF, BDNF, CNTF, GDNF). Specific active components have not been definitively identified.

routes.notes: IM and IV-only — oral not feasible due to peptide degradation. PK not well characterized due to undefined active species.

notes: Used in Eastern Europe, Russia, and parts of Asia for stroke, TBI, and dementia. Cochrane review (2017) suggests possible benefit in acute ischemic stroke and vascular dementia but evidence quality is moderate. Cannot be used orally. Theoretical TSE/prion risk from porcine brain raw material is regulated by source-country veterinary standards.

name: Chloral Hydrate

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Trichloroethanol (TCE) — the active metabolite — potentiates GABA-A currents at the barbiturate site (Lovinger & Peoples).
binding.notes: Chloral hydrate itself is essentially a prodrug for TCE.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug → TCE via ADH (very rapid, t1/2 minutes). TCE is the active GABA-A PAM and also a TTX-resistant Na+ channel modulator (BMC Anesth 2023). Chloral hydrate is genotoxic in itself (formaldehyde-like aldehyde) — chronic use linked to hepatic/renal toxicity.

routes.notes: Chloral hydrate t1/2 in plasma ~4 min (rapid ADH conversion). Active TCE t1/2 dominates clinical effect.

metabolism.notes: TCE is more potent than parent; UGT2B7 glucuronidation is rate-limiting for elimination.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 'Mickey Finn' — alcohol slows TCE clearance and TCE displaces ethanol from albumin → marked sedation.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: TCE displaces warfarin from albumin → transient INR increase
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Transient anticoagulant potentiation.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Chronic exposure linked to liver tumors in rodents; IARC Group 2A.

demographic_differences.age: Withdrawn for paediatric use in many countries due to genotoxicity concerns.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment slows TCE conjugation.

notes: Classical 'knockout drops' (Mickey Finn). Mostly replaced by BZs and other sedatives. TCE is the relevant pharmacologically active species.

name: Chloral-betaine

primary_targets: GABA-A (via TCE, after chloral hydrate release)
pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Complex of chloral hydrate with betaine — gastric dissociation releases chloral hydrate. All subsequent PK/PD is chloral-hydrate pharmacology.

notes: Adduct formulation intended to reduce gastric irritation. Long withdrawn.

name: Chlordiazepoxide

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: First benzodiazepine synthesized (Sternbach 1955); 2-methylamino-4-oxide moiety distinguishes it structurally. Metabolized to a cascade of active species (desmethylchlordiazepoxide → demoxepam → nordazepam → oxazepam).

routes.notes: t1/2 5–30 h (mean 12 h); demoxepam t1/2 14–95 h.

metabolism.notes: Demoxepam t1/2 14–95 h; further metabolized to nordazepam → oxazepam.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs accumulate nordazepam more.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild due to long-acting active metabolites — preferred for alcohol withdrawal (CIWA protocols).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked CL reduction; metabolite accumulation.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic disease: demoxepam t1/2 up to 346 h reported.

notes: Sternbach's 1955 discovery; first benzodiazepine. Cascade metabolism gives 'self-tapering' withdrawal that suits alcohol detoxification.

name: Chloroform

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Volatile anaesthetic; abandoned ~1900s due to hepatotoxicity (CYP2E1 → phosgene) and cardiac arrhythmia (catecholamine sensitisation).

metabolism.notes: Hepatotoxic reactive metabolite.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Sudden cardiac death from VF with even minor adrenergic stress.

notes: Historic; IARC Group 2B carcinogen.

name: Chlorpheniramine

binding.tissue_or_cell: cloned human H1 (recombinant) — value is for the active dexchlorpheniramine (S)-(+) enantiomer
binding.notes: (R)-(-)-levochlorpheniramine Ki is 211–361 nM at the same receptor — ~80-fold weaker. Racemic chlorpheniramine maleate is the marketed preparation; dexchlorpheniramine carries virtually all H1 activity.

binding.reference: Wikipedia compendium citing PDSP Ki database (https://pdsp.unc.edu/databases/kidb.php)
binding.notes: Aggregated tabulation; PDSP record is the primary source.

Chlorpheniramine is a weak anticholinergic relative to e.g. diphenhydramine; the M1-M5 Ki values (25–78 µM range) are well above therapeutic free plasma concentrations (typically <30 nM), so clinical anticholinergic burden at antiemetic/antihistamine doses is modest.

Chlorpheniramine is essentially equipotent to many marketed SSRIs at SERT and was the original lead Tabakoff/Carlsson worked from in the 1960s. It has clinical relevance: chlorpheniramine + an SSRI has triggered serotonin syndrome in case reports (pmid:16413139).
Weak; ~95× less potent than at SERT.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Inverse agonism at H1 (constitutively active GPCR; chlorpheniramine and other first-gen H1 antagonists stabilize the inactive conformation, reducing Gαq → PLCβ → IP3/DAG signalling). SERT inhibition is purely competitive at the central binding site (S1) with no demonstrated allosteric activity at the S2 site at clinically achievable concentrations.

neuroimaging.finding: Clinical (sedating) oral chlorpheniramine 4 mg produces ~40-50% brain H1 receptor occupancy measured with [11C]-doxepin in healthy volunteers, accounting for its sedation; second-generation antihistamines (fexofenadine, bilastine) produce <10% occupancy at therapeutic doses.
neuroimaging.reference: pmid:9482876 (Tagawa et al., 2001; J Clin Pharmacol)

routes.reference: pmid:7106172 (Peets EA, Jackson M, Symchowicz S — Pharmacokinetics of chlorpheniramine after IV and oral administration, 1982; J Pharmacol Exp Ther)
routes.notes: Range of half-life observed: 19–43 h. Bioavailability from 10 mg oral solution 34–59%; from 8 mg tablets 25–44% (extensive gut wall first-pass metabolism).
Mean t1/2 ~20 h IV, longer (28 h mean) after PO due to flip-flop kinetics.

concentration_effect.reference: researchgate:232794187 (Simons FE — Chlorpheniramine plasma concentration and histamine H1 receptor occupancy)

metabolism.reference: pmid:11994058 (Yasuda SU, Zhang L, Huang SM — The roles of CYP2D6 and stereoselectivity in the clinical pharmacokinetics of chlorpheniramine; Br J Clin Pharmacol 2002)

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Coadministered quinidine prolonged (S)-(+)-chlorpheniramine elimination half-life from 18.0 ± 2.0 h to 29.3 ± 2.0 h and increased AUC, confirming the dominant role of CYP2D6 in stereoselective clearance.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs and patients on CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine, bupropion) show ~50–60% increased AUC and prolonged sedation duration. The (S)-(+) (active) enantiomer is preferentially metabolised by CYP2D6 and accumulates relative to the inactive (R)-(-) form in PMs.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: H1 sedation tolerance develops within ~3-7 days of regular dosing; receptor-level mechanism not formally measured for chlorpheniramine specifically but presumed analogous to other H1 inverse agonists (no robust H1 internalisation in heterologous systems; tolerance likely reflects compensatory glutamatergic/noradrenergic adaptation rather than receptor downregulation).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No formal withdrawal syndrome. Chronic users (e.g. for sleep) may report rebound insomnia and anxiety on cessation, lasting 2-7 days.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: IC50 15.6 µM at 0 mV in Xenopus oocytes (Hong & Jo 2009); authors estimate ~2 µM IC50 in mammalian (HEK/cardiomyocyte) systems. Therapeutic free plasma chlorpheniramine is 12.5–30 nM, giving a ~70× safety margin in normal use. Overdose plasma concentrations of 1.25–2.75 µM approach hERG IC50 and have been associated with prolonged QT and wide-QRS arrhythmia.

Class IA-like sodium channel block contributes to wide-QRS and Brugada-pattern ECG findings in massive overdose; treated with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate. Quantitative Nav1.5 IC50 not separately characterised in mammalian patch-clamp.

demographic_differences.age: Children clear chlorpheniramine faster than adults (shorter t1/2 ~10-13 h vs 20-28 h adult); elderly show prolonged t1/2 and elevated steady-state concentrations.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal failure modestly prolongs t1/2 due to reduced metabolite clearance; severe hepatic impairment substantially reduces clearance (CYP2D6 hepatic).

data_gaps_remaining: Primary source for individual M1-M5 Ki values (PDSP compendium values cited; original Bolden 1992 / Stanton 1993 papers not directly accessed)
No human PET occupancy curve at multiple doses
No fraction of clearance per CYP isoform quantified
notes: Chlorpheniramine is unusual among first-generation antihistamines for its potent SERT activity (Ki 15.2 nM) — comparable to some marketed SSRIs — and its weak muscarinic activity (Ki >15 µM at M1-M5). It is the H1 antagonist most often implicated in case-reported serotonin syndrome with SSRIs. The 'anticholinergic' grouping is partially misleading: chlorpheniramine's anticholinergic load is modest compared to diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, or promethazine. Stereoselectivity is pharmacologically meaningful — dexchlorpheniramine alone is marketed in some regions and is ~80× more H1-potent than the (R)-(-) enantiomer.
