name: Cinolazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Austrian-marketed hypnotic (Gerodorm). Pre-drug-like — 3-hydroxylated to active metabolite.

notes: Marketed in Austria; minor benzodiazepine hypnotic.

name: Citalopram

binding.notes: Racemate; S-enantiomer carries activity. Hyttel JCP 1994 reports Ki ~1-4 nM for citalopram across multiple preparations.
Highest off-target among citalopram receptors; underlies sedation.
Weakest sigma-1 affinity among SSRIs aside from paroxetine.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acute SERT blockade raises synaptic 5-HT; chronic dosing produces somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitisation (delayed onset of antidepressant effect).

neuroimaging.finding: 20 mg/day citalopram produces ~80% striatal SERT occupancy measured by [11C]-DASB; occupancy plateaus above 40 mg/day.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Citalopram AUC ↑ ~40%; pushes plasma into QTc-risk range at >20mg.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs show 2-3× citalopram AUC and elevated QTc; CPIC recommends max 20 mg/day for PMs. UMs may have subtherapeutic exposure. 5-HTTLPR S-allele homozygotes show worse response.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitisation 2-3 weeks in humans (PET evidence)
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: SSRI discontinuation syndrome — flu-like symptoms, dizziness, paresthesias ('brain zaps'), anxiety; onset 2-3 days, peak 5-7 days, duration 1-3 weeks. Less severe than paroxetine due to longer t1/2.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QTc prolongation, torsade de pointes; FDA black-box restriction limits dose to 40 mg (20 mg in elderly/CYP2C19 PMs).
DDCT/DCT metabolite shows greater hERG potency than parent; contributes to QTc effect.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: clearance ↓ ~30%; FDA limits dose to 20 mg in ≥60 years.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: clearance ↓ ~37%, t1/2 doubles. Dose limit 20 mg/day.

notes: Racemate; R-enantiomer is pharmacologically inactive at SERT but contributes to hERG affinity and antagonises the active S-enantiomer via allosteric site (basis for escitalopram development).

name: Citicoline

primary_targets: choline + cytidine donor for Kennedy pathway phosphatidylcholine synthesis
pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hydrolyzed in gut to cytidine + choline; both cross BBB independently. Brain reassembles into CDP-choline → phosphatidylcholine via Kennedy pathway. Cytidine is converted to uridine in humans (humans cannot use cytidine directly), providing UTP for membrane phospholipid synthesis.

routes.notes: Biphasic plasma levels: peak at 1 h (free choline + cytidine) and second peak at 24 h (after CNS incorporation/release cycle). 62.8% of [14C] dose appears as brain phospholipids.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: no tolerance

data_gaps_remaining: controlled human cognitive endpoint data in healthy adults
notes: Differs from alpha-GPC by additionally supplying cytidine (→ uridine in humans) for nucleotide pool. Best-evidenced use is ischemic stroke recovery (ICTUS trial neutral; meta-analyses positive at higher doses). Nootropic effect in healthy adults is modest in controlled trials.

name: Clobazam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 1,5-benzodiazepine (rather than 1,4), gives mild α2-subunit preference → relatively less sedation/cognitive impairment than diazepam at equipotent anxiolytic doses. Anticonvulsant for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (Onfi FDA approval 2011).

routes.notes: Clobazam t1/2 36–42 h; N-desmethylclobazam (norclobazam) t1/2 71–82 h.

metabolism.notes: ~2/3 of clobazam undergoes N-demethylation. Norclobazam is ~25% as potent but at chronic dosing reaches plasma concentrations 8–20× clobazam.
CYP2C19 PMs have 5× higher norclobazam levels — clinically important for dosing in Asian populations.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Norclobazam levels 2–3× higher; clinically significant in Dravet syndrome co-treatment
Norclobazam AUC increased ~3–4×; major clinical interaction in Lennox-Gastaut and Dravet co-treatment

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs: norclobazam plasma levels 5× higher than EMs; recommend lower starting dose. ~15% of East Asians are CYP2C19 PMs.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Anticonvulsant tolerance develops in ~30% within 6 months.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild relative to 1,4-benzos but can precipitate status in epileptic patients; long t1/2 buffers it.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: prolonged metabolism.

notes: Structural outlier among benzos (1,5- rather than 1,4-). Lower sedation per equipotent anxiolytic dose. Norclobazam carries most of the chronic-dosing effect.

name: Clobromazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Combination of 2'-Cl + 8-Br + triazolo features → predicted very high GABA-A affinity (QSAR log 1/c 10.14, Manchester 2022). Among most-monitored designer benzos by EMCDDA post-2017.

notes: Synonymous with 'Phenazolam' as vendor name. EMCDDA monitoring since 2018.

name: Clomethiazole

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thiazole derivative. Potentiates GABA-A and glycine. Used for alcohol withdrawal (especially UK), elderly insomnia. High addictive potential restricts use.

routes.notes: Massive first-pass (~90%) in healthy adults; reduced first-pass in cirrhosis → 5-10x higher exposure (dose adjust).

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Both PD + PK (ethanol inhibits clomethiazole metabolism)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Markedly enhanced sedation/respiratory depression — actively dangerous in active drinkers.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked accumulation.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Cirrhosis: dose ~50% normal.

notes: UK-specific clinical use; high abuse liability noted in early trials.

name: Clonazepam

binding.notes: Sub-nanomolar to low-nanomolar at all α subunits; among the highest-affinity classical benzodiazepines.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective high-affinity benzodiazepine-site PAM. The 7-nitro group is metabolically reduced to 7-amino-clonazepam — pharmacologically inactive in vivo but accumulates and may compete for binding after chronic dosing.

metabolism.notes: Nitroreduction to inactive 7-amino metabolite (major); minor 3-hydroxylation. 7-amino subsequently acetylated by NAT2 to 7-acetamido-clonazepam.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased clonazepam exposure; sedation potentiation
Reduced clonazepam exposure; potential breakthrough seizures

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: NAT2 slow acetylators show altered metabolite profile but minor clinical impact.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Anticonvulsant tolerance prominent within weeks-to-months at therapeutic doses (~30–50% of patients lose efficacy). Anxiolytic tolerance slower.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 1–7 days (long t1/2 buffers it); protracted withdrawal common (months). Severe in long-term users; among the more difficult benzos to taper.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: prolonged t1/2.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: prolonged t1/2.

notes: Long t1/2 (30–40 h) makes clonazepam useful for sustained anxiolysis/anticonvulsant action but contributes to accumulation and protracted withdrawal.

name: Clonazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolam + 7-nitro group (combines triazolam scaffold with clonazepam's nitro substitution). Among the most potent benzodiazepines; active at 0.1–0.5 mg.

metabolism.notes: Parallel to clonazepam nitroreduction.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe; triazolo + nitro structure gives both high intrinsic activity and prolonged tail.

notes: First synthesized 1971 (Hester); appeared as NPS ~2014. Recreational doses 0.25–1 mg. Notorious for blackouts, paradoxical disinhibition, and acute respiratory depression risk when combined with opioids/alcohol.

name: Clonidine

binding.notes: Partial agonist (~70% Emax vs noradrenaline).

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Bousquet — I1 binding correlates better with antihypertensive potency than α2A binding; classical 'central sympatholytic' mechanism is now revised to include I1.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Central α2A presynaptic autoreceptor activation → reduced sympathetic outflow + I1 receptor activation in RVLM contributes. Used clinically for hypertension, ADHD (Kapvay), opioid/nicotine/alcohol withdrawal symptom relief.

routes.notes: t1/2 12-16 h. 40-60% renal unchanged.
Catapres-TTS weekly patch.

metabolism.notes: ~50% renal unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced antihypertensive efficacy.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe rebound hypertension on abrupt discontinuation (catecholamine surge); taper required.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: prolonged t1/2.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal impairment: prolonged t1/2.

notes: The I1 imidazoline receptor is poorly recognised in clinical pharmacology curricula — clonidine is the prototype I1 agonist.

name: Cloniprazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-cyclopropylmethyl clonazepam analogue; designer benzo.

notes: Sparse data; community-reported potent.

name: Clonitazene

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO cells stably expressing human MOR/KOR/DOR; functional via [35S]GTPγS
binding.notes: n=3; full MOR agonist relative to DAMGO

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO cells stably expressing human MOR/KOR/DOR; functional via [35S]GTPγS
binding.notes: n=4; full MOR agonist relative to DAMGO

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO cells stably expressing human MOR/KOR/DOR; functional via [35S]GTPγS
binding.notes: n=3; full MOR agonist relative to DAMGO

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist at MOR (Emax 104%) but partial at KOR/DOR. Synthesized 1956 by Ciba; one of the original nitazenes.

notes: Original Ciba nitazene from 1950s. Para-Cl substitution gives ~20× weaker MOR Ki than ethoxy isomer (etonitazene).

name: Clorazepate

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug: rapidly decarboxylated to nordazepam in acidic gastric environment (chemical hydrolysis, not enzymatic). All pharmacology mediated by nordazepam.

routes.notes: Parent not detected systemically; nordazepam t1/2 50–100 h.

metabolism.notes: Decarboxylation requires acidic pH — antacids/PPIs can reduce conversion and onset.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Slower onset and reduced peak nordazepam levels

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inherited via nordazepam — CYP2C19 PMs accumulate more.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: avoid accumulation.

notes: Prodrug — nordazepam carries all activity. Reduced gastric acidity impairs conversion.

name: Clotiazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienodiazepine (like etizolam structurally). Used in Japan/Italy/France as a short-acting anxiolytic.

notes: Thienodiazepine sister to etizolam; widely marketed in Japan (Rize, Trecalmo).

name: Cloxazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Oxazolam-type prodrug — opens the oxazoline ring to release delorazepam.

notes: Oxazolobenzodiazepine prodrug.

name: Cocaine

binding.notes: Han & Gu 2006 — Ki range 0.2-0.7 µM across DAT/NET/SERT; rank order DAT>SERT>NET.
High-affinity site (0.2 nM Kd) from striatal saturation; low-affinity site Kd 1.5 nM. Rank order RTI-55>GBR-12909>mazindol>WIN-35,428>methylphenidate>cocaine.

functional.notes: 0.3-0.6 mg/kg IV cocaine blocks 60-77% of striatal DAT (Volkow et al. 1997); subjective high correlates with occupancy.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Increases extracellular DA/NE/5-HT by transporter blockade; stabilises DAT in outward-facing open conformation (fast binding/dissociation). Striatal DA spike drives D1/D2 signalling responsible for reinforcement.

neuroimaging.finding: 60-77% striatal DAT occupancy at recreational IV doses (0.3-0.6 mg/kg); time course of striatal cocaine parallels subjective high

routes.notes: Smoked free-base (crack) — onset within seconds; subjective 'liking' higher than IV at matched plasma.

metabolism.notes: Norcocaine is hepatotoxic (further oxidized to nitroxide radical).
Transesterification when co-ingested with ethanol; cocaethylene has DAT Ki similar to cocaine, longer t1/2 (~2.5h), and 5x greater hERG block (IC50 1.2 µM).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QT prolongation at supratherapeutic plasma cocaine; cocaethylene metabolite is 4x more potent (IC50 1.2 µM)
Use-dependent Na block; QRS widening, arrhythmia, sudden cardiac death; treatment of cocaine wide-QRS is sodium bicarbonate

demographic_differences.sex: Women: AUC ~40% higher in luteal vs follicular phase (smoked route); no large differences in men vs women at matched dose (doi:10.1038/sj.npp.1395344)
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: BChE deficiency (atypical pseudocholinesterase) markedly prolongs half-life and increases toxicity risk

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative biased signalling data (DAT is not a GPCR)
notes: Prototype fast-binding/fast-dissociation DAT inhibitor — the paradigmatic 'cocaine-like' kinetic profile against which atypical DAT inhibitors are contrasted.

name: Codeine

binding.notes: Codeine MOR Ki ~200× weaker than morphine; analgesia depends almost entirely on CYP2D6 O-demethylation to morphine (~10% of dose).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Codeine itself is a weak MOR agonist; activity derives from CYP2D6 → morphine. Codeine-6-glucuronide (UGT2B7) is a minor active metabolite.

metabolism.notes: Rate-limiting bioactivation step; PMs get ~96% lower morphine AUC, UMs get supratherapeutic morphine from normal codeine doses.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Phenoconverts EM to PM → loss of codeine analgesia

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 UM (≥3 functional copies, ~1-2% Caucasian, 30% Ethiopian): risk of fatal morphine intoxication from standard doses — multiple infant deaths reported in breastfeeding UM mothers and post-tonsillectomy children → FDA contraindicated codeine <12 yo (2017). CYP2D6 PM (~5-10% Caucasian): no analgesia. CPIC strongly recommends genotype-guided dosing or alternative.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild morphine-type withdrawal at chronic doses.

demographic_differences.age: AVOID in children <12 y and adolescents <18 y post-tonsillectomy (FDA black box).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal failure: morphine and M6G accumulate; reduce dose.

notes: Codeine is the textbook CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics example — PMs get no analgesia, UMs get respiratory depression. NEJMa041888 reports the seminal infant death case.

name: Coluracetam

functional.cell_system: hippocampal synaptosomes; chronic in-vivo dosing 0.3-3 mg/kg PO

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Proposed mechanism: enhancement of choline uptake via CHT1 in cholinergic terminals, increasing ACh synthesis rate. Original characterization (MKC-231, Murai et al.) showed restoration of HACU and hippocampal ACh in rats with AF64A-induced cholinergic lesions. Direct molecular interaction with CHT1 has not been demonstrated; the HACU enhancement may be indirect (e.g., upregulation of transporter trafficking).

data_gaps_remaining: No direct binding constant for CHT1
Phase 2a major depressive disorder trial by BrainCells failed to meet primary endpoint (BCI-540); detailed PK never published
No human EEG or fMRI signature
notes: Originally MKC-231 (Mitsubishi Tanabe); licensed to BrainCells as BCI-540. Failed in MDD Phase 2a (2008-2009). Mechanism (HACU enhancement) is genuinely unusual but rests on a small number of rat papers; the entire human evidence base is essentially absent. Treat all anecdotal human dose ranges with skepticism.

name: Crack

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Identical molecular pharmacology to cocaine HCl. Only the route (smoked, free-base vaporises ~98°C vs salt decomposes ~195°C) changes kinetics.

routes.notes: Arterial venous gradient produces a brain bolus ~6-8 sec post-inhalation; sharper peak than IV at matched dose; subjective 'liking' higher than IV.

notes: Pharmacologically identical to cocaine; PK differences derive entirely from inhalation route. See Cocaine record for full data.

name: CRL-40,941

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug-like — hydroxamic acid analogue of fladrafinil. Animal data (Lafon patent CA1192222A) show sedation→excitation biphasic pattern at 64-256 mg/kg in mice.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Hepatotoxicity risk inferred from adrafinil class; no human data

data_gaps_remaining: No human PK; no quantitative binding data outside patent.
notes: Bisfluoro analogue of adrafinil; pharmacology entirely from Lafon patent and analogy.

name: CX-1739

functional.readout: synaptic potentiation in hippocampal slice; in vivo respiratory rescue from opioid-induced depression
functional.cell_system: rat hippocampus; human respiratory rate studies

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Low-impact AMPAkine (Type II) — preferentially attenuates desensitization with limited effect on deactivation. Cortex/RespireRx claims ~5x potency over CX-717 (no published peer-reviewed Ki). Mechanism class predicts no Gq-coupled ER calcium release and therefore lower seizure liability than high-impact compounds.

concentration_effect.concentration_unit: n/a — not reported as PK/PD curve

data_gaps_remaining: Phase 2 efficacy data in sleep apnea (results never disclosed publicly)
notes: Lead respiratory-stimulant AMPAkine from RespireRx (post-Cortex). Phase 2a in opioid-induced respiratory depression was conducted at Duke (NCT02735629); top-line readout was positive directionally but compound has not progressed. Almost all 'data' in the public domain are RespireRx press releases — treat as such.

name: CX-1942

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Water-soluble injectable analog from the CX-1739 series (RespireRx), intended for parenteral use in acute opioid-induced respiratory depression. No primary literature with binding constants or functional EC50 has been published; all references are RespireRx corporate communications.

data_gaps_remaining: Everything — structure, Ki, EC50, PK, all unpublished
notes: Listed in RespireRx pipeline materials as an injectable, water-soluble companion to CX-1739. No peer-reviewed primary literature exists; treat as an effectively unverified compound.

name: CX-516

functional.readout: field EPSP amplitude in hippocampal CA1
functional.notes: EC50 ~170 µM for ~50% potentiation of fast EPSPs; potency ~10-fold higher than aniracetam in same prep.

functional.readout: deactivation slowing of glutamate-evoked currents in excised patches
functional.notes: CX-516 is the prototypical 'high-impact' / Type I benzamide AMPAkine: slows deactivation strongly with only modest desensitization block. Arai-defined high-impact class.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: As a high-impact AMPAkine, CX-516 belongs to the subclass shown by Karst et al. (2024) to trigger Gq-coupled, IP3-mediated ER Ca2+ release at suprathreshold concentrations — proposed mechanism for the convulsant liability that has limited high-impact AMPAkines in clinical development.

routes.subject_demographics: Phase 2 schizophrenia adjunct (Goff et al.) and Alzheimer/MCI studies

off_targets.target: Gq / IP3R (via AMPA receptor metabotropic coupling)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: class-shared convulsant signal in animal models at high concentrations; CX-516 itself was tolerated in clinic but development was halted for low potency / short half-life rather than seizures.

data_gaps_remaining: Numerical human PK parameters (Cmax, Vd, CL never published as full PK)
Direct Ki at any AMPA subunit (no binding-site occupant — modulates allosterically)
notes: First clinical-stage AMPAkine; the eponymous 'high-impact' (Type I) benzamide. Multiple Phase 2 trials (schizophrenia adjunct to clozapine, mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's, Fragile X syndrome). All failed primary endpoints, generally attributed to low potency (EC50 ~170 µM) and ~2h half-life requiring frequent dosing. Cortex Pharma stopped development around 2006-2007.

name: CX-546

functional.readout: deactivation slowing of glutamate-evoked currents in outside-out patches
functional.cell_system: HEK293 expressing GluA1-4 with TARPs; outside-out patch
functional.notes: CX-546 slows deactivation ~10-fold following 1 ms glutamate pulses; reduces desensitization more potently than CX-516 or IDRA-21 but less than cyclothiazide. Classified as 'low-impact / Type II' by some authors and 'intermediate' by others — operates primarily through desensitization-block axis.
Modulation magnitude depends strongly on GluA subunit and TARP partner; effect varies by brain region — implies functional selectivity that has not been fully exploited pharmacologically.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Benzamide-type, like CX-516, but mechanistically closer to the desensitization-blocker subclass; preclinical-only.

notes: Cortex research tool; never advanced to clinic. Notable for being one of the first AMPAkines characterized to have GluA-subunit/TARP-dependent modulation magnitude, hinting at the possibility of brain-region selectivity that no compound has yet exploited successfully.

name: CX-614

functional.readout: block of desensitization in outside-out patches
functional.notes: Blocks desensitization with EC50 ~44 µM; slows deactivation 8.4-fold (1 ms glutamate pulses). Synaptic fEPSP potentiation EC50 20-40 µM. Belongs to the benzoxazine subgroup — structurally rigid and more potent than the benzamide series.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triggers AMPAR-coupled, Gq-mediated IP3R-dependent ER Ca2+ release in cortical neurons (Karst et al., 2024, Synapse) — proposed unifying explanation for the convulsant liability of high-impact AMPAkines including CX-614 and cyclothiazide.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: calcium-dependent neuronal toxicity and convulsions at supratherapeutic concentrations; primary reason this and other high-impact AMPAkines did not reach clinic.

data_gaps_remaining: No human PK or clinical exposure
notes: The high-impact AMPAkine reference compound for the desensitization-block axis. Frequently mislabeled in popular sources — note that 'high impact' refers to the magnitude of receptor modulation and Gq coupling, NOT to the mechanism (which is desensitization block rather than deactivation slowing). Both deactivation-slowers (CX-516) and strong desensitization-blockers (CX-614, cyclothiazide) can be high-impact; the unifying biomarker is Gq/ER-Ca2+ recruitment.

name: CX-691

functional.readout: kainate-evoked Ca2+ flux potentiation; field EPSP
functional.cell_system: rat hippocampal slice; clinical EEG-correlated psychometric battery in humans
functional.notes: Benzothiadiazine class — same family as IDRA-21 but more potent. EEG signature at active doses is increased fast-frequency power. Higher-impact than CX-516.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Benzothiadiazine high-impact AMPAkine. Cardiotoxicity signal reported as one rationale for discontinuation (though specific QT data not in public domain).

neuroimaging.finding: Increased fast-frequency (gamma) power and altered ERP amplitudes at memory-encoding intervals after 500 mg oral; observed in healthy elderly volunteers (Wezenberg et al., 2007).

routes.subject_demographics: healthy elderly volunteers (60-80 y), Wezenberg single-dose crossover

off_targets.clinical_consequence: developmental termination attributed to cardiac toxicity findings; specifics not published

data_gaps_remaining: Direct AMPA EC50 in recombinant system
notes: Co-developed by Cortex and Organon (Schering-Plough, then Merck). Multiple Phase 2 trials in schizophrenia (NCT00425815 — terminated), depression, and elderly cognition. The Wezenberg 2007 paper is striking for showing dissociable memory effects — short-term memory enhanced, episodic memory impaired — within a single dose, hinting at the complex dose-response of AMPA potentiation.

name: CX-717

functional.readout: fEPSP potentiation; respiratory rhythm rescue in opioid-treated rats
functional.cell_system: hippocampal slice; preBötzinger complex respiratory model
functional.notes: Classified as low-impact (Type II) AMPAkine; preferentially attenuates desensitization without strong Gq coupling. This profile is the rationale for safer respiratory-stimulant use vs. high-impact compounds.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Low-impact AMPAkine; does not trigger Gq/ER Ca2+ release at therapeutic concentrations, consistent with absence of convulsant signal in human Phase 1/2 studies.

neuroimaging.finding: Restored sleep-deprivation-impaired BOLD signal in DARPA-funded Phase 2 sleep deprivation study (Wesensten et al., 2007).

routes.subject_demographics: Phase 2a ADHD (recently published, 2025); also DARPA sleep-deprivation Phase 2

data_gaps_remaining: Published binding/functional EC50 in standardized assay
notes: The most-characterized low-impact AMPAkine; DARPA funded both rodent and human work as a sleep-deprivation countermeasure. 2025 Phase 2A in adult ADHD reported a 'promising therapeutic profile' — RespireRx is the current sponsor.

Reduces clearance, prolongs t1/2 to >20 h

name: Dextromethorphan

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Assay performed in absence of Mg2+/glutamate, which inflates apparent affinity vs physiological conditions
binding.notes: Ki ~7.25 microM in original Wong et al. study; parent DXM is a low-affinity blocker. Dextrorphan (metabolite) is the more potent NMDA antagonist.
Chou et al. 1999; DXM vs dimemorfan comparison. Sigma-1 agonism contributes to antidepressant-like and anticonvulsant effects.
Nguyen & Matsumoto 2014; DXM has higher SERT affinity than ketamine. This SERT inhibition underlies serotonin-syndrome risk with MAOIs/SSRIs.
Nguyen & Matsumoto 2014; moderate NET inhibition contributes to dose-dependent stimulant overlay.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: DXM/dextrorphan blockade of NMDA receptors reduces glutamate-evoked Ca2+ influx in neurons. Sigma-1 agonism modulates IP3-receptor Ca2+ release from ER and chaperones BiP dissociation, contributing to neuroprotective and antidepressant effects.

routes.notes: Capon et al. 1996 — EM bioavailability 1-2%, t1/2 ~2-4 h; poor metabolizers (PMs) bioavailability ~80%, t1/2 ~24 h with 5-fold higher DXM Cmax and DXO concentrations only 3% of EM values.
PMs accumulate DXM with markedly longer t1/2 and stronger dissociative effect at recreational doses.

metabolism.notes: O-demethylation. Dextrorphan is the principal NMDA-active metabolite (Ki ~900 nM at PCP site, ~8x parent).
N-demethylation. Becomes major pathway in CYP2D6 PMs (~2.8-fold higher 3-MM normalised to activity).
Conjugated dextrorphan is ~100x more abundant than free DXO in plasma.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Converts EM to phenocopy PM; DXM AUC increases 20-40 fold (basis for Nuedexta DXM/quinidine combo).
Persistent CYP2D6 inhibition (kinact 0.17 min-1); markedly elevated DXM exposure and serotonin syndrome risk.
Increases DXM exposure; documented serotonin syndrome cases with DXM cough syrup + fluoxetine.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic — DXM SERT inhibition + MAO blockade
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Severe serotonin syndrome and hyperpyrexia; contraindicated combination.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs (~7% of Caucasians, ~1% Asians): 5-fold higher DXM Cmax, t1/2 ~24 h vs ~3 h in EMs, DXO concentrations only 3% of EM values. UMs (CYP2D6 gene duplication) experience minimal subjective dissociation. PMs are at high risk of dose-dependent dissociation and serotonin syndrome at recreational doses; UMs at risk of opioid-like sedation from rapid DXO formation in rare cases.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Reverse tolerance / kindling-like phenomenon reported anecdotally in chronic DXM users (autoinduction of CYP2D6 has been hypothesised but not confirmed in humans).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Chronic high-dose users may develop psychological dependence with insomnia, dysphoria, craving, mild dysautonomia lasting 1-2 weeks. No major physical withdrawal syndrome.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QTc prolongation reported with supratherapeutic doses and CYP2D6 inhibitor co-administration; case reports of arrhythmia at recreational doses.
May contribute to anti-addictive effects observed in animal models.

demographic_differences.age: Pediatric DXM clearance higher per kg; recreational paediatric overdose particularly dangerous due to combination products (acetaminophen, chlorpheniramine, pseudoephedrine).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment expected to increase DXM exposure (CYP2D6-dependent); no formal dedicated study published.

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative human PET imaging of NMDA channel occupancy at recreational doses
notes: DXM is the prototype non-arylcyclohexylamine morphinan NMDA antagonist. Parent compound is a relatively weak NMDA blocker; pro-drug-like behaviour of the active metabolite dextrorphan (formed by CYP2D6) drives most dissociative pharmacology. The σ1 + SERT polypharmacology explains the affective overlay (euphoria, depersonalisation tinged with serotonergic activation) that differs qualitatively from ketamine. CYP2D6 phenotype is the single most important pharmacogenetic variable for DXM safety and effect intensity.

notes: Pharmacologically identical to base DXM; primary distinguishing feature is the bromide counterion load with chronic recreational use. Refer to Dextromethorphan record for full receptor and CYP data.

name: Diazepam

binding.tissue_or_cell: L(tk-) cells expressing recombinant human α1β2γ2
binding.notes: Hadingham et al. 1993 — canonical Ki values for human recombinant receptors. Classical 'non-selective' profile across α1/α2/α3/α5 with single-digit nM affinity.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prototypical non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM. Enhances GABA-A Cl- conductance by increasing channel-opening frequency at GABA-bound receptors. Roughly equal affinity across α1/α2/α3/α5; β-subunit identity has minor effect on diazepam Ki.

neuroimaging.finding: Brain occupancy of central benzodiazepine sites measured by [11C]flumazenil displacement reaches ~25% at 10 mg p.o.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults — Greenblatt clinical pharmacokinetics review
routes.notes: Parent t1/2 ~20–48 h; active metabolite nordazepam t1/2 50–100 h dominates effective duration on chronic dosing.

metabolism.notes: 3-hydroxylation
N-demethylation — primary route. Nordazepam t1/2 ~50–100 h; further metabolized to oxazepam (CYP3A4 hydroxylation) then UGT2B15-glucuronidated.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Decreased CL of diazepam by ~25–50% in CYP2C19 EMs (no effect in PMs)

name: Dizocilpine

binding.tissue_or_cell: rat cerebral cortical membrane / rat whole brain
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Mg2+-free; agonist-stimulated assay (glu/gly); use- and voltage-dependent binding to open channel.
binding.notes: Ki of (+)-enantiomer at PCP site; (-)-enantiomer is ~10-fold weaker. Kd 37 nM (Wong et al. 1986). MK-801 has extremely slow channel exit kinetics (koff ~0.01 s-1) — accumulates with repeated activation and produces sustained block, the molecular reason it is neurotoxic (Olney) and unsuitable for clinical use.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Trapping channel blocker — channel can close while drug is inside, requiring re-opening for drug egress. This trapping mechanism produces durable blockade and underlies both the long behavioural duration and the Olney's-lesion neurotoxicity (excessive disinhibition of cortical glutamate -> heat-shock response in retrosplenial neurons).

routes.notes: MK-801 was developed by Merck for anticonvulsant indications but abandoned after Olney's lesions and severe psychotomimetic effects in Phase I trials at sub-anticonvulsant doses. No published controlled human PK in the modern literature; remains a research tool only.

metabolism.notes: Limited human metabolism data.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Tolerance develops within days of repeated dosing in animals; NMDA receptor upregulation following chronic blockade documented (Williams et al.).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No clinical syndrome described in humans (limited exposure). Animal studies show rebound hyperexcitability and seizure threshold reduction.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Originally claimed as sigma ligand; subsequent work shows the apparent sigma binding was actually low-affinity off-target — dizocilpine is highly selective for the NMDA PCP site.

notes: Dizocilpine ((+)-MK-801) is the canonical high-affinity, slow-koff, trapping channel blocker of the NMDA receptor and the standard reference compound for NMDA-channel-blocker pharmacology. The contrast with memantine is paradigmatic: same binding site, ~3-orders-of-magnitude koff difference. Olney's lesions (vacuolisation in retrosplenial cortex layers III/IV) seen in rats given systemic MK-801 mapped the neurotoxicity risk of NMDA channel blockade and informed Merck's decision to halt development.

name: Fenfluramine

binding.notes: Rothman/Setola 2000 — parent fenfluramine has weak 5-HT2B; the danger is its metabolite norfenfluramine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acute: SERT release → anorexia, satiety. Chronic: metabolite norfenfluramine accumulates → 5-HT2B-mediated mitogenesis on cardiac valves → fibrous valvular thickening (mitral and aortic), pulmonary hypertension. Now reformulated for Dravet syndrome (Fintepla) at much lower doses, with REMS for echocardiography. Anticonvulsant action likely involves σ1 modulation (Sourbron 2017 doi:10.1111/epi.13691).

routes.notes: Caccia 1986 — fenfluramine t1/2 13–30 h (mean ~19 h depending on enantiomer); active metabolite norfenfluramine t1/2 1.5–2× longer (~30 h), accumulates with chronic dosing

metabolism.notes: Norfenfluramine is 400× more 5-HT2B-active than parent (Ki 52 nM vs 4134 nM); also has 5-HT2C activity (Ki 557 nM)

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: additive monoamine release; phentermine has no 5-HT2B activity (fen alone was the valve culprit)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Synergistic weight loss; valvulopathy/PPH driven by fen/norfen, not phen. 'Phen-fen' withdrawn 1997.
Reduces 5-HT2B exposure — potentially safer in PMs
Lethal serotonin syndrome; absolute contraindication

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs may have less norfenfluramine formation → potentially less valvulopathy risk but variable. UMs make norfen faster.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Cardiac valvulopathy and primary pulmonary hypertension on chronic dosing — basis for 1997 market withdrawal

notes: Fenfluramine itself is a relatively safe SERT releaser; the danger is its metabolite norfenfluramine, which is a potent 5-HT2B agonist (Ki 52 nM, EC50 ~18 nM, Emax ~73%). After 24+ months chronic dosing ~30% of patients develop echocardiographic valvulopathy. Reformulated as Fintepla for Dravet syndrome 2020 at sub-anorectic doses with REMS.

name: Fentanyl

binding.notes: Same paper measured IC50 1.23 nM in rat brain (Filizola 2019).

functional.notes: log(EC50) = -6.41; not significantly biased vs DAMGO.

biased_agonism.interpretation: Fentanyl is NOT significantly biased compared to DAMGO at the μ-opioid receptor (Ramos-González 2023). Earlier claims that fentanyl is 'arrestin-biased' have not survived re-analysis with operational-model bias factors.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist. Activates Gαi/o → adenylyl cyclase inhibition, opens GIRK channels, closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels. Also recruits β-arrestin2 and undergoes ~25% receptor internalisation at saturating concentrations.

neuroimaging.finding: [11C]carfentanil PET displacement quantifies MOR occupancy during fentanyl administration in humans; analgesia threshold ~50% MOR occupancy.

routes.notes: Terminal t½ 3-7 h; Vd large due to lipophilicity; context-sensitive t½ ~250 min after 4h infusion.
Apparent elimination half-life is depot-controlled (18-22 h) — much longer than IV t½.
Intranasal fentanyl bioavailability 71-89% across studies.

concentration_effect.notes: Plasma 0.5-2 ng/mL = post-op analgesia; ≥3 ng/mL = anaesthesia / respiratory depression begins.

metabolism.notes: Tateishi 1996 — CYP3A4 N-dealkylation is the dominant pathway; norfentanyl is essentially inactive. CYP3A5 contributes minor fraction.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced fentanyl clearance, increased AUC, risk of overdose; FDA black-box warning.
Modest AUC increase for oral / mucosal fentanyl formulations.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP3A4*22 carriers have reduced clearance. OPRM1 A118G (rs1799971) — G-allele carriers need higher fentanyl doses for equivalent analgesia (Park 2007). ABCB1 (P-gp) polymorphisms affect brain efflux.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: MOR internalisation occurs within minutes; receptor recycling t½ ~30 min. Chronic exposure causes desensitisation rather than downregulation.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 8-24h (transdermal slower), peak 36-72h, duration 7-10 days. Symptoms: lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, mydriasis, gooseflesh, GI cramping, muscle aches, anxiety, insomnia, dysphoria.

off_targets.target: diaphragm / chest wall musculature (chest wall rigidity)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: Rapid IV bolus or high-dose smoked / IV illicit use causes 'wooden chest syndrome' — laryngeal closure + thoracic skeletal muscle hypertonia via central MOR-dopaminergic pathway. Sudden ventilatory failure within seconds-minutes of dose; reversible with naloxone OR neuromuscular blockade.

demographic_differences.sex: Women have ~30% slower clearance than men in some studies (Hess 1985); clinical relevance modest.
demographic_differences.age: Neonates and elderly have reduced clearance (decreased CYP3A activity and Vd changes).
demographic_differences.weight: Obese patients: dosing on lean body mass preferred — Vd does not scale linearly with TBW.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment markedly prolongs t½ (>50% reduction in clearance in cirrhosis).

notes: Reference compound for the class. ~80-100× morphine potency parenteral. Wooden chest syndrome is the #1 acute mechanism of sudden death (especially with very-rapid-onset routes — IV bolus, smoking). Naloxone reverses but high cumulative doses may be required for illicit-route exposures.

Weak 5-HT release; 4-F shifts profile less than 4-Cl, retains DA selectivity

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Catecholamine-selective substrate-releaser. 4-fluoro substitution is the smallest halogen and minimally perturbs DA/5-HT balance — flephedrone is more methcathinone-like than 4-CMC.

notes: 4-fluoro is the only halogen that doesn't strongly SERT-shift cathinones (unlike 4-Cl/4-Br which produce SNDRA profiles). Smaller VdW radius preserves DA selectivity.

name: Flmodafinil
notes: Duplicate of Bisfluoromodafinil — see canonical record above.

name: Flualprazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Alprazolam with 2'-fluoro substitution on phenyl. Predicted GABA-A affinity exceptionally high by Manchester QSAR (log 1/c 10.13). Roughly twice the t1/2 of alprazolam in rat PK studies.

routes.subject_demographics: Estimated from rat PK + post-mortem cases (Rice/Hikin 2019)
routes.notes: Rat PK: Vd and CL ~2× alprazolam; t1/2 ~2× longer (extrapolation to human ~18 h).

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe — comparable to alprazolam but t1/2 nearly doubled.

notes: Major designer benzo of late 2010s. Nine-case post-mortem series by Rice & Hikin 2019; deaths involved poly-drug intoxication, none attributed to flualprazolam alone.

name: Flubromazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 1,4-benzodiazepine designer benzo with 7-bromo + 2'-fluoro substitution; long-acting like phenazepam. Predicted GABA-A Ki similar to diazepam by QSAR (Manchester 2022).

routes.notes: Moosmann 2013 self-experiment. t1/2 ~106 h. Detection in urine for 28 days, serum for 23 days.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Very prolonged — t1/2 >100 h means clinical effects can extend 3+ weeks per single dose.

notes: Extremely long t1/2 (106 h) — among the longest of any benzodiazepine. 4 mg dose produces detectable serum levels for nearly a month.

name: Flubromazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine — alprazolam analogue with 8-bromo + 2'-fluoro substitution. Predicted GABA-A binding affinity exceptionally high (log 1/c ~10 by Manchester 2022 QSAR). High intrinsic activity contributes to rapid tolerance.

routes.notes: Huppertz 2018 self-experiment, 0.5 mg. t1/2 ~10–20 h. Detection in urine up to 8 days.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Triazolobenzodiazepines (alprazolam-class) show especially rapid tolerance and severe withdrawal.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe even at low cumulative doses; multiple post-mortem cases reported.

data_gaps_remaining: Population PK; subunit Ki not published
notes: Active oral dose 0.25–0.5 mg — among the most potent benzodiazepines synthesized. Post-mortem-case-series subject in 5+ studies (Hikin/Abdul 2020, Lewis 2019). Rat PK studies show ~2× larger Vd and CL vs alprazolam (doi:10.1016/j.taap.2023.116481).

name: Flubrotizolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienotriazolodiazepine — fluoro analog of brotizolam (4'-fluoro substitution). RC; potent BZ-like PAM by class analogy. See benzos enrichment file for thienodiazepine class context.

notes: Designer BZ analog; see benzos file.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Thienotriazolodiazepine. QSAR-predicted log 1/c 8.91 (Manchester 2022).

name: Fluetizolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Fluoro-etizolam; thienotriazolodiazepine designer benzo.

notes: Designer benzo; sparse peer-reviewed data.

notes: Aminorex analogue, abandoned anorectic.

name: Flunitrazepam

binding.notes: Used as the canonical radioligand for benzodiazepine binding studies.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: High-affinity non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM. The 1-methyl + 7-nitro motif gives extremely potent sedation/amnesia.

metabolism.notes: Km 108 μM CYP3A4 / 11 μM CYP2C19 — CYP2C19 is the high-affinity contributor at low concentrations.
Nitroreduction by CYP3A4 + nitroreductase; inactive but the primary forensic urinary marker.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C19 PMs may show higher parent exposure / lower desmethyl formation.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Similar to other intermediate-duration benzos; abuse-related dependence prominent.

notes: Schedule III in US (others IV); reformulated with blue dye to deter DFSA (drug-facilitated sexual assault) use.

name: Flunitrazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolo + nitro + fluoro — combines features of flunitrazepam and clonazolam. Extreme potency expected.

notes: Designer benzo, active oral dose reported ~0.1 mg. Insufficient peer-reviewed PK.

notes: Duplicate of Hydrafinil — see canonical record.

name: Fluorexetamine

binding.notes: No formal Ki published. Expected affinity similar to MXE (~300 nM) based on F-for-MeO bioisostere logic in the 3-position (smaller F → less H-bonding → likely modestly lower NMDA affinity).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Fluorinated MXE analogue. Subjective duration reported shorter than MXE.

notes: Note alias collision: the name 'Fluorexetamine' has been used for both 3-F-MXE-like compounds and 2'-F-MXE — verify identity per source. Canket entry covers the 2'-F variant.

name: Fluorolintane

binding.notes: Wallach et al. 2019 (Eur J Pharmacol). Ki 87.92 nM at NMDA PCP site; voltage-dependent fEPSP inhibition and LTP block in rat hippocampal slices confirmed.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Notable feature: DAT affinity is higher than NMDA affinity for fluorolintane — among the diarylethylamines, this profile is the closest approximation to a 'dissociative-stimulant' hybrid; users report substantial arousal vs the more dissociative-typical diphenidine.

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative DAT/NET/SERT Ki values for fluorolintane specifically
notes: 1,2-diarylethylamine with pyrrolidine (5-ring) rather than piperidine (6-ring) on the nitrogen, and 2-fluoro on one aryl. The pyrrolidine analogue (vs piperidine) generally raises monoamine transporter affinity (compare alpha-PVP vs alpha-PHP) — fluorolintane shows the same SAR shift, with DAT affinity exceeding NMDA affinity (a hallmark of the cathinone-pyrrolidines). Two isomeric series exist; the 2-fluoro isomer is the canonical street form.

name: Fluorophenibut

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 4-Fluorophenibut.

notes: Duplicate library entry for 4-Fluorophenibut.

name: Fluoxetine

binding.notes: Tatsumi et al. 1997 — definitive monoamine transporter Ki table for antidepressants.
Competitive reversible 5-HT2C antagonism is functionally relevant — disinhibits prefrontal DA/NE release.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: SERT blockade plus 5-HT2C antagonism produces secondary disinhibition of frontal cortex DA/NE — accounts for activating profile distinct from other SSRIs.

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 1-3 days acute; 4-6 days chronic. Norfluoxetine t1/2 ~7-15 days (essentially eliminates need for tapering).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Strong CYP2D6 inhibition persists 4-6 weeks after stopping due to long t1/2. Reduces tamoxifen → endoxifen conversion; phenocopies CYP2D6 PM.
Moderate inhibitor; raises levels of midazolam, alprazolam.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs: fluoxetine AUC ↑, norfluoxetine AUC ↓. Because norfluoxetine has comparable SERT potency to parent and longer t1/2, total active drug exposure is similar across phenotypes — fluoxetine is unusually robust to CYP2D6 polymorphism.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: 5-HT1A autoreceptor desensitisation 2-3 weeks
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mildest discontinuation among SSRIs because norfluoxetine self-tapers over weeks. Rarely requires dose taper.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Minimal QTc effect at therapeutic doses.

demographic_differences.age: Pediatric (8-18y): faster clearance — same mg/kg dosing achievable. Elderly: clearance unchanged but t1/2 prolonged due to comorbidity.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: t1/2 doubles; halve dose.

notes: The long half-life of norfluoxetine (~7-15 days) makes fluoxetine the SSRI most likely to cause serotonin syndrome when switching to MAOIs (requires 5-week washout) and most robust to occasional missed doses.

name: Flurazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Parent compound has short t1/2 (2–3 h); virtually all clinical effect mediated by N-desalkylflurazepam (norflurazepam), t1/2 47–150 h (mean ~71 h).

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 2.3 h; active metabolite N-desalkylflurazepam dominates effect.

metabolism.notes: t1/2 47–150 h; accumulates with chronic dosing.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild due to long-acting metabolite; significant daytime sedation hangover on initiation.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked accumulation of norflurazepam; avoid.

notes: Effectively a prodrug; all chronic effect mediated by N-desalkylflurazepam (= norflurazepam).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Japanese-marketed (Coleminal); N-hydroxyethyl analogue. Metabolized to N-desalkyl-flutazolam.

name: Flutoprazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Japanese long-acting anxiolytic (Restas). N-cyclopropylmethyl substitution.

notes: Japan only.

name: Fluvoxamine

binding.notes: Highest sigma-1 affinity in the SSRI class; fluvoxamine is the prototypical sigma-1 agonist among prescribed antidepressants. Sigma-1 agonism implicated in pro-cognitive and ER-stress-attenuating effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Sigma-1 agonism translocates the chaperone from ER mitochondria-associated membranes to plasma membrane, modulating IP3 receptor Ca2+ release and ER stress response.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Clozapine AUC ↑ 5-10×; can produce severe sedation/agranulocytosis risk. Sometimes used deliberately to lower clozapine dose requirements.
Theophylline clearance ↓ 60-70%; can cause toxicity at standard theophylline doses.
Tizanidine AUC ↑ 33×, Cmax ↑ 12×; severe hypotension/sedation. Contraindicated combination.
Caffeine half-life roughly 5×; clinically meaningful insomnia/anxiety.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs show higher fluvoxamine exposure but clinical impact is less than for fluoxetine/paroxetine.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Similar to other SSRIs
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Shortest t1/2 SSRI besides paroxetine → discontinuation syndrome onset within 1-3 days, can be severe.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Plasma melatonin levels ↑ 17× due to CYP1A2 inhibition of melatonin metabolism.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: t1/2 ~17-26 h vs 13-16 h in younger adults.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: dose reduction recommended.

notes: Strongest CYP1A2 inhibitor among SSRIs — clinically defining interaction profile.

data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor
notes: Tryptophan metabolic derivative or peptide. Not directly psychoactive. Either upstream of serotonin synthesis or a chemical intermediate / analytical reference compound.

name: Focalin

binding.notes: d-threo eutomer; ~5-10x more potent than l-threo at DAT and NET.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Same as racemic MPH but with cleaner stimulant profile (l-enantiomer largely inert at CNS targets but contributes to PK variability and some peripheral NE effects).

routes.notes: d-MPH alone — same first-pass CES1 hydrolysis; PK linear 2.5-20 mg.

notes: Pure d-threo eutomer of methylphenidate; preferred when avoiding peripheral l-enantiomer NE-driven side effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Water-soluble diazepam analog with phosphono group at N-1. Pro-drug-like in vivo conversion to diazepam-like activity. See benzos file.

name: Furanylfentanyl

binding.tissue_or_cell: rat brain membrane or CHO hMOR depending on source
binding.notes: Ki 0.028 nM (Goggin 2017) — extremely high MOR affinity. EC50 2.52 nM in CHO hMOR GTPγS (7× more potent than fentanyl 17.9 nM in same assay). Hydroxy-furanyl metabolite is one of the major in-vivo species.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist via Gαi/o. β-arrestin bias not reliably established for most fentalogs — fentanyl class is broadly unbiased per Ramos-González 2023.

metabolism.notes: Class-default CYP3A4 N-dealkylation pathway shared with fentanyl. Also 4-ANPP (4-anilino-N-phenethylpiperidine) from amide hydrolysis is a marker of synthesis.
Furan ring undergoes epoxidation then dihydrodiol formation — distinctive metabolic pathway.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased AUC, overdose risk.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inferred from fentanyl-class — no analogue-specific human data.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Classical opioid; typically shorter than morphine due to higher lipophilicity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Wooden chest syndrome — class-shared; rapid IV / smoked / IV illicit exposure.

notes: Ki 0.028 nM (Goggin 2017) — extremely high MOR affinity. EC50 2.52 nM in CHO hMOR GTPγS (7× more potent than fentanyl 17.9 nM in same assay). Hydroxy-furanyl metabolite is one of the major in-vivo species.

name: Gaba

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Exogenous oral GABA does NOT meaningfully cross the BBB (extremely polar zwitterion). Marketed supplement effects are largely placebo or via gut/enteric nervous system signalling. Any 'GABAergic' effect attributed to oral GABA supplements likely reflects bias.

routes.notes: BBB permeability very low; central effects not pharmacologically expected.

notes: Oral GABA supplements unlikely to produce direct central effects.

name: Gabapentin

primary_targets: α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cav)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Suman-Chauhan et al. 1993 — original characterisation of the α2δ binding site. Gomez et al. confirmed in recombinant α2δ-1: Kd ~59 nM at α2δ-1 vs 153 nM at α2δ-2.
binding.notes: Note: NOT a GABA receptor ligand despite the name. Does NOT bind GABA-A, GABA-B, or GABA-T. Therapeutic effect via Cav α2δ-1 binding → reduced trafficking of Cav2.1/2.2 to presynaptic terminals → ↓glutamate release. Effect manifests over hours-days, not seconds.

functional.notes: Reduces stimulated glutamate release ~25-40%; effect requires hours-days of treatment, reflecting reduced trafficking of α2δ-1-containing Cav channels to the membrane rather than acute channel block.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Binds α2δ-1 → disrupts trafficking and surface expression of Cav2.1/Cav2.2 at presynaptic terminals → reduced glutamate, noradrenaline, substance P release at hyperexcitable synapses. Also disrupts α2δ-1 / thrombospondin interaction (Eroglu 2009) → modulates excitatory synaptogenesis in development. The slow onset of analgesic/anxiolytic effect (days-weeks) reflects these trafficking and structural mechanisms.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults; PK is dose-dependent due to saturable LAT1 absorption.
routes.notes: F% drops from ~60% at 300 mg → ~47% at 600 mg → ~34% at 1200 mg → ~25% at 3600 mg due to saturation of LAT1 (SLC7A5, L-type amino acid transporter) in gut. t1/2 5-7 h (longer in renal failure: CL closely tracks CrCl). Negligible protein binding. ~100% renally excreted unchanged.

concentration_effect.notes: Therapeutic range approximate; no formal therapeutic drug monitoring established.

metabolism.notes: Excreted essentially unchanged in urine. No CYP involvement. No drug-drug interactions via CYP.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Separate doses by ≥2 h.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic synergy at respiratory depression; mild PK interaction (morphine ↑gabapentin AUC ~44%)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Major OD-risk amplifier — multiple coronial reports of gabapentinoid-opioid combined deaths.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: LAT1 polymorphisms may explain inter-individual variability in F% (~20-30%) but no clinically validated genotype guidance.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Long-term gabapentin increases α2δ-1 expression in some animal models — possible mechanism for tolerance and rebound hyperalgesia.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12-48 h after abrupt discontinuation. Anxiety, insomnia, GI upset, diaphoresis, tachycardia; case reports of seizures, particularly in patients with epilepsy or co-existing AUD/BZ dependence. Less severe than benzodiazepine or phenibut withdrawal but real.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Disruption of excitatory synaptogenesis — relevant to in-utero exposure and developing CNS.

demographic_differences.sex: No major sex difference in PK.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced proportional to renal function; dose-adjust by CrCl.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: CrCl <60: reduce dose; CrCl <15: 100-300 mg/day. Hepatic impairment irrelevant (no metabolism).

notes: The name 'gabapentin' is misleading — it has no direct action at any GABA receptor. The mechanism is Cav α2δ-1 binding with downstream effects on glutamate (not GABA) release. Saturable LAT1 absorption makes dose-response flatten at high doses.

name: Galantamine

functional.notes: Reversible, competitive AChE inhibitor with IC50 ~800 nM (less potent than donepezil ~6 nM, more potent than rivastigmine).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual mechanism debated. Pereira's work claimed positive allosteric modulation of α4β2 and α7 nAChRs at the 'APL' site, but Kowal et al. 2018 (doi:10.1111/bph.14329) reported negative results in carefully controlled assays on human α4β2 and α7 nAChRs — calling the PAM mechanism into question. AChE inhibition remains the universally accepted dominant mechanism.

routes.notes: Oral F ~90%, low protein binding (18%), t½ ~7 h. Cleared by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 + renal.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased galantamine exposure, increased cholinergic side effects

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs have ~25% higher galantamine AUC; UMs have lower exposure. Modest clinical impact since CYP2D6 contributes only ~25% of clearance.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: modest mAChR downregulation with chronic dosing
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Abrupt cessation in AD can worsen cognition (loss of cholinergic support).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly require dose titration
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Reduce dose in moderate hepatic/renal impairment

data_gaps_remaining: definitive resolution of nAChR APL mechanism controversy
notes: FDA-approved for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease. Lower AChE potency than donepezil but with proposed (controversial) nicotinic positive allosteric modulation. Significant CYP2D6 contribution to clearance — relevant for poor metabolizers.

name: GBL

primary_targets: GHB (via rapid in vivo lactonase hydrolysis)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: GBL itself is essentially inactive at GHB/GABA-B; its effects derive from peripheral and tissue-lactonase conversion to GHB.
binding.notes: Lettieri & Fung 1979; Roth & Giarman 1968. The lactone form is extremely lipophilic → faster absorption and more rapid onset than equimolar GHB. F% approaches 100% (vs 25% for GHB) due to bypass of first-pass GHB-saturable metabolism.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See GHB. GBL is a prodrug; the half-life of conversion in human plasma is <1 minute (serum paraoxonase / arylesterase activity). Onset ~5-10 min vs ~20-30 min for GHB.

routes.subject_demographics: Lettieri & Fung 1979 — GBL t1/2 in plasma ~1 min; GHB Cmax higher and Tmax shorter after GBL than equimolar GHB.
routes.notes: Equimolar conversion: 1 mL GBL ≈ 1.6 g GHB equivalent (density 1.13 g/mL, MW 86.1 vs GHB MW 104.1). Faster onset and higher peak make GBL more dangerous than GHB even at 'equivalent' doses.

metabolism.notes: Conversion is essentially complete and very rapid (t1/2 <1 min in plasma at 37°C). All subsequent PK/PD is GHB pharmacology.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Major respiratory-depression risk; common in club-drug overdoses.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: PON1 Q192R polymorphism alters lactonase activity — may modestly affect onset speed, but conversion is so fast that polymorphism likely has limited clinical impact.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Same as GHB.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Identical to GHB withdrawal; often more severe because GBL users dose more frequently (faster onset / shorter perceived effect).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Pure GBL is caustic at high concentrations — oral/oesophageal burns reported with undiluted ingestion.

notes: GBL is operationally indistinguishable from GHB after the first minute, but the faster onset and higher F% make it disproportionately overdose-prone. Per-volume potency is ~1.6x GHB.

name: GHB

binding.target: GHB-specific high-affinity binding site (distinct from GABA-B)
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Maitre lab — multiple papers from 1980s identifying stereoselective, saturable binding distinct from GABA-B. NCS-382 (Maitre 1990) is the selective antagonist (Ki ~340 nM) that does NOT bind GABA-B.
binding.notes: Castelli et al. 2004 (Neurosci Lett) — confirmed by molecular evidence that [3H]GHB does NOT bind HEK293 expressing GABA-B R1/R2. Identity of the GHB receptor cloned in 2003 (Andriamampandry, Maitre — pmid:14555562) as GPR172A is contested; the true molecular identity remains uncertain.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Lingenhoehl et al. 1999 (pmid:10591456) — GHB is a low-potency weak partial agonist at GABA-B (EC50 ~150-500 μM, Emax ~25-30% of baclofen). At clinically achieved brain conc. (~250-500 μM at recreational doses) GHB activates GABA-B sufficiently to produce sedation and respiratory depression — GABA-B is the target responsible for the intoxicating effects.
binding.notes: CRITICAL: low-dose GHB (~10-30 mg/kg) reaches conc that activates only the high-affinity GHB receptor → mild stimulation, euphoria. High-dose (>50 mg/kg) GHB reaches ~250-500 μM and engages GABA-B → sedation, coma. This biphasic dose-response is mechanistically explained by the two binding sites.

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 + Xenopus oocytes expressing human α4β3δ
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Absalom et al. 2012 — GHB is a low-potency (EC50 ~140 μM) but quite efficacious agonist at α4β1δ and α4β3δ GABA-A; partial inverse agonism at α4β3γ2 at higher conc. δ-selective effect parallels neurosteroid pharmacology.
binding.notes: PNAS paper proposes that δ-GABA-A contributes to GHB's absence-seizure liability and to the dose-dependent switch from euphoria to sedation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual-receptor model: at low brain concentrations (<100 μM) GHB selectively activates the high-affinity GHB receptor (Maitre receptor) which produces dopamine modulation and the stimulatory/pro-cognitive low-dose effects observed in rodents and at sub-medical doses in humans. At high brain concentrations (>200 μM, reached at recreational/medical Xyrem doses) GABA-B activation dominates → GIRK opening → hyperpolarisation, ↓cAMP, sedation, GH release, respiratory depression. The δ-GABA-A activation at ~140 μM may contribute to absence-seizure-like EEG and the deep stage-3/4 sleep pattern seen with Xyrem.

neuroimaging.finding: Xyrem (sodium oxybate) increases slow-wave sleep (N3) duration and amplitude in narcolepsy; produces 2.5-3 Hz spike-wave discharges (absence-like) in some species at supratherapeutic doses.

routes.subject_demographics: Brenneisen et al. 2004 healthy volunteers, 25 mg/kg PO; t1/2 = 30.4 ± 2.45 min, Vd 52.7 ± 15 L.
routes.notes: F% low (~25%) due to extensive first-pass and pre-systemic decarboxylation; absorption AND elimination are capacity-limited — doubling dose more than doubles AUC and Cmax. Food reduces Cmax by ~70%. Within the recreational dose range, half-life lengthens from ~30 min (low dose) to ~60-90 min (high dose) as metabolism saturates.

concentration_effect.notes: Couper & Logan: plasma >50 mg/L drowsiness; >150 mg/L unconsciousness; >250 mg/L deep coma. Toxic range overlaps recreational range — narrow therapeutic index.

metabolism.notes: GHB → SSA → succinate → CO2 + H2O. Endogenous pathway, saturable (Km ~50-100 μM). β-oxidation pathway also contributes. Renal excretion of unchanged GHB <5%.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic: shared GABA-B and respiratory depression; ethanol also competes for ADH/aldehyde dehydrogenase
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Marked synergistic respiratory depression; ethanol prolongs GHB half-life ~30%.
Markedly elevated GHB AUC and prolonged half-life; contraindicated with Xyrem.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: SSADH deficiency (Aldh5a1 -/-) accumulates GHB and GABA, causing intellectual disability and seizures — illustrates the saturable metabolism vulnerability.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Chronic GHB → GABA-B receptor desensitization and downregulation (rodent studies); contributes to severe withdrawal.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 1-6 h after last dose (very short — driven by short t1/2). Mild: tremor, anxiety, insomnia, tachycardia. Severe: delirium, psychosis, hallucinations, autonomic instability — closely resembles severe alcohol/benzo withdrawal; can be life-threatening. Treatment: high-dose benzodiazepines + baclofen + sometimes phenobarbital. The protracted course (psychiatric sequelae weeks-to-months) is attributed to GABA-B receptor downregulation.

off_targets.target: endogenous opioid release (dopamine via GABA-B disinhibition)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: Reinforcing properties partly opioid-mediated; naloxone partially blocks GHB-induced dopamine release in some studies.

demographic_differences.sex: Females may have higher GHB AUC than males at same mg/kg (rat data); limited human evidence.
demographic_differences.weight: Dose typically scaled to lean body mass given low Vd (~0.4 L/kg) and dose-dependent kinetics.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment prolongs t1/2; renal excretion minimal so renal failure has little effect on parent GHB.

data_gaps_remaining: Molecular identity of the high-affinity GHB receptor in humans (GPR172A controversial)
Quantitative human PK-PD model for narrow therapeutic window
notes: The dual-receptor pharmacology (high-affinity GHB receptor at low doses; GABA-B at high doses) is the single most important and most-overlooked fact about this compound. Maitre's group (Strasbourg, 1980s-2000s) did the foundational work characterising the GHB-specific binding site; Couper & Logan provided forensic concentration-effect data.

name: HARMINE

binding.notes: Herraiz 2010: IC50 2–5 nM at human MAO-A; potent, reversible, competitive (RIMA)
Weak MAO-B inhibition; >10,000-fold selectivity
Bain 2007: ATP-competitive DYRK1A inhibitor; relevant to β-cell proliferation interest

Hypertensive crisis risk lower than irreversible MAOIs due to RIMA character, but cautious avoidance still wise

name: Herkinorin

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Originally reported as a selective MOR agonist with µ/κ binding ratio of 0.13 (Harding et al. 2005, J Med Chem); μOR Ki ≈ 45 nM is the widely cited value (MedChem Express, vendor sheet citing primary literature).
binding.notes: First salvinorin-scaffold MOR-selective agonist. Selectivity reversed from Sal A by replacing C-2 acetate with a benzoate.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: µ/κ ratio ≈ 0.13 implies KOR Ki ≈ 90 nM (back-calculated from MOR Ki 45 nM and reported ratio).
Reported as having very little affinity for DOR

biased_agonism.interpretation: Originally reported as a strongly G-protein-biased MOR agonist (Groer et al. 2007 — induces MAPK signalling but does not recruit β-arrestin-2 or internalise MOR even with GRK2 overexpression). Later studies (Manglik/Shoichet group) reported similar β-arrestin recruitment to DAMGO depending on assay/cell-system — bias is contested. The original observation made herkinorin a landmark tool compound for MOR-biased agonism research.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR Gαi/o coupling; G-protein-mediated MAPK activation; minimal β-arrestin-2 recruitment / internalisation in HEK293 + GRK2 assay (Groer 2007); contested by later studies.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Hypothesised to be slower than morphine — minimal internalisation should mean reduced tolerance development. Not formally measured in humans.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Residual KOR activity (~2× weaker than MOR) means herkinorin is not pure MOR-selective.

notes: The exception in the salvinorin family — replacement of the C-2 acetate with benzoate inverts opioid receptor selectivity from KOR to MOR. Originally celebrated as the first G-protein-biased MOR agonist (Groer 2007), this bias claim has been challenged; remains a key reference compound in MOR-biased-agonism discussions.

name: Heroin

binding.notes: Heroin itself binds MOR with low intrinsic affinity; pharmacology is dominated by rapid hydrolysis to 6-MAM and morphine.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acts predominantly as a lipophilic prodrug; rapid esterase hydrolysis (t½ ≈ 2-3 min) to 6-MAM then morphine. The fast onset/'rush' reflects BBB penetration of the diester rather than direct receptor activity.

routes.notes: Parent heroin half-life ~2-6 min; undetectable by 10-40 min. Effects driven by 6-MAM then morphine.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Same OPRM1 sensitivity as morphine; CES1 polymorphism could in principle alter hydrolysis but is not clinically established.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: As morphine but more abrupt — onset 4-8 h, peak 36-72 h, duration 5-10 d.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal failure prolongs M6G accumulation — same caveat as morphine.

notes: Heroin is functionally a lipophilic morphine pro-prodrug. Naloxone reverses heroin overdose by antagonising MOR occupied by 6-MAM/morphine.

notes: Often confused with N-ethylhexedrone (Hexen/NEH); pure hexedrone is the N-methyl analogue. NEH (N-ethyl) is the clinically more prevalent compound.

name: Huperzine A

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Ki 24.9 nM, IC50 82 nM in rat cortex; 900-fold selectivity for AChE over BuChE
binding.notes: Reversible, mixed-type inhibitor with longer duration of action than donepezil due to slow off-rate from peripheral anionic site.

functional.notes: Non-competitive, voltage-independent NMDA inhibition with IC50 ~126 μM — ~5000× weaker than AChE. Clinically negligible at typical doses (200 μg).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: AChE inhibition is the dominant clinical mechanism — same target as donepezil/galantamine/rivastigmine. The much higher concentrations required for NMDA antagonism mean the 'dual-mechanism' marketing for neuroprotection is largely theoretical at oral doses.

routes.notes: Oral t½ 10-14 h. High BBB penetration. Effective doses 50-200 μg PO BID.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Bradycardia, nausea, cholinergic crisis at supratherapeutic combined exposure

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Chronic AChE inhibition leads to modest mAChR downregulation similar to other AChE-Is.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Abrupt cessation may unmask cholinergic deficit (e.g., worsening cognition in AD).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: 900× selectivity for AChE means low peripheral cholinergic side-effect burden compared to less-selective AChE-Is.

data_gaps_remaining: validated human plasma PK at OTC supplement doses
notes: Mechanistically equivalent to FDA-approved AChE inhibitors (donepezil et al.) — natural-product status does not reduce the cholinergic pharmacology. The NMDA antagonist component (IC50 ~126 μM) is too weak to contribute clinically at oral OTC doses. Should be treated with the same caution as prescription AChE inhibitors regarding co-administration with anticholinergics, neuromuscular blockers, and other cholinergic agents.

name: Hydroxetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 3-OH analogue of MXE. By analogy to 3-HO-PCP (μ-opioid Ki 39-60 nM) — likely μ-opioid agonist + NMDA antagonist. Could be hazardous combination.

notes: 3-Hydroxy MXE analogue. Major safety concern: meta-OH arylcyclohexylamines (3-HO-PCP, 3-HO-PCE) have shown high μ-opioid affinity, raising respiratory depression risk uncharacteristic of pure NMDA antagonists.

name: Hydroxynorketamine

binding.notes: Suzuki 2017: (2R,6R)-HNK does NOT block NMDA at antidepressant-relevant concentrations (≤10 μM). Earlier Moaddel 2013 claim of NMDA antagonism not replicated. HNK binds closed/desensitized NMDA receptors at much higher concentrations (Lumsden 2019)

functional.notes: Marcantoni 2024: HNK (not ketamine) acts via α7-nAChR. Selective α7 antagonist or Chrna7 KO abolishes HNK-induced synaptic and nuclear regulations.
Zanos 2016: (2R,6R)-HNK potentiates AMPA via presynaptic mechanism. AMPA blockade by NBQX abolishes antidepressant effect.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Proposed mechanism (Zanos/Gould): presynaptic α7-nAChR activation → glutamate release → AMPA potentiation → BDNF → TrkB → mTOR → synaptogenesis WITHOUT NMDA blockade or dissociation. This decoupling drove HNK as a non-dissociative antidepressant candidate (Phase 1 NIH 2023).

routes.notes: NIH Phase 1 single ascending dose study (Zarate group); preliminary data shows oral bioavailability adequate for therapeutic exposure

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Predicted minimal (no NMDA blockade, no dissociation)

notes: Major mechanism controversy. Zarate/Gould (NIH) push α7-nAChR + AMPA mechanism (Zanos 2016 Nature, Marcantoni 2024 Transl Psychiatry). Moaddel 2013 originally claimed NMDA antagonism but Suzuki 2017 PNAS showed no NMDA block at antidepressant-relevant doses. Different from parent ketamine — should NOT be tagged NMDA-antagonist.

name: Hydroxyzine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Higher H1 affinity than diphenhydramine; metabolised to cetirizine.

binding.notes: 5-HT2A contributes to anxiolysis.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: H1 dominant sedation + 5-HT2A anxiolysis. Less anticholinergic than DPH. Major active metabolite = cetirizine (CYP3A4-mediated oxidation) — non-sedating peripheral H1 antagonist responsible for most steady-state H1 effect at the systemic level but not in CNS (cetirizine is P-gp substrate, low BBB penetration).

metabolism.notes: Cetirizine is itself a marketed antihistamine.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: H1 tolerance within days.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QT prolongation at high doses; FDA warning 2015.

notes: Useful anxiolytic in BZ-sparing protocols.

name: Ibogaine

binding.notes: Popik et al. 1995, 1997 — Ki ~1 μM at PCP site (one report); other groups have reported higher values (~3 μM). NMDA antagonism is widely accepted as one mechanism of anti-addictive action.
Sweetnam et al. 1995; Glick & Maisonneuve attribute anti-addictive effects partly to kappa agonism. Lower-affinity than noribogaine.
Glick et al. 1995 originally reported high mu affinity — that work used non-standard conditions. Standard radioligand displacement gives Ki ~5 μM.
Non-competitive inhibition of SERT (distinct from typical SSRI competitive mechanism).
Sigma-2 is the highest-affinity ibogaine target identified; functional consequences less well-mapped than NMDA/kappa.
Glick & Maisonneuve 1998 — weak 5-HT2A agonism may contribute to the visionary/oneirogen subjective effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Multi-target polypharmacology with no single dominant mechanism. NMDA channel block (low-μM) acts synergistically with kappa-opioid G-biased agonism (via metabolite noribogaine) and SERT inhibition. The 'iboga experience' itself may reflect transient combined NMDA antagonism + 5-HT2A agonism (oneirogenic visions); the sub-acute anti-addictive effect (days-weeks) likely reflects the long-acting noribogaine metabolite acting at kappa-opioid and SERT.

routes.subject_demographics: Glue et al. healthy volunteer ascending dose study; mixed CYP2D6 genotype
routes.notes: t1/2 in EMs ~7 h, longer in PMs (paroxetine-pretreated subjects had ~2x exposure to active moiety). CYP2D6 is the dominant clearance pathway — phenotype correlates r=0.77 with ibogaine Cmax.

metabolism.notes: O-demethylation. Noribogaine has 10x higher SERT affinity, longer t1/2 (28-49 h), and is the kappa-opioid G-biased active metabolite responsible for sustained anti-addictive effect.
Drug transporters P-gp and OATP1B1 affect ibogaine/noribogaine pharmacokinetics; CYP3A4 (despite presence of methoxy group) is NOT a major contributor to clearance.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 2-fold increase in active moiety (ibogaine + noribogaine) exposure; markedly increased cardiotoxicity risk.
Severe QTc prolongation, torsades risk — absolutely contraindicated combinations.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs have markedly higher and longer-lasting ibogaine exposure → higher cardiotoxicity risk. UMs have rapid clearance → less effect at standard doses but rapid noribogaine accumulation. PM genotype is essentially a contraindication for full-dose ibogaine without dose adjustment.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: No conventional tolerance described — ibogaine is typically dosed once or in widely spaced 're-treatments'. No physical dependence syndrome.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QTc prolongation, torsades-de-pointes, sudden cardiac death. The dominant lethal hazard. Documented at standard anti-addictive doses (8-10 mg/kg) in healthy individuals without pre-existing cardiac disease.
May contribute to anti-addictive efficacy.

demographic_differences.weight: mg/kg dosing standard; very high doses (>20 mg/kg) approach lethal range.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment increases exposure due to CYP2D6 dependency.

data_gaps_remaining: Functional NMDA receptor electrophysiology (open vs trapping block, on/off kinetics)
Quantitative human PET imaging of NMDA / kappa-opioid / SERT occupancy
Mechanistic dissection of which target drives which subjective effect
notes: Ibogaine is more a polypharmacology cocktail than a classical NMDA antagonist; its clinical effect (anti-addictive, particularly opioid-craving suppression) cannot be reproduced by any single-target ligand. The dominant safety hazard is hERG blockade (IC50 3.5 μM) producing QT prolongation and torsades — multiple deaths documented at therapeutic doses, especially with CYP2D6 PM genotype or QT-prolonging co-medications. The active metabolite noribogaine (formed by CYP2D6) likely carries most of the sub-acute therapeutic effect via 10x higher SERT affinity and kappa-opioid G-biased agonism with 28-49 h half-life.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methadone analogue with carbonyl replaced by sulfone (bioisostere). Roughly methadone-equipotent in animals; human reports inconsistent.

name: Idebenone

primary_targets: mitochondrial complex III (electron donor, bypassing complex I)

functional.target: Complex III of electron transport chain
functional.readout: oxygen consumption restoration in Complex-I-inhibited mitochondria
functional.notes: Idebenone acts as a short-chain ubiquinone analog. NQO1 reduces it to idebenol, which donates electrons directly to Complex III — bypassing Complex I defects. The metabolite QS10 also restores electron transfer.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Tissues with high NQO1 (RPE, hepatocytes) benefit most; neurons have low NQO1 expression which may limit CNS efficacy. EU approval for LHON (Raxone, 900 mg/day) and conditional approval for Friedreich's ataxia historically (withdrawn).

routes.notes: Very low oral F due to extensive first-pass metabolism; mainly circulates as glucuronide/sulfate conjugates. Improved absorption with high-fat meal.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: NQO1 polymorphism (C609T, *2 allele) reduces enzyme activity → reduced idebenone reduction → reduced efficacy in tissues dependent on cytosolic reduction.

notes: EMA-approved for LHON (Raxone). Nootropic claim in healthy adults is not supported by controlled data; effective dose for LHON is 900 mg/day, far above typical nootropic regimens.

name: IDRA-21

functional.cell_system: Xenopus oocyte / HEK293 expressing human GluA
functional.notes: 70 µM IDRA-21 doubles charge transfer; slows deactivation and attenuates desensitization. ~10-30x more potent than aniracetam in behavioral reversal of scopolamine/alprazolam amnesia.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Benzothiadiazine PAM. Both deactivation slowing and desensitization block contribute. (+)-IDRA-21 is the eutomer.

neuroimaging.finding: Improved delayed matching performance in aged rhesus monkeys at 1-5 mg/kg PO (Buccafusco et al., 2004).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Inhibits synaptic and extrasynaptic NMDA receptor-mediated events in cerebellar granule cells — net effect inhibitory at NMDA despite AMPA potentiation.

notes: The prototypical benzothiadiazine AMPAkine and progenitor of many later compounds. Popular as a research chemical for self-experimentation; absence of human PK or formal safety data makes any consumer use a leap. Activity is enantioselective — racemic material from grey-market vendors has half-strength.
