name: Jenkem

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Not applicable. 'Jenkem' is an unverified preparation of fermented human waste (faeces and/or urine), the fumes of which are allegedly inhaled for psychoactive effect. There is no defined active pharmaceutical ingredient. Putative volatile constituents of anaerobic faecal fermentation include hydrogen sulfide (H2S), methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3), volatile organic acids, indole, skatole, and methyl mercaptan — none of these are recognised hallucinogens. H2S at very high concentrations causes CNS depression and is acutely toxic (cytochrome c oxidase inhibition); ammonia causes mucosal injury. No coherent pharmacological mechanism for euphoria or hallucination has been proposed in the peer-reviewed literature.

off_targets.target: Inhalational toxicity (H2S, NH3, methyl mercaptan, biological pathogens)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: If actually inhaled, fecal fermentation gases pose risks of cytotoxic anoxia (H2S → cytochrome c oxidase inhibition), respiratory irritation, and bacterial / viral / parasitic infection from aerosolised pathogens (enteric bacteria, hepatitis A, helminth ova). No evidence of meaningful psychoactivity.

data_gaps_remaining: Most authoritative sources (Snopes, toxicology reviews) classify it as urban legend / media hoax with isolated, unverified African street-children case reports
notes: Jenkem does NOT belong in the anticholinergic-deliriants category. It is not an anticholinergic compound and likely does not produce reliable psychoactive effects at all. Origin: 2007 US media panic based on a 1995 BBC report about Zambian street children — the actual psychoactive substance abused by those children was overwhelmingly inhalant solvents (glue, petrol), not faecal gas. Recommendation: remove Jenkem from the substance database, or reclassify under 'hoax/unverified substances' if retention is needed for harm-reduction education purposes. If retained: warning copy should emphasise (a) likely hoax status, (b) genuine biological/chemical inhalation risks if attempted, (c) no expected psychoactive benefit.

name: JJC8-088

name: JWH-018

binding.tissue_or_cell: rat cerebellar membranes (Aung 2000); also reported on hCB1-CHO
binding.notes: Aung et al 2000 founding measurement; ~4× more potent than Δ9-THC at CB1 AND full agonist (~100% efficacy vs THC's ~25%). This combination is what makes JWH-018 dramatically more dangerous than cannabis.

biased_agonism.interpretation: Synthetic cannabinoids including JWH-018 show modest β-arrestin bias relative to THC; arrestin recruitment correlates with tachycardia and seizure liability

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full CB1 Gi-cAMP inhibition; potent β-arrestin recruitment; large internalisation — explains rapid tolerance and withdrawal severity in heavy users.

routes.notes: No controlled human PK; only post-mortem and emergency-room concentrations reported (0.1–199 ng/mL parent in blood).

metabolism.notes: Mono- and dihydroxylated metabolites retain high CB1 affinity (Ki 4-50 nM) — extending pharmacodynamic effect. Some metabolites act as neutral CB1 antagonists (Brents 2012, pmid:21942375).

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Limited data; expected slower clearance in CYP2C9 PMs.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Rapid CB1 internalisation (hours); robust desensitisation within days. Heavy users develop severe physical dependence with prolonged withdrawal compared to cannabis.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset within 24 h, peak 2-7 d, can persist 2-4 weeks. Anxiety, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, tremor, GI distress, severe insomnia, craving. More severe than cannabis withdrawal.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Some JWH-series compounds show minor 5-HT2B activity; clinical relevance unclear

notes: Prototype 'K2/Spice' synthetic cannabinoid. The combination of high CB1 affinity AND full intrinsic activity (vs THC's partial agonism) drives the severe toxicity profile: seizures, acute kidney injury, myocardial infarction, psychosis, hyperthermia, agitated delirium. Schedule I (US) since 2011.

metabolism.notes: Monohydroxylated metabolites retain CB1 affinity (intermediate to high); some act as neutral antagonists/partial agonists (pmid:22323737).

name: Ketamine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Used as the reference comparator in Roth 2013 (MK-801 Ki ≈ 5.7 nM in same assay)
binding.notes: Racemic ketamine; widely cited canonical value
S-ketamine ~4× higher affinity than R-ketamine
R-ketamine Ki ≈ 27,000 nM, S-ketamine Ki ≈ 131,000 nM at σ1; substantial enantioselectivity
Very weak; clinical relevance unclear
Hirota et al. 1997; functional agonism debated. Williams 2018 naltrexone trial showed naltrexone blocks ketamine antidepressant effect but Yoon 2019 reanalysis questioned methodology

functional.cell_system: HEK293 expressing HCN1; cortical pyramidal neurons
functional.notes: EC50 ~8-16 μM for racemate; S-ketamine ~2× more potent (EC50 ~7 μM). Within clinically anesthetic free plasma range (5-10 μM). Chen et al. 2009 — HCN1 knockout abolishes ketamine hypnosis

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acute: blocks open NMDA channel (use-dependent, voltage-sensitive). Disinhibits cortical pyramidal cells via preferential blockade of GABAergic interneuron NMDARs → glutamate surge → AMPA activation → BDNF/TrkB → mTORC1 → synaptogenesis (Duman/Aghajanian model). HCN1 inhibition contributes to hypnosis. The major active metabolite (2R,6R)-HNK potentiates AMPA via α7 nAChR-dependent presynaptic mechanism (Marcantoni 2024, doi:10.1038/s41398-024-02744-y).

neuroimaging.finding: Acute ketamine increases prefrontal/ACC BOLD signal and decreases default-mode network connectivity in humans; matches subjective dissociation
Acute ketamine increases gamma power (30-80 Hz), decreases alpha power; biomarker of dissociation and rapid antidepressant response
[11C]-(+)-PHNO displacement studies show ketamine increases striatal dopamine release ~20% at subanesthetic doses (consistent with ~3% D2/D3 occupancy by displaced DA)

routes.notes: Clements & Nimmo 1981. Terminal t½ ~2.5 h (range 2-4 h)
Yanagihara et al. report 45% absolute bioavailability; some studies give 25-50% range
Grant et al. 1981; oral bioavailability 17-20% due to extensive first-pass; norketamine/ketamine ratio ~6.4 in plasma with oral route

concentration_effect.notes: Plasma ketamine ~640-1000 ng/mL produces unconsciousness; recovery at <500 ng/mL
Subanesthetic plasma ~100-200 ng/mL during 0.5 mg/kg IV infusion produces analgesia and antidepressant response

metabolism.notes: Yanagihara 2002, Hijazi 2002. CYP2B6 demethylates S- and R-ketamine equipotently
CYP3A4 demethylates S-ketamine faster than R-ketamine; primary in human liver microsomes per some reports
HNK does NOT block NMDA at antidepressant-relevant doses (Zanos 2016, Suzuki 2017 doi:10.1073/pnas.1816071116); acts via α7 nAChR and AMPA potentiation

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Oral ketamine AUC increased ~2.6× by clarithromycin (strong CYP3A4 inhibitor)
Reduces ketamine and S-ketamine AUC ~80%
Inhibits norketamine formation; increases ketamine AUC

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2B6*6/*6 carriers (~3-5% Caucasians) show ~50% lower oral ketamine clearance; norketamine exposure increased. Clinical relevance for oral/sublingual ketamine in TRD treatment.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Rapid tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing (hours to days); use-dependence of NMDA blockade reduces with sustained channel blockade
cross_tolerance: DXM (partial, via different NMDA site kinetics)
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild compared to opioids/benzos. Onset 24-72h after cessation in heavy users: craving, dysphoria, anhedonia, fatigue, GI distress. Lasts 1-2 weeks. Urinary tract symptoms (ketamine cystitis) may persist months.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Contributes to hypnotic action; HCN1 KO mice resistant to ketamine anesthesia
Minor at clinical concentrations; indirect sympathomimetic effects dominate cardiovascular profile
Inhibition at supratherapeutic doses; not clinically dominant
Ulcerative cystitis in chronic high-dose users (>1 g/day); norketamine implicated as direct urothelial toxin

demographic_differences.sex: Women have slightly lower CL/F and higher peak exposure on weight-normalized basis
demographic_differences.age: Pediatric CL/kg higher than adult; elderly show decreased CL
demographic_differences.weight: Standard weight-based dosing; obese patients may need lean-body-weight calculation
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment reduces CL significantly; renal impairment minor effect on parent but HNK glucuronides accumulate

data_gaps_remaining: definitive μ-opioid functional agonism vs allosteric modulation; mechanism of urothelial toxicity
notes: Reference compound for the entire class. Zhang 2021 Nature (doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03769-9) revealed S-ketamine binds NMDA channel central vestibule with two distinct sub-poses; key residues GluN2A-L642 and GluN1-N616. R-ketamine has longer-lasting/stronger antidepressant effect in rodents despite lower NMDA affinity (Hashimoto group).

name: Lamotrigine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: IC50 strongly voltage-dependent: 280 μM at -120 mV holding potential, 28.8 μM at -95 mV — use-dependent block of inactivated channels
binding.notes: Use-dependent / state-dependent — preferentially binds inactivated state. Stabilises Na channel inactivation, reduces glutamate/aspartate release.
Cardiac Na channel block underlies FDA warning for ventricular arrhythmia in patients with structural heart disease (2020).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Use-dependent Na channel block selectively dampens high-frequency neuronal firing (epileptic foci) and reduces glutamate release; mood-stabilising mechanism less well-defined but likely involves glutamate normalisation in limbic circuits.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Lamotrigine t1/2 ↑ to ~70 h; AUC ↑ 2× — major SJS risk factor; half all doses when combined.
Lamotrigine t1/2 ↓ to ~14 h; AUC ↓ 50% — double dose typically needed.
Lamotrigine clearance ↑ ~50% during active pill weeks; spikes during pill-free week.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: HLA-B*15:02 carriers (predominantly Han Chinese, SE Asian) have ~1000× higher SJS/TEN risk — pre-prescription testing recommended in these populations. HLA-A*31:01 also confers risk in European populations. UGT1A4*2/*3 alleles affect clearance.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Seizure rebound in epilepsy patients; mood instability in bipolar. Taper over ≥2 weeks recommended.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis in ~1/1000 (epilepsy) to ~1/2500 (bipolar). Slow titration (25 mg×2 wk, 50 mg×2 wk, then up to 100-200 mg) reduces risk roughly 10-fold. Risk amplified by valproate co-administration.
FDA 2020 warning: arrhythmia risk in patients with structural heart disease (Brugada-pattern ECG, conduction disease).

demographic_differences.sex: Women on combined oral contraceptives need ~50% higher doses during active pill weeks.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: clearance ↓ ~30%. Pediatric: weight-based dosing.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Severe hepatic impairment: clearance ↓ 50%; severe renal impairment: caution with metabolite accumulation.

notes: The slow 6-week titration schedule is non-negotiable for safety, not gradual dose-finding — rapid titration is the dominant SJS/TEN risk factor independent of total dose.

name: Levetiracetam

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO cells expressing human recombinant SV2A; human cortex membranes
binding.assay_buffer_notes: 37 C; Ki dependent on assay conditions — reported 0.8 µM to 8 µM range across labs
binding.notes: Often quoted as ~1.6 µM in CHO-hSV2A or 6-8 µM in brain tissue at 37 C — the difference reflects assay temperature and membrane composition rather than a true affinity discrepancy. Stereospecific: (R)-enantiomer is ~1000x weaker.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Binds SV2A on synaptic vesicles, modulating Ca2+-dependent neurotransmitter release in an activity-dependent way. Secondary actions reported include partial inhibition of N-type Ca2+ channels and IP3R-mediated Ca2+ release; these are not believed to drive clinical anticonvulsant efficacy. Critically: no AMPA receptor activity, despite the racetam scaffold and the historical lumping with piracetam family.

neuroimaging.finding: [11C]UCB-J PET shows dose-dependent SV2A occupancy of 10-90% across the 250-3000 mg dose range in humans.

routes.subject_demographics: healthy adults; values from FDA Keppra label and Radtke 2001

concentration_effect.effect: therapeutic plasma concentration for seizure control

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: No clinically relevant CYP-pharmacogenetic effects; metabolism is CYP-independent.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: no SV2A downregulation reported with chronic dosing
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: abrupt withdrawal can precipitate rebound seizures; taper recommended. Behavioral side effects (irritability, aggression, depression) can persist for days after discontinuation in susceptible patients.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: partial inhibition at high concentrations; not clinically dominant

demographic_differences.sex: no clinically significant sex difference in PK

Cmax ~5 nM at 100 µg; receptor occupancy of 5-HT2A estimated 50–70% at peak

name: MDMA

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 stably expressing human SERT, release of preloaded [3H]-5-HT
binding.notes: Simmler et al 2013, human transporter. Note that rat synaptosome assays (Baumann/Rothman) give SERT release EC50 ~75 nM — 70× more potent. The species difference is real and matters.
Rat synaptosome: 154 nM (much more potent at rat DAT).
MDMA is most potent at NET — explains the sympathomimetic profile.
Weak partial agonist. Functional data: 5-HT2A activation contributes little at clinical doses.
Setola & Roth 2003. 5-HT2B agonism is the proposed mechanism of MDMA-associated valvular heart disease (fenfluramine-like). Active metabolite MDA is more potent at 5-HT2B (Ki ~100 nM).
Human TAAR1 affinity is much weaker for amphetamines; rat data is not a good predictor.

functional.notes: Racemic and S-MDMA show weak partial agonism; R-MDMA has negligible functional activity despite higher binding affinity. Stereoselective dissociation between binding and function.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MDMA is primarily a transporter substrate, not a GPCR agonist of significance. It enters cells via DAT/NET/SERT, then triggers reverse transport (efflux) of monoamines through the same transporters. Inside the neuron, it also disrupts VMAT2 vesicular storage. The 5-HT release dominates the SSC subjective profile; concurrent NE release drives cardiovascular effects; weak DA release (low at human DAT) contributes to reinforcement. The mechanism-based inhibition of CYP2D6 — via reactive quinone/quinone-methide intermediates from the catechol metabolite HHMA — irreversibly inactivates the enzyme that clears MDMA itself, producing the well-documented nonlinear PK.

neuroimaging.finding: MDMA (100 mg PO) decreases amygdala reactivity to angry faces and increases ventral striatum response to positive social stimuli
Chronic heavy MDMA users show reduced SERT availability in cortical and subcortical regions; partial recovery after abstinence

metabolism.notes: Primary O-demethylenation pathway. CYP2D6 catalyses the demethylenation that generates the catechol HHMA, which then forms reactive ortho-quinones that covalently bind and inactivate CYP2D6 — this is the mechanism-based inhibition.

Blunts MDMA subjective effects (SERT competition); risk of serotonin syndrome at high combined doses.
Severe risk: massive 5-HT accumulation → serotonin syndrome, hyperthermia, fatality. Absolute contraindication.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PM status modestly increases MDMA exposure (~30% higher Cmax) and prolongs half-life, but the effect is much smaller than expected because MDMA itself rapidly inhibits CYP2D6 — within 1 h of a 100 mg dose, even EMs are functionally phenoconverted to PM status. The auto-inhibition takes ~10 days to resolve (slow CYP2D6 resynthesis). Practical implication: re-dosing within a week stacks exposure unpredictably regardless of genotype. COMT Val/Met polymorphism affects HMMA formation kinetics. 5-HTTLPR short/short carriers report stronger subjective effects.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Acute pharmacodynamic tachyphylaxis within hours of redosing (5-HT pools depleted, SERT downregulated). Chronic SERT downregulation in heavy users shows partial recovery over months of abstinence (PET [11C]-DASB studies).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No physical withdrawal syndrome. Post-acute 'comedown' (24-72 h) — dysphoria, fatigue, irritability, occasional depressive episodes — reflects depleted 5-HT stores rather than receptor adaptation. Resolves spontaneously; not pathognomonic of dependence.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Cardiac valvular fibrosis with chronic/repeated heavy use (fenfluramine-like mechanism). Epidemiological evidence supports increased VHD risk in regular MDMA users.

Weak hERG block at supratherapeutic concentrations; clinically relevant QT prolongation usually requires overdose or co-ingestion. Hyperthermia from MDMA toxicity is the dominant cardiac concern, not QT.

MDMA disrupts vesicular storage of monoamines. Combined with cytosolic redox stress from MDMA quinone metabolites, this drives the well-characterised serotonergic axonal pruning seen in animal models at high repeated doses.

demographic_differences.sex: Women show ~30-40% higher Cmax and stronger subjective effects per mg/kg, partly explained by lower body water and lower lean body mass. Women also have higher risk of MDMA-associated hyponatremia (combination of SIADH + polydipsia + smaller TBW).
demographic_differences.weight: Fixed-dose protocols (e.g., 125 mg flat) produce wide exposure range — light users get effective ~2 mg/kg, heavy users get ~1 mg/kg. Weight-adjusted dosing is preferred clinically.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment markedly extends half-life (CYP2D6 inhibition + reduced phase II capacity).

data_gaps_remaining: Exact human 5-HT2B Ki (Setola data sometimes cited as 500 nM, sometimes as higher)
notes: MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD: MAPS/Lykos submitted NDA Dec 2023 based on MAPP1 (NCT03537014, n=90) and MAPP2 (n=104) Phase 3 trials, both meeting primary endpoint (CAPS-5 reduction vs placebo+therapy). FDA issued Complete Response Letter Aug 2024 citing functional unblinding, AE underreporting, and concerns about therapy delivery — not efficacy. Drug listed in DEA Schedule I; FDA breakthrough designation 2017. The Holze 2024 enantiomer trial (NCT05277636) showed S-MDMA 100 mg ≈ racemic 125 mg ≈ R-MDMA 300 mg for overall effect intensity.

name: MDMB-4en-PINACA

binding.notes: Cannaert 2021. EC50 1.88–2.47 nM with Emax 221–299% relative to JWH-018 — super-efficacious. ~10× CB1 affinity of JWH-018. Pent-4-enyl side chain is novel and bypasses fluoropentyl analogue laws.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Super-agonist at CB1 (Emax >> reference); high β-arrestin recruitment likely contributes to severe toxicity.

notes: One of the most dangerous SCRAs identified. Super-efficacious CB1 agonist. The pent-4-enyl side chain is a 'designer evasion' of pentyl/fluoropentyl analogue scheduling. DEA Schedule I (2026).

name: MDOH

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-hydroxy variant of MDA. The N-OH is metabolically labile and rapidly reduced to MDA in vivo — MDOH effectively acts as a prodrug of MDA. PIHKAL #114; dose 100-160 mg, duration 3-6 h.

metabolism.notes: Rapid N-OH reduction to MDA in vivo. MDOH is functionally an MDA prodrug.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Inherits MDA's 5-HT2B agonism.

data_gaps_remaining: Direct binding/release data — only PIHKAL human dose-response is published
notes: PIHKAL #114. Functionally an MDA prodrug.

name: Mdpa

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methylenedioxyphenylacetamide. Sparse/no published pharmacology. The amide is likely metabolically labile or weakly active; no clear monoamine releaser activity reported.

notes: Negligible published data.

name: MDPBP

binding.notes: Luethi 2021 — MDPBP IC50 0.07 μM at hDAT; pure pyrrolidinophenone blocker, slightly weaker than MDPV (α-butyl vs α-pentyl)
DAT/SERT ratio 155 — high DAT selectivity, MDPV-like

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pure DAT/NET reuptake inhibitor, ~2× less potent than MDPV. Same pyrrolidinophenone mechanism.

notes: MDPBP is the α-butyl homologue of MDPV (α-pentyl). One carbon shorter, ~2× lower DAT potency.

name: MDPPP

binding.notes: MDPPP is the α-methyl homologue of MDPV — ~10× weaker; confirms α-chain length SAR (longer = more potent at DAT)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pyrrolidinophenone DAT/NET blocker; weaker than MDPBP and MDPV

notes: Shortest α-chain pyrrolidinophenone; weakest of the methylenedioxy series.

name: MDPR

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-propyl extension of MDA scaffold. Per Shulgin SAR — extension beyond N-ethyl progressively kills monoamine release activity at the human transporters. PIHKAL describes weak activity at ~200 mg.

notes: PIHKAL compound. N-propyl chain reduces potency. Limited published pharmacology.

name: Mdpv

binding.notes: Baumann 2013 Neuropsychopharmacology — MDPV is ~50× more potent than cocaine at DAT; pure blocker, NOT a substrate (no release evoked)
Luethi 2021 — IC50 0.03 μM at hDAT; confirms pure blocker mechanism
DAT/SERT selectivity >800 — the most DAT-selective monoamine drug yet characterized; explains 'pure dopaminergic' hyperstimulation profile
Luethi 2021 — MDPV inactive at hTAAR1 up to 30 μM; no TAAR1 brake on dopamine firing
Glennon 2014 reports moderate σ1 affinity for MDPV (low μM); contributes to psychostimulant profile and possibly proconvulsant effects

functional.notes: Kolanos 2015 ACS Chem Neurosci — S-(+)-MDPV ~270× more potent than R-(-)-MDPV at DAT; eutomer accounts for activity

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pure DAT/NET reuptake inhibitor with sub-nM eutomer potency. Persistent binding kinetics (slow off-rate at DAT compared to cocaine) explains prolonged in vivo effects beyond what plasma half-life predicts. The combination of (a) extreme DAT potency, (b) slow off-rate, (c) no TAAR1 feedback, and (d) no autoreceptor activation from released DA produces sustained dopaminergic activation responsible for flakka-style psychosis.

routes.notes: Compiled clinical estimates from forensic cases suggest t1/2 ~7-8 h in humans (rat t1/2 ~80-100 min, but humans accumulate due to lipophilicity). Exact controlled-administration PK NOT published — would be unethical given toxicity.

metabolism.notes: Strano-Rossi 2010 — CYP2D6, CYP1A2, CYP2C19 all contribute to O-demethylenation; catechol metabolite further methylated by COMT to 4-OH-3-MeO-PV (predominant urinary metabolite)

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced demethylenation may prolong half-life and increase toxicity risk

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6/CYP2C19 PMs likely show prolonged exposure; redundant metabolic pathways reduce magnitude of pharmacogenetic impact compared to mephedrone

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe stimulant withdrawal: anhedonia, hypersomnia, intense craving, depression; can persist weeks. Compulsive-redosing during use is the hallmark.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Direct hERG and KCNQ1 block at low-μM concentrations in zebrafish hearts produces conduction delay and bradyarrhythmia — distinct from sympathomimetic tachycardia; documented MDPV cardiac deaths often show conduction abnormalities
off_targets.notes: Tarapoulouzi 2024 — integrated cardiotoxicity assessment; MDPV-specific direct ion channel toxicity

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Possible contribution to seizures and psychosis at high doses

demographic_differences.weight: Lipophilicity (logP ~3.3) predicts increased tissue accumulation in obese users; clinical correlation reported in flakka epidemics

data_gaps_remaining: exact hERG IC50 in mammalian patch clamp
notes: MDPV is the canonical 'pure pyrrolidinophenone' — sub-nM DAT eutomer (S-MDPV), no SERT, no TAAR1, slow off-rate. The combination is uniquely dangerous; this profile drives most flakka/bath-salts emergency presentations. Direct hERG block (unlike most cathinones) adds cardiac risk distinct from sympathomimetic toxicity.

name: Mebroqualone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Bromo analog of mecloqualone. Quinazolinone; see Methaqualone.

notes: Quinazolinone analog.

name: Meclonazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: (S)-3-methylclonazepam. Originally developed as anti-schistosomal; never marketed for that. Active (S)-enantiomer; designer benzo.

notes: Developed as anti-schistosomal. Hester 1971 patent.

name: Medazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug — metabolized to diazepam, nordazepam, and finally oxazepam. Lacks 2-oxo group of diazepam.

notes: Prodrug — metabolized to diazepam then nordazepam.

name: Medifoxamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Weak DAT inhibition (preferential) and even weaker SERT inhibition; 5-HT2A/2C antagonism. Drug not well-characterised at modern cloned receptors.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Fulminant hepatitis cases led to withdrawal (Morocco 1999, France 2000). Mechanism likely reactive metabolite via diphenoxy moiety.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Withdrawn — do not use.

data_gaps_remaining: receptor binding Ki at modern targets
notes: Withdrawn 1999-2000 due to hepatotoxicity. No longer clinically available.

name: Mefloquine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Quinoline antimalarial. Not intentionally psychoactive but causes neuropsychiatric AEs (anxiety, depression, paranoia, vivid dreams) in 0.5-25% depending on series — FDA black-box 2013. Mechanism for AEs: connexin-43 gap-junction inhibition in brain, adenosine A2A binding, calcium dysregulation.

routes.notes: Extraordinarily long t1/2 ~14-21 days. Tmax 6-24 h. Large Vd (lipophilic). Hepatic CYP3A4.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Neuropsychiatric AEs (psychosis, suicidality) — FDA black-box 2013.

demographic_differences.sex: Women report higher rates of neuropsychiatric AEs.

notes: Not a primary psychoactive; included here only because of AE profile.

name: MELATONIN

binding.notes: Audinot 2003: subnanomolar
Quinone reductase 2 — antioxidant relevance

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MT1 sleep onset (Gαi→cAMP↓ + PLC activation); MT2 circadian phase shift; MT3 antioxidant. cAMP-PKA-CREB downstream. No serotonergic agonism at typical doses.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Up to 17-fold AUC increase
~30–50% AUC reduction
Complex; may increase oral exposure

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Slow CYP1A2 metabolisers have ~3× longer half-life and higher AUC at standard doses

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: MT1 internalisation after sustained agonist exposure; documented in chronic ramelteon use

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Very weak

demographic_differences.age: Elderly have lower endogenous melatonin; exogenous response often greater
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment markedly increases exposure

notes: Massive CYP1A2 substrate sensitivity drives most clinically meaningful DDIs. Fluvoxamine + melatonin essentially contraindicated.

name: MEM

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: α-methyl analogue of escaline (DOx with 4-ethoxy). PIHKAL active 20–50 mg, longer than escaline.

routes.notes: Active 20–50 mg, duration 8–16 h

notes: PIHKAL #117. Methoxyethyl-amphetamine M.

name: Memantine

primary_targets: NMDA-receptor (PCP site, low-affinity uncompetitive open-channel blocker)

binding.tissue_or_cell: cultured rat cortical / hippocampal neurons, whole-cell patch clamp
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Voltage-dependent (Mg2+-like), use-dependent open-channel blocker. IC50 strongly voltage-dependent: ~1 μM at -70 mV.
binding.notes: Parsons et al. 1995. Key kinetic feature: fast off-rate (koff ~5 s-1) that allows escape during physiological transient glutamate release — preserves synaptic plasticity while blocking tonic pathological activation.
Rammes et al. 2001 — non-competitive antagonism, potency similar to NMDA. May contribute to anti-emetic effect and tolerability.
Aracava et al. 2005 — memantine has higher affinity for alpha7 nAChR than for NMDA at resting potentials, an under-appreciated off-target.
Peeters et al. — moderate-affinity sigma-1 agonist; minor contribution at therapeutic doses.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Preferential block of extrasynaptic over synaptic NMDA receptors (Xia et al. 2010, J Neurosci 30:11246) — this selectivity arises from extrasynaptic NMDARs being more frequently activated by low ambient glutamate, allowing memantine's voltage- and use-dependent block to accumulate. Extrasynaptic NMDA activation drives pro-apoptotic CREB shutoff signalling, while synaptic NMDA activation drives pro-survival CREB activation; memantine's bias preserves the latter — the molecular basis for therapeutic utility in Alzheimer's.

routes.notes: F ~100%, Tmax 3-8 h, t1/2 60-80 h (mean ~70 h), Vd 9-11 L/kg, plasma protein binding ~45%. Linear PK. ~48% excreted unchanged in urine.

metabolism.notes: Three minor inactive metabolites; CYP450 system is NOT meaningfully involved in clearance — clinically negligible CYP-mediated DDI risk.
Excreted via OCT2/MATE-mediated tubular secretion; pH-dependent reabsorption. Urinary alkalinisation (e.g., heavy sodium bicarbonate) decreases clearance up to 9-fold.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Urinary pH ↑ → ↑ tubular reabsorption of protonated memantine
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Up to 9-fold increase in memantine plasma concentrations

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic — additive NMDA channel block + OCT2 competition
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased risk of CNS toxicity; combination not recommended.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Polymorphisms in OCT2/MATE1 affect tubular secretion; clinically modest. CYP genotype is largely irrelevant given negligible hepatic metabolism.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: No clinically meaningful tolerance to therapeutic effect over years in dementia trials; minimal recreational tolerance reported.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No physical withdrawal documented in therapeutic use. Abrupt discontinuation in dementia patients may produce cognitive rebound over weeks consistent with loss of NMDA blockade.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: May contribute to cognitive side-effects; under investigation.
Possibly contributes to low emetogenic profile vs other NMDA antagonists.
Weak D2 affinity reported; not clinically significant at therapeutic doses.

demographic_differences.sex: Women have ~45% higher AUC at same mg dose (lower body weight + lower renal clearance per kg).
demographic_differences.age: Elderly (target population) have reduced renal function — dose-adjust in CrCl 5-29 mL/min to 5 mg BID.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal impairment markedly increases exposure: mean AUC ↑ 4%, 60%, 115% in mild, moderate, severe renal impairment respectively. t1/2 increases up to 95%. Hepatic impairment: negligible effect (no CYP dependence).

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative human NMDA receptor occupancy at therapeutic vs recreational dose ranges (no PET ligand routine for this)
notes: The defining mechanism is fast-off-rate, voltage-dependent open-channel block (~5 s-1 koff vs ~0.01 s-1 for MK-801). This kinetic distinction — not affinity — is what makes memantine safe for chronic Alzheimer's therapy: it cleared from the channel rapidly enough during transient synaptic glutamate spikes to preserve LTP, while still accumulating block during the sustained low-glutamate elevation of neurodegeneration. The pharmacology is otherwise close to amantadine but with ~10x higher NMDA potency.

name: MEN 10376
data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor
notes: Novel or obscure tryptamine without published controlled pharmacology. Effects unknown in humans.

name: Mephedrone

binding.notes: Baumann 2012 Neuropsychopharmacology — racemic mephedrone, EC50 DA release 51 nM (similar to MDMA at NE but stronger at DA)
Baumann 2012 — EC50 NE release 58 nM
Baumann 2012 — EC50 5-HT release 122 nM; DAT/SERT release ratio ~2.4 = MDMA-like balanced profile
Simmler 2013 — weak rat TAAR1 partial agonist, but NEGLIGIBLE human TAAR1 activity (EC50 >10 μM hTAAR1, consistent with cathinone class)
Simmler 2016 — no functional activation at hTAAR1 up to 30 μM; this is the class-defining loss of TAAR1 brake

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: As a non-selective DAT/NET/SERT substrate, mephedrone drives reverse transport at all three transporters with roughly balanced potency (DA:5-HT EC50 ~1:2.4), more MDMA-like than methamphetamine-like. Unlike amphetamines, NO TAAR1 activation in humans means no PKA/PKC feedback inhibition of DAT firing — combined with rapid clearance (t1/2 ~2 h) this produces the characteristic compulsive-redosing pattern.

routes.subject_demographics: Recreational stimulant users, mostly male, age 21-32, supervised lab study
routes.notes: Olesti 2019 Clin Pharmacol Ther — single oral dose 50/100/150/200 mg, dose-linear PK; Cmax ~84 ng/mL at 150 mg, t1/2 2.15 h. CYP2D6 PMs had 2-3× higher mephedrone Cmax and AUC.
Papaseit 2020 J Anal Toxicol — controlled IN 100 mg; faster onset than oral but similar t1/2

concentration_effect.notes: Olesti 2019 — subjective and cardiovascular effects scaled linearly with plasma mephedrone

metabolism.notes: Primary N-demethylation by CYP2D6; CYP2D6 PMs show 2-3× higher parent AUC and worse adverse effects
Pozo 2017 AAPS J — most abundant urinary metabolite; tolyl methyl oxidized to carboxylic acid
Luethi 2021 Front Pharmacol — β-OH metabolite still functions as DAT/SERT substrate

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Predicted to phenocopy CYP2D6 PM status — 2-3× higher mephedrone exposure; case reports of severe toxicity in users co-using SSRIs

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs (~7% of Europeans) and IMs show 2-3× higher mephedrone Cmax/AUC and substantially greater cardiovascular and subjective effects. This is the single most important pharmacogenetic factor for mephedrone toxicity.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: DAT/SERT downregulation reported after repeated mephedrone in rats; no human data on receptor occupancy
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Anhedonia, dysphoria, fatigue, cognitive slowing; onset 6-24 h after binge; peak 2-4 days; partial resolution over weeks. No physical dependence syndrome.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Minimal direct hERG block (~9% inhibition at 30 μM); cardiotoxicity is sympathomimetic, not channel-mediated

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: CYP2D6 PM status dominates — see pharmacogenetics

data_gaps_remaining: definitive hERG IC50 from manual patch clamp at therapeutic concentrations
biased agonism (not applicable — not a GPCR ligand)
notes: Mephedrone is one of the best-characterized cathinones with controlled human PK, CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics, and full transporter profiles. The class-defining absence of hTAAR1 agonism (versus MDMA which is a hTAAR1 agonist) likely explains its higher compulsive-use signal.

name: Mephenmetrazine
notes: Duplicate/synonym for 4-Methylphenmetrazine — see canonical record.

name: Mescaline

binding.notes: Range across labs Ki 550–17,400 nM, EC50 88–30,200 nM, Emax 33–107%

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Classical psychedelic. 5-HT2A partial agonist with significant biased agonism at 5-HT2C. NOT amphetamine-like despite having an aminoethyl side chain (no α-methyl).

routes.notes: Recent re-analysis (2020s) gives t1/2 ~3.6 h (range 2.6–5.3 h), correcting earlier 6 h estimate. Onset 0.5–0.9 h; Tmax 1.6–2.3 h.

metabolism.notes: Mescaline is a poor substrate of purified human MAO; deamination pathway unclear. Not significantly metabolised by CYP2D6.

notes: Mescaline is a phenethylamine but a classical psychedelic, not a stimulant — included here because of phenethylamine class membership. Active metabolite of peyote (Lophophora williamsii).

name: Mesyl Sal B

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 transiently expressing FLAG-His6-tagged human KOR
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Ki = 0.59 ± 0.21 nM — described as the most potent KOR agonist identified to date (Yan et al. 2009, Biochemistry).
binding.notes: Note: literature commonly conflates 'Mesyl Sal B' (RB-64 / 22-methylsulfonyl Sal B) with 22-thiocyanatosalvinorin A; the latter is more rigorously what RB-64 refers to. They are closely related C-22 (oxymethylene-substituted Sal B) probes from the Roth lab. Treat the input compound name 'Mesyl Sal B / RB-64' as the irreversible covalent-tethered Roth probe.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Ki >> 10,000 nM — no significant MOR/DOR activity

biased_agonism.interpretation: Bias factor 96 toward G-protein over β-arrestin-2 (relative to Sal A as the unbiased reference). One of the most strongly G-protein-biased KOR agonists ever reported — the prototype for the 'Gi-biased KOR agonist = non-dysphoric analgesic' hypothesis. In vivo: analgesic without the locomotor incoordination seen with unbiased KOR agonists; retains aversion (so Gi bias does not fully eliminate dysphoria).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Strong Gαi/o-mediated cAMP inhibition and GIRK activation with markedly reduced β-arrestin-2 recruitment and receptor internalisation. Irreversible (covalent) tethering to KOR via the C-22 reactive group → very long-duration KOR activation.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Reduced KOR internalisation compared to unbiased agonists — predicted to develop tolerance more slowly, though formal time-course not in literature.

notes: Roth-lab covalent KOR probe (Yan et al. 2009). Reactive C-22 (thiocyanate/methanesulfonate) group tethers irreversibly to KOR → very high apparent potency and dramatically extended duration. Landmark proof-of-concept that strongly G-protein-biased KOR agonists can be analgesic with reduced motor side-effects, but still aversive in animals — so KOR-mediated dysphoria is not fully explained by β-arrestin-2 alone.

name: META-DOB

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Positional isomer of DOB; expected reduced 5-HT2A potency from loss of 2,5-substitution.

notes: PIHKAL #122. Meta-DOB.

name: META-DOT

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Positional isomer of 2C-T-series.

notes: PIHKAL #124.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Bromo-substituted benzodiazepine, German-marketed (Talis). N-demethylation → desmethylmetaclazepam active metabolite.

name: metanephrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Inactive metabolite of adrenaline; clinical use as urinary/plasma biomarker for pheochromocytoma. Miscategorised.

notes: Catecholamine metabolite; miscategorised.

name: Metaxalone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Central muscle relaxant; specific receptor target not definitively identified. Less sedating than cyclobenzaprine; minimal anticholinergic activity.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~9 h. Food markedly increases F% (~50% Cmax increase).

notes: Mechanism truly not well-characterised.

name: Methadone

binding.notes: R-methadone is the active opioid enantiomer; ~10× higher MOR affinity than S.
Bossert 2023 — S-methadone is a MOR partial agonist with selectively reduced efficacy at MOR-Gal1R heteromer; low abuse liability.
Non-competitive NMDA antagonist; both enantiomers equipotent. Believed to contribute to efficacy in opioid-tolerant patients and neuropathic pain.
Eap 2007 — (S)-methadone blocks hERG 3.5× more potently than (R).

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: S-methadone has selectively low efficacy at this complex, which is implicated in opioid reward; this is offered as a mechanism for low abuse liability of (S)-MTD (REL-1017/esmethadone).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR Gαi cascade + non-competitive NMDA antagonism + SERT/NET reuptake inhibition. The NMDA antagonism is hypothesised to reduce opioid tolerance and treat neuropathic pain.

routes.notes: Eap 2002 — half-life highly variable (8-59 h), median ~24 h. F% high but inter-individual variability is enormous.

concentration_effect.notes: Daily methadone dose >100 mg / serum >1000 ng/mL associated with increased TdP risk.

metabolism.notes: CPIC 2024 guideline — CYP2B6 dominant; CYP3A4/5 contributes <5% by recent modelling. CYP2D6 minimal.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Precipitates methadone withdrawal in maintenance patients
↑ methadone exposure, ↑ QT risk

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2B6 *6/*6 (slow metabolisers) have ~50% higher S-methadone plasma concentrations → 4.5× increased TdP risk (Eap 2007). CPIC 2024 recommends genotype-informed dosing.

cross_tolerance: all MOR full agonists (partial — NMDA antagonism modifies cross-tolerance)
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 36-72 h, peak 6-10 d, lasts 3-6 weeks; protracted dysphoria common.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: QT prolongation, TdP, sudden cardiac death. ECG before initiation and at steady state recommended; risk ↑ above 100 mg/d.
Binds σ1; clinical relevance unclear.
Weak monoamine reuptake inhibition; theoretical serotonin syndrome risk when combined with strong serotonergics.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: slower clearance, prolonged half-life — start low, go slow.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Modest changes with renal impairment; faecal excretion compensates. Hepatic impairment: caution.

notes: Methadone half-life >> analgesic duration (4-8 h) means accumulation is the killer — overdose deaths cluster in week 1 of initiation. Rotating from morphine equivalents requires the conservative methadone-specific conversion (not linear with morphine).

name: Methallylescaline

binding.notes: Notable 5-HT2C selectivity

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Higher 5-HT2C than 5-HT2A affinity in some reports; steep dose-response.

routes.notes: 40–65 mg; duration 12–16 h; steep dose-response

notes: PIHKAL #94.

name: Methamnetamine

binding.notes: Wee/Negus dataset. Balanced SNDRA, low-nM.
Lower-potency partial agonist.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Naphthyl ring replacement of phenyl gives a balanced SNDRA with very low nM potency. PAL-287 was investigated as a stimulant-use-disorder treatment because the 5-HT release dampens DA reinforcement. Methamnetamine is the N-methyl analogue.

metabolism.notes: Aromatic hydroxylation of the naphthalene ring is a major pathway in vitro.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome risk.

notes: Triple-monoamine releaser with research-pharmacology pedigree (PAL series). No published human controlled data; very limited recreational user-base data.

name: Methamphetamine

binding.notes: Nichols/Nguyen — micromolar σ1 affinity; activation implicated in methamphetamine-induced neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurotoxicity

functional.notes: d-meth EC50 8.5–24.5 nM (range across labs); ~3× more DA-potent than d-amphetamine
5-HT release EC50 ~1 µM — modest but non-trivial, accounts for some 'rush' euphoria distinguishing meth from amph
l-meth ~50× weaker than d-meth at DAT. This is the form released as metabolite of selegiline.
Only ~2× weaker than d-meth at NET; this is why l-meth (Vicks Vapor Inhaler) has decongestant action despite minimal CNS stimulation

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methamphetamine adds two features to amphetamine pharmacology: (1) σ1 agonism, which through chaperone effects on D1, BiP/GRP78, and microglial NF-κB drives chronic-use neurotoxicity (Nguyen Pharmacol Rev 2017, doi:10.1124/pr.116.012799); (2) the N-methyl group increases lipophilicity, raising brain:plasma ratio and intracellular accumulation in DA terminals. Reactive oxygen species from cytosolic DA auto-oxidation are the proximate cause of DAT terminal degeneration (McCann 1998 PMID 9504281).

neuroimaging.finding: Chronic high-dose meth users show 24% lower striatal DAT density that persists ≥3 years after cessation
0.25 mg/kg IV meth displaces striatal raclopride ~25%, ~5× greater than oral d-amphetamine on a molar basis

routes.notes: Cook et al. — d-meth oral t1/2 9–12 h, Vd 3–4 L/kg, F 67%; intranasal F 79%; smoked F 67–90%

metabolism.notes: ~15% of meth dose appears as amphetamine in urine; useful forensic marker
Highly pH-dependent like amphetamine

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs show slightly higher meth plasma exposure and lower amphetamine metabolite; small clinical effect.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Vesicular DA depletion — substrate of contributing to cytosolic DA → ROS → terminal neurotoxicity

notes: Listed entry is racemic; clinical/illicit material is overwhelmingly d-meth. d-meth is ~3× more DA-potent than d-amphetamine; this and the σ1 component drive its higher abuse potential and chronic neurotoxicity profile.

name: Methaqualone

primary_targets: GABA-A (transmembrane β+/α- intersubunit site; etomidate-like pocket)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Hammer et al. 2015 — methaqualone PAM at α1,2,3,5β2,3γ2S with EC50 ~1-10 μM. Diverse functionalities at α4,6β1,2,3δ subtypes ranging from inactive → negative AM → positive AM → super-agonist.
binding.notes: Binding site distinct from BZ and barbiturate sites — overlaps with etomidate/propofol intersubunit transmembrane site. Crystal structure: methaqualone widens TM2 ion-conducting pore.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: GABA-A PAM at the propofol/etomidate pocket. Quinazolinone scaffold inserts deeper into subunit interface than BZ-site ligands.

routes.notes: t1/2 20-60 h. Extensive hepatic hydroxylation (CYP3A4 likely). Lipophilic, large Vd.

notes: Hammer 2015 (Mol Pharmacol) is the definitive modern characterisation. The etomidate-site binding distinguishes it from BZ and barbiturate-site modulators.

name: Methcathinone

binding.notes: Rothman 2003 — S-(-)-methcathinone is the eutomer; DA release potency similar to methamphetamine
DA/5-HT selectivity ~35 — methamphetamine-like profile; minimal 5-HT release

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Catecholamine-selective substrate releaser, the cathinone analogue of methamphetamine. Lower CNS penetration than methamphetamine (~10×) due to β-keto polarity.

routes.notes: Estimated t1/2 ~4 h from forensic data

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: By analogy with mephedrone, PMs likely have elevated exposure

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Stimulant withdrawal; severe psychosis with chronic use (especially Russian 'jeff' epidemics from KMnO4-contaminated synthesis with manganese parkinsonism)

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Street methcathinone from KMnO4-mediated synthesis is contaminated with Mn²⁺, causing irreversible extrapyramidal syndrome (manganese parkinsonism) in chronic users
off_targets.notes: Distinct from intrinsic methcathinone pharmacology — a synthesis-contaminant toxicity

notes: Methcathinone is the cathinone analogue of methamphetamine. Critical clinical caveat: Russian/Eastern European users of street 'jeff' present with manganese parkinsonism from KMnO4 synthesis contamination, NOT from methcathinone itself.

name: Methedrone

functional.notes: SERT-preferring; β-keto + para-methoxy combination shifts to serotonergic

routes.notes: Reported t1/2 ~26 h — unusually long for a cathinone

notes: β-keto cathinone with para-methoxy. Caused fatal serotonin-syndrome poisonings in Sweden 2010. Note: belongs to cathinone group, may be better categorised there.

name: Methoxetamine

binding.notes: Roth 2013 reported 259 ± 76 nM (some texts cite 337). ~3× higher NMDA affinity than ketamine.
S-(+)-MXE Ki 320 nM, R-(-)-MXE Ki 510 nM. Confirmed functional SERT inhibitor (Hondebrink 2017).
Ki >10,000 nM — surprisingly weak vs 3-MeO-PCP (42 nM)

functional.notes: Botanas 2021: MXE behavioral effects partially blocked by 5-HT2 antagonists; suggests indirect 5-HT2 activation via SERT block

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: NMDA blockade dominant; SERT inhibition contributes serotonergic component that may underlie the longer-duration and 'antidepressant-like' subjective profile vs ketamine.

routes.notes: Hill 2012; t½ ~3-6 h

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Cravings, anxiety, depression after heavy use; case reports of dependence syndrome

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Lower-reported cystitis incidence than ketamine but case reports exist

notes: Most-studied of the post-2010 RC dissociatives. Combination of high-affinity NMDA blockade (Ki 259 nM) + SERT inhibition (Ki 481 nM) is the canonical 2'-oxo + 3-methoxy + N-ethyl pharmacophore. Designed by Lee 2010 (UK patent) as a putative analgesic.

name: Methoxmetamine
notes: N-methyl analogue of MXE (N-methyl instead of N-ethyl). Predicted similar NMDA affinity (200-400 nM) and SERT activity but no published binding data.

name: Methoxphenidine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Tris-HCl, low-Mg2+; Wallach et al. methodology.
binding.notes: ~2-fold lower affinity than diphenidine; consistent with users reporting needing higher MXP than DPH dose.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Voltage- and use-dependent NMDA channel block. The 2-methoxy substitution reduces affinity vs diphenidine but does not fundamentally change the binding pose. The 3-methoxy isomer (3-MeO-PCP-like geometry) is substantially more potent (Ki 19 nM); the 4-methoxy isomer collapses to Ki 461 nM — a steep SAR demonstrating the importance of meta-substitution on the aryl ring for PCP-site engagement.

routes.notes: Postmortem blood concentrations: case 1 femoral 24.0 mg/L; case 2 femoral 606 μg/L; case 3 not detailed. No controlled human PK study published. Hydroxy-2-MXP on piperidine ring is the primary urinary metabolite.

metabolism.notes: Geyer et al. forensic toxicology — metabolites identified in postmortem urine.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Anecdotal rapid tolerance; cross-tolerance to ketamine reported.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Moderate affinity reported in Wallach screen.

data_gaps_remaining: No information on isomeric purity of street samples (2-MXP vs 3-MXP — pharmacologically very different)
notes: Multiple confirmed fatalities (Elliott et al. JAT 2015; Hofer et al. Clin Toxicol 2015). The 2-MeO regiochemistry is less potent than the 3-MeO isomer (Wallach 2016), which is forensically important because street 'MXP' samples have on rare occasions been mis-sold or contaminated with the more potent 3-MeO isomer with predictable consequences. The compound has comparatively narrow therapeutic index — postmortem blood concentrations of fatalities (606 μg/L to 24 mg/L) overlap with concentrations reported in survivors after recreational use (~200-500 μg/L), suggesting toxicokinetic variability is the main risk driver.

name: Methoxyacetyl-fentanyl

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist via Gαi/o. β-arrestin bias not reliably established for most fentalogs — fentanyl class is broadly unbiased per Ramos-González 2023.

metabolism.notes: Class-default CYP3A4 N-dealkylation pathway shared with fentanyl. Also 4-ANPP (4-anilino-N-phenethylpiperidine) from amide hydrolysis is a marker of synthesis.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased AUC, overdose risk.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inferred from fentanyl-class — no analogue-specific human data.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Classical opioid; typically shorter than morphine due to higher lipophilicity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Wooden chest syndrome — class-shared; rapid IV / smoked / IV illicit exposure.

notes: ~30% of fentanyl potency (rat ED50 0.053 mg/kg vs 0.018). Major metabolites: O-demethyl-methoxyacetylfentanyl, 4-ANPP.

name: Methylene blue

primary_targets: mitochondrial complex IV / cytochrome c oxidase (alternate electron carrier)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Ki 27 nM; IC50 ranges 70-164 nM depending on enzyme/substrate concentration
binding.notes: Ramsay et al. 2007 — confirms predicted MAO-A inhibition that explains the serotonin syndrome risk when MB is co-administered with SSRIs/SNRIs.
~80× selectivity for MAO-A over MAO-B.

functional.readout: oxygen consumption / electron transfer rescue in Complex I/III inhibited mitochondria
functional.species: various (human cell lines, rat brain mitochondria)
functional.notes: MB cycles between oxidized (MB) and reduced (MBH2/leucomethylene blue) forms, donating electrons to cytochrome c and rescuing electron transport when Complex I or III are inhibited. Effect is biphasic — low doses (0.5-4 mg/kg) enhance respiration; high doses (>10 mg/kg) inhibit.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Biphasic mitochondrial effects: low doses enhance ATP synthesis via Complex IV electron shunting and induce mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1α; high doses uncouple respiration. Inhibits soluble guanylate cyclase (basis for use in refractory vasodilatory shock) and methemoglobin reductase activity (FDA-approved for methemoglobinemia). MAO-A inhibition is potent enough at therapeutic doses to cause clinically dangerous serotonin syndrome.

neuroimaging.finding: Low-dose MB (0.5-4 mg/kg PO) in healthy humans increases task-related BOLD activity in cortex and hippocampus; correlates with improved short-term memory.

routes.notes: Oral F ~72%, terminal t½ 10-18 h, very large Vd reflecting tissue distribution especially to brain (lipophilic + cation transport). Metabolized to leucomethylene blue (active reduced form).
FDA-approved IV use for methemoglobinemia (1-2 mg/kg).

metabolism.notes: Redox cycling between MB and leucomethylene blue is the mechanistic basis for mitochondrial electron-transfer effects.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Serotonin syndrome — FDA black-box-equivalent warning. Multiple deaths reported.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: G6PD-deficient patients can develop hemolytic anemia or paradoxical methemoglobinemia from MB administration — relevant for parenteral/high-dose use.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: no formal tolerance described; MAO-A inhibition is reversible.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Used therapeutically for vasoplegia (vasodilatory shock); at high doses can cause hypertension.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: biliary + urinary excretion of metabolites; renal impairment may prolong t½.

data_gaps_remaining: concentration-effect curve for cognitive enhancement in humans
notes: MB is a POTENT reversible MAO-A inhibitor (Ki 27 nM) and this is the clinically dominant pharmacology at the doses used for cognitive enhancement (0.5-4 mg/kg). Serotonergic-drug combinations have caused fatal serotonin syndrome. The mitochondrial electron-shunt mechanism is real but biphasic — efficacy peaks at low doses and reverses at high doses.

name: methylenedioxydeschlorobupropion

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: By bupropion analogy (cathinone with tert-butyl on N at meta-chloro ring), this 'deschloro-bupropion' analogue is expected to be a DAT/NET reuptake inhibitor (cocaine-like) rather than a substrate, due to tert-butyl bulk. Methylenedioxy adds modest SERT engagement

notes: By bupropion's N-tert-butyl analogy, predicted to be reuptake inhibitor (not substrate). Bupropion itself has weak DAT/NET binding (Ki ~10 μM); this MDx analogue likely similar potency.

Reported to slow caffeine metabolism (extending caffeine t½) when co-administered, while caffeine does not alter methylliberine PK.

routes.notes: Linear PK, t½ ~1.5 h, onset 15-60 min — faster and shorter than caffeine.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Methylliberine prolongs caffeine half-life; caffeine does not alter methylliberine PK.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: adenosine receptor upregulation similar to caffeine plausible but unstudied

data_gaps_remaining: receptor binding Ki at A1, A2A
notes: Marketed as 'fast caffeine alternative' (Dynamine). Plausible adenosine antagonism but binding affinities have not been quantitatively published.

name: Methylmethaqualone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methaqualone analog with 4'-methyl on 3-aryl ring. Reportedly more convulsant than parent (additional Na+ channel or excitatory effect). Quinazolinone.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Reported pro-convulsant in animals.

notes: Reported convulsant liability.

name: Methylone

binding.notes: Baumann 2012 — methylone is ~2× less potent than mephedrone at DA release
DA:5-HT release ratio ~0.5 — slightly SERT-leaning, MDMA-like balanced entactogen profile
Simmler 2016 — methylone shows negligible activation at hTAAR1 (cathinone class effect); rat TAAR1 EC50 ~2 μM partial agonist

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Substrate-type releaser at DAT/NET/SERT, mechanistically similar to MDMA but with weaker potency at all three transporters and significantly reduced VMAT2 disruption. The result is a shorter, more stimulating, less empathogenic profile.

routes.subject_demographics: 12 healthy male volunteers, mean 23 y, recreational psychostimulant users
routes.notes: Poyatos/Papaseit 2022 IJMS — dose-linear across 50–200 mg; 200 mg: Cmax 604 ng/mL, t1/2 6.4 h, Tmax 2 h. Methylone PK is linear (unlike MDMA which auto-inhibits CYP2D6).

metabolism.notes: HMMC is the major urinary metabolite (Cmax 10-14× lower than parent, AUC 21-29× lower); pathway parallels MDMA but methylone does NOT autoinhibit CYP2D6, hence linear PK

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Less pronounced than MDMA because methylone does not autoinhibit CYP2D6; PM status expected to elevate AUC by 30-50% but not produce the runaway accumulation seen with repeat MDMA dosing

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild post-acute dysphoria similar to MDMA 'Tuesday blues'; binge-pattern users report 2-4 day low mood and serotonergic depletion symptoms

demographic_differences.sex: Only male subjects in published PK; sex differences not characterized

notes: Methylone is being developed as MDMA-alternative psychotherapy adjunct (Transcend Therapeutics); linear PK and lack of CYP2D6 autoinhibition is a clinical advantage over MDMA. 5-HT2B activity not yet quantified — important to characterize given chronic-use proposal.

name: Methylphenidate

binding.notes: Pan et al. 1994; racemic d,l-threo-MPH.
Higher NET than DAT affinity in vitro.
Essentially inactive at SERT.

functional.notes: Volkow et al. — 0.5 mg/kg oral methylphenidate produces >50% striatal DAT occupancy in adults.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cocaine-like fast-binding DAT inhibitor; NET inhibition in PFC drives prefrontal DA increase (since PFC DA clearance is NET-dominated). Dexmethylphenidate (d-threo) is the eutomer ~10x more potent than l-threo.

neuroimaging.finding: Oral 0.5 mg/kg occupies ~60% of striatal DAT and ~70-80% of NET in thalamus

routes.notes: d-MPH bioavailability 22±8%, l-MPH only 5±3% due to first-pass CES1 hydrolysis; protein binding 10-33%.

metabolism.notes: Stereoselective: l-MPH cleared 5-10x faster than d-MPH. CES1 G143E (rs71647871, ~3% allele freq) reduces clearance, increases AUC.
Transesterification — analogous to cocaethylene; increases d-MPH exposure and euphoria.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased d-MPH AUC, ethylphenidate formation, enhanced euphoria

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CES1 G143E (rs71647871) carriers have 2-7x higher MPH AUC; CES1 SNPs explain ~15-30% of interindividual PK variation.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Limited downregulation at therapeutic doses; recreational IV dosing produces cocaine-like tolerance over weeks
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild dysphoria, fatigue, sleep rebound on discontinuation; no severe physical withdrawal

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Weak partial 5-HT1A agonism at high doses possibly contributes to mood effects

demographic_differences.age: Children clear MPH faster per kg than adults; CES1 expression increases through childhood
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment minor effect (CES1 expression preserved in mild cirrhosis)

notes: Cocaine-like kinetic class (fast binding/dissociation) despite differing structure; therapeutic oral dosing achieves slower brain pharmacokinetics, which is thought to reduce abuse liability vs IV/insufflated routes.

notes: Used in former USSR as oral radioprotectant for cosmonauts and radiologists (50 mg).

name: Mexedrone

binding.notes: McLaughlin et al 2017 — only weak SERT releasing activity. Inactive as DAT/NET releaser.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: β-methoxy modification of mephedrone scaffold collapses transporter activity — only weak SERT release remains, with no DA/NE release. Subjective effects in users are weak compared to mephedrone, consistent with this. Sold as a 'legal' mephedrone replacement; actually weakly active.

notes: Sold 2015+ as legal mephedrone alternative. Pharmacology disappointing; actual recreational potency may reflect contamination with active congeners.

name: MGM-15

binding.notes: Matsumoto 2014 — μ/δ dual agonist; greater hMOR and hDOR affinity than 7-OH-mitragynine.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual μ/δ Gαi full agonist with high oral bioavailability — pharmacology of an addictive opioid despite the kratom-natural-product framing.

notes: Matsumoto/Horie 2014 dual μ/δ agonist derived from 7-OH-mitragynine. Has appeared in vendor markets recently as a 'kratom alternative' but exhibits the canonical pharmacology of an addictive full opioid agonist.

name: Midazolam

binding.notes: Imidazobenzodiazepine; pH-dependent ring-opening enables water solubility at acidic pH for IV/IM formulation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Imidazobenzodiazepine PAM; preferential occupancy of α1-containing receptors at sub-sedative concentrations (associated with anterograde amnesia). Used clinically as IV/IM sedative and probe drug for CYP3A4 activity (single highest-confidence in vivo CYP3A4 phenotyping substrate).

routes.notes: Extensive first-pass (CYP3A4 in gut wall and liver).

metabolism.notes: Kronbach 1989 / Gorski review; 1-OH-midazolam ≈ 20% of parent's BZ-receptor affinity. Active metabolite contributes to clinical effect, especially in renal failure where glucuronide can accumulate.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Oral AUC increased ~16-fold; t1/2 prolonged ~3×
Oral AUC reduced >95%; renders midazolam nearly inactive orally

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP3A5 expressers (CYP3A5*1 carriers) clear midazolam ~25% faster than non-expressers. Population-level variability in CYP3A4 activity manifests as 5–10× variation in midazolam clearance — why midazolam is the gold-standard CYP3A4 probe substrate.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Tolerance develops rapidly with continuous IV infusion (days); rebound seizures reported on abrupt cessation.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Acute withdrawal on cessation of continuous infusion in ICU patients: agitation, seizures, tachycardia. Less commonly seen with single-dose use.

demographic_differences.sex: Mild — females slightly higher CL.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: CL reduced ~30%, t1/2 prolonged; neonates have very low CL (immature CYP3A).
demographic_differences.weight: Obese: increased Vd.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: prolonged t1/2 and reduced CL. Renal failure: 1-OH-midazolam glucuronide accumulates and contributes to prolonged sedation.

notes: Imidazobenzodiazepine designed for IV use — pH-dependent ring opens at pH <4 (water-soluble open form), closes at physiological pH (lipophilic active form). Massive intersubject variability in oral PK due to CYP3A4-dependent first pass.

name: Mirtazapine

binding.notes: Among the most potent H1 antagonists in clinical use — accounts for sedation, weight gain, appetite stimulation.
5-HT3 antagonism gives anti-nausea property and avoids GI side-effects typical of SSRIs.
Central α2 autoreceptor antagonism on noradrenergic neurons disinhibits NE release; heteroreceptor blockade on serotonergic terminals enhances 5-HT release. Core 'NaSSA' mechanism.
Weak muscarinic affinity → minimal anticholinergic effects.
Mirtazapine has negligible SERT/NET binding — does not directly inhibit reuptake.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: α2 antagonism increases NE release; NE acts on serotonergic cell bodies α1 to increase 5-HT cell firing; 5-HT2A/2C/3 blockade channels the released 5-HT specifically to 5-HT1A. The 'noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant' (NaSSA) mechanism.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Mirtazapine AUC ↑ 50%, Cmax ↑ 40%.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs show modestly higher mirtazapine exposure; clinically minor.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: H1 sedation tolerance develops within 1-2 weeks (paradoxically: 15 mg more sedating than 30 mg because α2 antagonism — which is alerting via NE release — emerges at higher doses)
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Generally mild; flu-like symptoms, anxiety, insomnia possible. Onset 1-3 days, duration 1-2 weeks.

demographic_differences.sex: Women have ~25% higher AUC than men.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: clearance ↓ ~40%.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Severe renal impairment: clearance ↓ ~50%.

notes: Dose-dependent sedation paradox: 15 mg is more sedating than 30 mg because at higher doses α2-mediated noradrenergic alerting offsets H1-mediated sedation. Frequent off-label use as a sleep aid uses the low end.

name: Mitragynine

binding.notes: Várfi/Kruegel 2016, JACS — Ki ~233 nM (also reported 161-700 nM across labs). Partial agonist, low intrinsic efficacy (Emax ~30-50% of DAMGO).

functional.notes: Kruegel/Majumdar 2016 — essentially no β-arrestin-2 recruitment → strongly G-protein biased.

biased_agonism.interpretation: Mitragynine is G-protein biased (recruits β-arrestin-2 essentially not at all), which is the proposed mechanism for kratom's apparently lower respiratory depression at equianalgesic doses vs morphine. The 'biased agonism = safer opioid' hypothesis is now controversial (Conibear & Kelly 2019 / doi:10.1016/j.tips.2019.04.002) — much of the safety may come from low intrinsic efficacy / partial agonism, not bias per se.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR partial Gαi without β-arrestin-2; some α2-adrenergic and weak 5-HT2 activity contribute to subjective profile. CYP3A4 converts mitragynine to 7-hydroxymitragynine in vivo — 7-OH-MG is the dominant pharmacologically active species after oral kratom (Kruegel 2019).

routes.notes: Trakulsrichai 2015 — Tmax 0.83 h, t½ 23 h (range 9-43 h, dose-dependent). Cmax dose-dependent.
Huestis 2024 — t½ 42.9 h after high single dose, 61 h after multiple dosing.

metabolism.notes: Kruegel 2019 — CYP3A4 generates 7-OH-MG in vivo; 7-OH-MG is the dominant analgesic species after oral kratom.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Tanna 2024 — itraconazole ↑ mitragynine AUC ~3× and reduces 7-OH-MG (less bioactivation).
Mitragynine inhibits CYP2D6 (IC50 0.45 mM in HLM); clinical relevance modest.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP3A inhibition reduces 7-OH-MG formation and may reduce kratom's opioid effects; OPRM1 sensitivity applies to the MOR component.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild-moderate opioid withdrawal — rhinorrhoea, myalgia, anxiety, restlessness, insomnia; usually milder and shorter than full agonists but well-documented (10-15% of chronic users meet DSM criteria).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Some in vitro hERG block at supratherapeutic concentrations; rare QT signal in case reports.

data_gaps_remaining: definitive biased-agonism quantification in matched-lab conditions
notes: Mitragynine is a partial MOR agonist with G-protein bias, but in vivo most of kratom's opioid effect after oral dosing comes from CYP3A4-derived 7-hydroxymitragynine, which is a near-full MOR agonist (Kruegel 2019).

name: Moclobemide

binding.notes: Reversible competitive MAO-A inhibitor (RIMA). Selectivity ratio MAO-A:MAO-B ~10:1 in vitro, higher in vivo because the reversibility means MAO-B remains available.

name: Morphine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 60 min at 25 °C
binding.notes: Chen 1991. In the Volpe 2011 uniform-assay ranking of recombinant human MOR (PMC, doi:10.1016/j.yrtph.2010.12.007) morphine fell in the Ki=1-100 nM bin.

binding.tissue_or_cell: CHO membranes expressing recombinant human MOR
binding.notes: Volpe et al. 2011 — morphine classified in Ki = 1–100 nM bin; uniform-assay re-ranking.

functional.notes: Morphine recruits β-arrestin-2 with intermediate efficacy compared with DAMGO; this is the comparator against which 'G-protein biased' opioids (TRV130, mitragynines) are normalised.

biased_agonism.interpretation: Morphine is the canonical reference compound used to define β-arrestin-2 over-recruitment liability; some analyses place it as marginally arrestin-biased relative to DAMGO, but the 'biased agonism rescues respiratory depression' hypothesis (originating from Bohn 1999/2000, KO mice) is now contested.

receptor_oligomerisation.functional_consequence: Morphine binding at μ in μ/δ heteromer shifts pharmacology; δ-antagonists potentiate morphine analgesia and slow tolerance.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Gαi/o coupling → inhibition of adenylyl cyclase (decreased cAMP), activation of GIRK potassium channels (hyperpolarisation), inhibition of N/P/Q-type Cav channels (decreased neurotransmitter release). Repeated activation drives GRK-mediated phosphorylation, β-arrestin-2 recruitment, receptor desensitisation and internalisation (morphine internalises MOR poorly compared with DAMGO/etorphine — the 'RAVE' paradox).

neuroimaging.finding: Morphine displaces [11C]carfentanil from MOR in human striatum, thalamus, and cingulate cortex; displacement correlates with analgesic and euphoric ratings.

routes.notes: F% ranges 20-40% due to high first-pass UGT2B7 glucuronidation; oral AUC ratios M3G:morphine ≈ 30:1, M6G:morphine ≈ 5:1.

metabolism.notes: M3G has been implicated in opioid-induced hyperalgesia/neuroexcitation (TLR4) but is not an MOR agonist.
M6G accumulates in renal failure → prolonged sedation/respiratory depression. Penetrates BBB poorly but acts at MOR with higher intrinsic potency than parent.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: decreased morphine AUC; rare loss of analgesia

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: OPRM1 118G carriers show ~2x lower brain MOR binding potential, need ~30% more morphine for the same analgesia, but are paradoxically protected against morphine-induced respiratory depression (OR 5.6 for AA vs G-carriers). UGT2B7*2 alters M6G/M3G ratio. COMT Val158Met affects pain processing and morphine requirement.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Receptor internalisation by morphine is paradoxically weaker than DAMGO; tolerance is driven more by signalling adaptation than receptor loss. Functional desensitisation occurs over days.
cross_tolerance: all MOR full agonists (heroin, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl)
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 6-12 h after last dose; peak 36-72 h; lasts 5-10 days. Symptoms: rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, mydriasis, piloerection, myalgia, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, autonomic hyperactivity, dysphoria.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Proposed mechanism for opioid-induced hyperalgesia; clinical importance debated.

demographic_differences.sex: Women report stronger analgesia from morphine at equivalent plasma concentrations; mechanism likely receptor sensitivity rather than PK.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly (>65) have ~50% reduced clearance and higher Cmax; reduce dose 25-50%.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal failure: M6G/M3G accumulate dramatically → reduce dose, lengthen interval, or switch to hydromorphone/fentanyl.

data_gaps_remaining: definitive human cloned MOR Ki measured in same lab as comparators
notes: Morphine is the reference opioid; all relative potencies in clinical use are anchored to it.

name: Myristicin

binding.notes: Weak MAO inhibitor — lacks basic nitrogen typical of MAOIs, so the activity is mild. Probably contributes to nutmeg's monoaminergic effects.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Itself an aromatic ether with no primary amine — not a classical entactogen. Hypothesised to be metabolised in humans to MMDA (3-methoxy-4,5-MDA) via an aminotransferase/CYP-mediated process that adds an amine to the allyl side chain — this proposed amphetamine metabolite would then act on 5-HT2A. The metabolic conversion has been demonstrated in rodent in vitro systems but the in vivo human conversion is debated and quantitatively small. Nutmeg's psychoactivity probably stems from a combination of weak MAO inhibition, slow generation of trace amphetamine metabolites, and CNS effects of other constituents (elemicin, safrole).

routes.notes: Onset of nutmeg intoxication 3-8 hours; duration 24-48 h. Pharmacokinetics dominated by extensive first-pass metabolism.

metabolism.notes: Aminotransferase-mediated formation of 3-methoxy-4,5-MDA in rodents. Quantitative role in humans unclear.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Additive risk.

notes: Nutmeg primary aromatic ether. Not a true entactogen — included in this group because of the methylenedioxy ring. Psychoactivity is delayed (3-8 h onset) and dysphoric/deliriant rather than empathogenic.

name: Nicotine

binding.notes: Reference Ki ~1 nM at α4β2 — the high-affinity neuronal nicotinic target.
~770× lower affinity than α4β2 but still functionally activated at smoked-tobacco brain concentrations.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Activates pre-synaptic α4β2/α6β2 nAChRs on VTA dopamine neurons → mesolimbic DA release → reinforcement. Rapid desensitization explains tolerance and the cycle of repeated dosing. α7 activation in hippocampus contributes to cognitive enhancement and sensory gating.

routes.notes: Smoked nicotine reaches brain in 7-19 s (fastest of any nicotine route).
Buccal absorption; first-pass metabolism reduces F.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased clearance of caffeine, clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline in smokers

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2A6 slow metabolizers (e.g., *4, *9, *17 variants) have prolonged nicotine t½, lower smoking quantity, and reduced cessation success on nicotine replacement. Common in East Asian populations.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: nAChR UPREGULATION (not down) with chronic exposure — opposite of most agonist classes. Reverses over weeks of abstinence.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 4-24 h, peak 2-3 days, duration 2-4 weeks. Irritability, anxiety, dysphoria, concentration impairment, increased appetite, cravings.

demographic_differences.sex: Women clear nicotine ~10-15% faster than men; estrogen induces CYP2A6. Oral contraceptives further increase clearance.

notes: Despite being categorized as 'nootropic' in this dataset, nicotine is a Schedule-equivalent abuse-potential alkaloid with high addiction liability. Pure nicotine without combustion products still produces dependence, cardiovascular effects, and adolescent neurodevelopmental harm. The cognitive enhancement is real but modest and largely a withdrawal-relief phenomenon in dependent users.
