pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cl- channel potentiation via GABA-A allostery.

routes.notes: t1/2 16.5–48 h; ~29 h young, ~40 h elderly

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-A subunit downregulation within days; benzodiazepine cross-tolerance is full
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Anxiety, insomnia, tremor, seizures (10–14 day taper recommended)

demographic_differences.age: Elderly have ~40 h t1/2 vs 29 h in younger
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment prolongs t1/2

notes: Class-misfit — benzodiazepine, not a phenethylamine psychedelic.

name: Nitrazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Nitro-substituted triazolobenzodiazepine; designer benzo with potency between nitrazepam and clonazolam.

notes: Designer benzo with combined triazolo + nitro features.

name: Nitrous

binding.tissue_or_cell: cultured rat hippocampal neurons; Xenopus oocytes expressing NR1/NR2 subunits
binding.radioligand_or_probe: Whole-cell NMDA currents; inhibition >50% at 80% atm N2O at -60 mV
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Non-competitive antagonism at the channel; molecular site unresolved. Inhibits NMDA receptor function across NR2A-D subunits roughly equally.
binding.notes: Jevtović-Todorović et al. 1998 — landmark paper showing N2O is an NMDA antagonist, neuroprotectant against NMDA-evoked toxicity, and (paradoxically) Olney-lesion-positive at high concentrations.

binding.action: indirect agonist via endogenous enkephalin/dynorphin release in periaqueductal grey (PAG)
binding.radioligand_or_probe: Microdialysis of enkephalin / antinociception blockade by naloxone
binding.notes: N2O analgesia is blocked by naloxone; mechanism is N2O-induced release of endogenous opioid peptides that activate mu-opioid receptors on GABAergic interneurons in PAG, disinhibiting descending bulbospinal noradrenergic neurons. The descending noradrenergic system mediates analgesia via spinal α2-adrenergic receptors.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual mechanism: (1) NMDA channel blockade driving rapid-onset dissociation, euphoria, and (when sustained) Olney's lesions; (2) Endogenous opioid release in PAG driving analgesia via descending noradrenergic pathways. The opioid arm explains why N2O analgesia is reversed by naloxone and why it shows cross-tolerance with morphine. Antidepressant effects (Nagele et al. 2015, 2021) likely driven by NMDA antagonism analogous to ketamine. Recent literature also implicates two-pore K+ channels (TREK-1) and modest HCN1 inhibition in anaesthetic effects.

neuroimaging.finding: N2O at sub-anesthetic concentrations produces increased BOLD in anterior cingulate cortex and posterior cingulate cortex with reduced default-mode network connectivity — pattern overlapping with ketamine.

routes.notes: Blood:gas partition coefficient 0.47 (very low — fastest equilibration of any anaesthetic gas). MAC ~104% (weak anaesthetic; cannot achieve surgical anaesthesia at 1 atm pressure as a sole agent). Onset and offset within minutes. Excreted unchanged via the lungs; <0.004% metabolised in gut by anaerobic bacteria to N2 with possible enterotoxicity in chronic users. Causes 'second gas effect' enhancing uptake of volatile anaesthetics.

metabolism.notes: N2O oxidises the cobalt(1+) of methylcobalamin to inactive cobalt(3+), permanently inactivating methionine synthase (MTR). This blocks the conversion of homocysteine to methionine, depleting S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) — required for myelin sheath maintenance. Result: subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal column demyelination), peripheral neuropathy, and macrocytic anaemia in chronic users. Effect on a single B12 molecule is irreversible — recovery requires synthesis of new MTR and replenishment of active cobalamin (B12 + methionine supplementation accelerates recovery).

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Oxidation of MeCbl Co1+ → Co3+ inactivates methionine synthase
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Megaloblastic anaemia; subacute combined degeneration of cord; sensorimotor neuropathy. Onset over weeks to months of heavy use; cases reported with chronic ~10 canister/day use.
Increased risk of bone marrow suppression and neurotoxicity.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: MTHFR C677T TT homozygotes have lower baseline methionine synthase activity and are at elevated risk of N2O-induced neurotoxicity. Hyperhomocysteinaemia-associated genetic variants compound the risk.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Rapid acute tolerance (tachyphylaxis) within a single session of repeated balloons due to brief PK exposure. Tolerance to euphoria reported in heavy users.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild psychological dependence; craving, dysphoria, occasional autonomic hyperactivity in chronic heavy users. No prominent physical withdrawal.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Contributes to anaesthetic effect.
Modest inhibition may contribute to anaesthetic and analgesic effects.

demographic_differences.age: Adolescents and young adults overrepresented in recreational use case series; rapid onset of myelopathy in heavy users <25 y.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: No meaningful effect — pulmonary excretion bypasses both.

data_gaps_remaining: Direct human in-vivo NMDA occupancy measurement
Dose-response curve for B12 inactivation in humans
notes: The outlier of this class — a gaseous, non-organic NMDA antagonist with extremely fast onset/offset (5-10 min) due to low blood-gas partition coefficient (0.47). Mechanistically dual: NMDA antagonism + endogenous opioid release in PAG (naloxone-reversible analgesia). The defining chronic harm is irreversible B12 inactivation: each oxidation of methylcobalamin's Co1+ to Co3+ is permanent, and chronic heavy use (multiple canisters/day) reliably produces subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, peripheral neuropathy, and macrocytic anaemia within months. Important harm-reduction: oral methylcobalamin supplementation does NOT prevent neurotoxicity (cobalamin keeps being inactivated); only abstinence does.

name: Nm-2-ai

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyl-2-aminoindane. Without the methylenedioxy ring, much weaker than MDAI. Pure 2-aminoindane scaffold is itself an NRI; N-methylation slightly shifts profile. Limited direct data.

notes: Aminoindane variant.

name: NMT
data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor
notes: Novel or obscure tryptamine without published controlled pharmacology. Effects unknown in humans.

name: Noctec

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Trade name for chloral hydrate.

notes: Trade name duplicate — see Chloral Hydrate.

name: Noopept

primary_targets: AMPA receptor positive modulation (via cycloprolylglycine metabolite)

functional.notes: The endogenous metabolite cyclo-Pro-Gly (cyclic prolylglycine, cPG) is a positive AMPA-receptor modulator. Noopept itself has weak direct receptor activity — most pharmacology is mediated by cPG.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Noopept is a prodrug: rapid esterase hydrolysis to the free acid, then cyclization to the endogenous dipeptide cyclo-Pro-Gly (cPG). cPG is an AMPA receptor positive modulator and TrkB activator, with documented neuroprotective and BDNF/NGF-upregulating effects. The short plasma t½ (<90 min) of parent compound contrasts with the longer functional effect, consistent with active metabolite mediation.

routes.notes: Parent t½ <90 min; small-molecule (not peptide) chemistry permits oral absorption despite peptide-like structure. Russian clinical use: 10-30 mg TID.

metabolism.notes: cPG is endogenous and is the active species — explains the disconnect between short parent t½ and prolonged effect.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: no documented tolerance

data_gaps_remaining: controlled human cognitive trials outside Russia
direct receptor binding at clinically relevant concentrations
notes: Russian-developed and -approved (Noopept brand) for cognitive impairment of vascular origin. Often miscategorized as a racetam — it is a glycyl-proline dipeptide ester, not a 2-oxopyrrolidine. Active species in vivo is cyclo-Pro-Gly.

name: norbaeocystin

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dephosphorylates to 4-HT (no methyls); peripheral, no HTR in mice — like norpsilocin, BBB-limited

data_gaps_remaining: any quantitative receptor data on 4-HT itself
notes: Glatfelter 2022 SAR: removing both N-methyls eliminates psychedelic activity in mice.

name: Nordazepam

binding.notes: Comparable affinity to diazepam; the long-acting backbone of diazepam, prazepam, clorazepate, halazepam metabolism.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Active common metabolite of multiple parent benzos; the long t1/2 (50–100 h) of nordazepam dominates pharmacology on chronic dosing of diazepam, clorazepate, prazepam, etc.

routes.notes: t1/2 50–100 h; accumulates substantially on chronic dosing.

metabolism.notes: 3-hydroxylation → oxazepam → UGT2B15 glucuronidation.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild due to very long t1/2 (acts as self-tapering).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked accumulation; substantial CL reduction.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: prolonged t1/2.

notes: Marketed alone in France/Italy (Nordaz). Also the active metabolite of diazepam, clorazepate, prazepam, halazepam, medazepam, ketazolam — anything that eventually demethylates to a 1,4-benzodiazepin-2-one without N1 substituent.

name: norepinephrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous catecholamine + clinical vasopressor. NOT a GABAergic depressant — miscategorised.

notes: Endogenous; miscategorised.

name: Norflurazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-desalkylflurazepam = norflurazepam. Long-acting active metabolite of flurazepam and quazepam; sold as a designer benzo. t1/2 47–150 h.

notes: Identical to N-desalkylflurazepam. Active metabolite of flurazepam (Dalmane) and quazepam (Doral).

name: Norketamine

binding.notes: Ebert 1997. S-norketamine Ki ~1700 nM; R-norketamine Ki ~13,000 nM. About 3× less potent than parent ketamine at NMDA. After oral ketamine, norketamine plasma >> ketamine plasma (ratio ~6:1) — major contributor to oral PD.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Same use-dependent NMDA channel block as parent. Higher norketamine/ketamine ratio with oral route makes norketamine a major active species in oral ketamine PD.

routes.notes: Norketamine forms via first-pass; plasma half-life ~5-6 h, longer than parent ketamine

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2B6 PMs show prolonged norketamine exposure

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Proposed primary mediator of ketamine cystitis in chronic users

notes: Tag 'no-human-data' is wrong — norketamine is detected in every human ketamine PK study; it's an active metabolite, not a research chemical.

name: normetanephrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Inactive metabolite of noradrenaline; clinical biomarker for pheochromocytoma. Miscategorised.

notes: Catecholamine metabolite; miscategorised.

name: norpsilocin

binding.notes: Sherwood/Glatfelter 2022: norpsilocin Ki ~13 nM; ~2× higher 5-HT2A affinity than psilocin in same assay; full Emax

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: More potent than psilocin in vitro but does not produce HTR in mice — Glatfelter 2022/2025 demonstrate poor BBB penetration due to secondary amine + 4-OH log-D

notes: Critical SAR finding: N-methyl removal increases potency but kills CNS bioavailability. Same finding for baeocystin → norpsilocin in mushrooms.

name: NSI-189

functional.readout: BrdU incorporation, neurosphere formation, neurite outgrowth
functional.notes: Stimulates adult hippocampal neurogenesis at sub-μM concentrations in vitro; molecular target unidentified despite extensive screening.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Unknown primary receptor; downstream effects include hippocampal volume increase in rodents and neurotrophic gene expression. Did not show classical antidepressant receptor binding (SERT/NET/DAT/5-HT receptors).

routes.notes: Mean t½ 17.4-20.5 h; steady-state at 96-120 h. Dose-proportional AUC across cohorts.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: no data

notes: Benzylpiperazine-aminopyridine developed by Neuralstem Inc. for MDD. Phase 2 (n=220, 40 and 80 mg vs placebo, 12 weeks) FAILED its primary MADRS endpoint, though some secondary cognition endpoints improved. Despite the marketing as a 'neurogenic antidepressant', no defined receptor target has been published. Treat as preliminary / unproven for nootropic use.

name: O-desmethyltramadol

binding.notes: Raffa 1992 — (+) enantiomer is the potent MOR agonist; ≈400× more potent than parent (+)-tramadol.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR Gαi cascade; retains tramadol-like monoamine effects but with much greater opioid contribution.

routes.notes: As metabolite of tramadol or when administered directly (desmetramadol clinical trials NCT04683926).

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Bypasses CYP2D6 phenoconversion when administered directly; OPRM1 sensitivity applies as for any MOR agonist.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Inherits tramadol's seizure liability via mono­amine reuptake inhibition.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal failure: accumulates.

data_gaps_remaining: direct human Cmax for orally administered O-DSMT alone
notes: O-DSMT is the true opioid in tramadol therapy. When sold as a research chemical it bypasses CYP2D6 phenoconversion, making dosing more predictable but eliminating tramadol's 'self-limiting' poor-metaboliser safety margin.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 2'-oxo (ketone) analogue of PCP. The β-keto group restricts conformation similar to ketamine. By Abelian 2024 SAR analysis, 2'-oxo substitution shifts subjective profile toward 'heavier/holier' character vs non-keto PCP — possibly via preferential occupation of one of the two PCP-site binding poses (Zhang 2021).

notes: Hybrid of PCP scaffold + ketamine-style β-keto. No formal binding data.

name: octopamine

functional.notes: One of four endogenous TAAR1 agonists (PEA, tyramine, octopamine, synephrine)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine; 400–2000× weaker than NE at mammalian adrenergic receptors. Does not cross BBB readily.

notes: Endogenous trace amine. Major neurotransmitter in invertebrates (analogue of NE in insects).

name: oglufanide
data_gaps_remaining: Ki at any human cloned receptor

name: Olanzapine

binding.notes: Bymaster et al. 1996 — definitive olanzapine receptor profile.
5-HT2A:D2 ratio of ~3:1 is the canonical 'atypical' fingerprint.
5-HT2C antagonism is a key driver of olanzapine-induced weight gain and metabolic syndrome.
Major contributor to sedation and weight gain.
Strong M1 antagonism. Anticholinergic effects, but also protects against EPS.
M3 antagonism on pancreatic β-cells implicated in insulin secretion impairment and type 2 diabetes risk.
Orthostatic hypotension.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 5-HT2A antagonism enhances frontal-cortex DA release while D2 blockade reduces mesolimbic DA — the classic 'atypical' separation of antipsychotic from EPS effect.

neuroimaging.finding: 10 mg/day olanzapine produces ~63% striatal D2 occupancy ([11C]-raclopride) and >85% 5-HT2A occupancy ([18F]-setoperone). 20 mg/day pushes D2 to ~80%, above which EPS risk rises sharply.
M2 muscarinic occupancy in patients on therapeutic doses ~40-60% ([123I]-IQNB).

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Olanzapine AUC ↑ ~2×; dose reduction recommended.
Smokers require ~30-40% higher dose; abrupt smoking cessation → toxicity risk.
Olanzapine AUC ↓ ~50%.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP1A2*1F induction-prone allele plus smoking → significantly lower exposure. UGT1A4 polymorphisms have modest effect.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: D2 supersensitivity may develop with chronic use → tardive dyskinesia risk (cumulative >1 year).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Cholinergic rebound (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, insomnia) due to abrupt unmasking of muscarinic activity. Dyskinesia possible.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Insulin secretion impairment → type 2 diabetes (independent of weight gain).

demographic_differences.sex: Women have ~30% lower clearance than men.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: clearance ↓ ~30%.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Minor changes.

notes: Combines highest weight-gain liability among atypicals (H1 + 5-HT2C + M3) with potent antipsychotic efficacy approaching clozapine — the classic efficacy/metabolic trade-off.

name: Opium

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Crude raw opium contains morphine 10-12% by weight (dominant analgesic alkaloid), codeine 0.5-3%, thebaine 0.5-2%, plus the smooth-muscle alkaloids papaverine and noscapine. CNS pharmacology dominated by morphine.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Same as morphine + codeine.

notes: Crude plant material; effects dominated by morphine content. Variable alkaloid content per source.

name: Org 26576

functional.readout: spatial reference memory enhancement in rats
functional.notes: 3 and 10 mg/kg enhanced spatial learning acquisition. Profile suggests low-impact AMPAkine; no convulsant signal in approved-dose ranges.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Originally Organon, later Schering-Plough then Merck (MK-8777). Phase 2 in MDD (NCT00610649) and ADHD; failed to demonstrate efficacy.

notes: Merck inherited from Schering-Plough/Organon. Failed depression Phase 2; no further development. Detailed mechanism characterization in literature is thin compared to LY/CX series.

name: ORTHO-DOT

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Positional isomer of DOT series.

notes: PIHKAL entry; minimal published data.

name: Oxazepam

binding.notes: Lower potency than diazepam; clinically used as anxiolytic with intermediate t1/2.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective benzodiazepine-site PAM; the 3-hydroxy group eliminates need for CYP-mediated metabolism — directly glucuronidated.

routes.notes: t1/2 3–21 h (mean ~8 h); slowest oral absorption of any benzo (Tmax ~2–4 h).

metabolism.notes: Court 2002 — S-isomer almost exclusively glucuronidated by UGT2B15. R-isomer uses UGT2B7 and UGT1A9.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: UGT2B15 D85Y polymorphism reduces S-oxazepam glucuronidation. Women have longer t1/2 than men.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Mild relative to short-acting benzos; preferred in elderly alcohol withdrawal.

demographic_differences.sex: Women: ~20% longer t1/2.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: preserved CL (glucuronidation not impaired).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Preferred benzo in hepatic disease (LOT: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam — no CYP metabolism).

notes: Terminal metabolite of nordazepam pathway (oxazepam is what diazepam ultimately becomes). Marketed as Serax. LOT rule.

name: Oxazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Oxazolobenzodiazepine prodrug — releases nordazepam upon gastric hydrolysis.

notes: Japanese-marketed (Serenal); prodrug.

name: oxedrine

functional.notes: Low-potency TAAR1 partial agonist

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Weak α1-selective adrenergic agonist + low-potency TAAR1 agonist. p-Synephrine (Citrus aurantium) — distinct from m-synephrine (phenylephrine) which is ~100× more potent at α1.

notes: Found in bitter orange (Citrus aurantium); common in fat-burner supplements. Very weak compared to m-synephrine (phenylephrine).

name: oxidopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Selectively taken up by DAT and NET into catecholaminergic neurons where auto-oxidation generates ROS → mitochondrial dysfunction → selective DA/NE neuron death. Standard research lesioning agent for Parkinson's disease models.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Selective dopaminergic neurotoxicity — research-only, not for human use

notes: 6-OHDA is the classic experimental neurotoxin for selective DA terminal lesions. Standard tool in Parkinson's disease animal models.

name: Oxiracetam

functional.readout: [3H]choline uptake in rat hippocampal synaptosomes after chronic dosing
functional.cell_system: hippocampal synaptosomes; 100 mg/kg/day x several days
functional.notes: Repeated 100 mg/kg PO increased HACU by 31% in hippocampus. Direct receptor binding for AMPA is essentially absent — cognitive effect is downstream of cholinergic activation.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hippocampal/cortical cholinergic activation (HACU upregulation, ACh release); modest effects on phospholipid turnover. Like piracetam, the direct molecular target remains poorly defined — the functional effects sit downstream of cholinergic tone.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Effectively none — non-metabolized renally cleared

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: renal impairment dramatically prolongs t½ (8 h → 10-68 h); dose reduction required

data_gaps_remaining: Direct receptor binding constants (essentially none exist because target is ill-defined)
notes: Approved as cognitive enhancer in Italy and parts of Asia; never in US/UK. Bioavailability 56-82% depending on study. Like piracetam, the molecular target is essentially unknown — the consensus 'mechanism' is downstream cholinergic activation.

name: Oxycodone

binding.notes: Volpe 2011 uniform assay; ~15× weaker than morphine at hMOR but oral F% and BBB transport compensate.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR Gαi cascade; some active influx transport into rat brain (parental oxycodone, not metabolites, dominates CNS effect in humans).

metabolism.notes: Lalovic 2006 — major pathway; noroxycodone has negligible MOR activity.
Oxymorphone has 40-60× higher MOR affinity than oxycodone but contributes only ≈15% of analgesia in EMs because plasma exposure is low.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: ↑ oxycodone AUC 2-3×
↓ oxycodone AUC ≥85%; loss of analgesia
Reduces oxymorphone formation; small reduction in subjective effects

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 status modulates oxymorphone formation but oxycodone's parent activity means PM/UM effect is smaller than for codeine/tramadol. CYP3A inhibition is the bigger clinical lever.

demographic_differences.sex: Women: 25% higher Cmax/AUC than men.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: ~25% reduced clearance.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: 2× AUC, halve dose. Renal failure: parent accumulates.

notes: Unlike codeine/hydrocodone, oxycodone has meaningful intrinsic MOR activity, so CYP2D6 status is less critical clinically.

name: Oxymorphone

binding.notes: Volpe 2011 — sub-nanomolar, one of the highest-affinity classical opioids. 40-60× more potent than oxycodone at MOR.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: MOR Gαi.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Less CYP-dependent than oxycodone; few clinically significant pharmacogenetic interactions.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment dramatically increases oral F%; avoid in moderate-severe cirrhosis.

notes: Bypasses CYP-mediated metabolism; useful in patients on enzyme inhibitors.

notes: Iqbal lab (NY State Inst. for Basic Research) developed in rodent AD models. Five published peer-reviewed studies, all from single group, all preclinical. No human data.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cyclopyrrolone partial agonist at BZ site; developed for anxiety and panic disorder, later investigated for stuttering. Failed Phase III. Subunit-selective PAM concept similar to subtype-selective bretazenil.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Possible BZ-like, attenuated by partial agonism.

notes: Not a recreational psychedelic. Peptide hormone analogue, oncology probe, neuropeptide ligand, or unrelated approved drug; included in parent dataset due to indole or tryptophan substructure. No psychedelic pharmacology relevant.

name: Para-Methoxyamphetamine

functional.notes: Blough 2008 — PMA DA release EC50 166 nM
Potent SERT releaser; combined with MAO-A inhibition this is the killing mechanism

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: SERT release + MAO-A inhibition (IC50 300–600 nM) → massive cytosolic 5-HT accumulation → serotonin syndrome with malignant hyperthermia. Onset is delayed (4–6 h) compared to MDMA (~1 h), causing users to redose thinking they got bad ecstasy.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Lethal serotonin syndrome with hyperthermia and delayed onset

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs have markedly impaired O-demethylation and clear PMA more slowly → higher risk of fatal toxicity. Multiple PMA deaths linked to PM genotype.

notes: PMA is the canonical 'fake MDMA' killer compound. Often sold as ecstasy. Delayed onset → redosing → fatal hyperthermia. CYP2D6 PMs are at multiplied risk.

name: Parafluorobutyrfentanyl

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist via Gαi/o. β-arrestin bias not reliably established for most fentalogs — fentanyl class is broadly unbiased per Ramos-González 2023.

metabolism.notes: Class-default CYP3A4 N-dealkylation pathway shared with fentanyl. Also 4-ANPP (4-anilino-N-phenethylpiperidine) from amide hydrolysis is a marker of synthesis.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased AUC, overdose risk.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inferred from fentanyl-class — no analogue-specific human data.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Classical opioid; typically shorter than morphine due to higher lipophilicity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Wooden chest syndrome — class-shared; rapid IV / smoked / IV illicit exposure.

notes: 4-F on anilino phenyl + butyryl chain. p-F substitution typically improves potency vs butyrfentanyl (SAR).

name: Parafluorofentanyl

binding.tissue_or_cell: rat brain membrane or CHO hMOR depending on source
binding.notes: Ki 4.2 nM at human MOR (~2.5× weaker than fentanyl Ki 1.6 nM). Changes selectivity from μ>κ>δ to μ>δ≥κ. EC50 4.2 nM (electrophysiology) or 79 nM (GTPγS). In rat brain Cmax exceeds fentanyl by 1.5× per Canfield 2024 PK study.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist via Gαi/o. β-arrestin bias not reliably established for most fentalogs — fentanyl class is broadly unbiased per Ramos-González 2023.

metabolism.notes: Class-default CYP3A4 N-dealkylation pathway shared with fentanyl. Also 4-ANPP (4-anilino-N-phenethylpiperidine) from amide hydrolysis is a marker of synthesis.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increased AUC, overdose risk.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Inferred from fentanyl-class — no analogue-specific human data.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Classical opioid; typically shorter than morphine due to higher lipophilicity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Wooden chest syndrome — class-shared; rapid IV / smoked / IV illicit exposure.

notes: Ki 4.2 nM at human MOR (~2.5× weaker than fentanyl Ki 1.6 nM). Changes selectivity from μ>κ>δ to μ>δ≥κ. EC50 4.2 nM (electrophysiology) or 79 nM (GTPγS). In rat brain Cmax exceeds fentanyl by 1.5× per Canfield 2024 PK study.

name: Paroxetine

binding.notes: Highest SERT affinity of any approved SSRI. Crystal structure of paroxetine-hSERT complex resolved (Coleman et al. 2020).
Highest NET affinity of any SSRI — paroxetine functions as a weak SNRI at higher doses.
Most anticholinergic SSRI — accounts for dry mouth, constipation, cognitive blunting.
Lowest sigma-1 affinity of any SSRI.
Novel NOS inhibition (Finkel et al. 1996) — paroxetine is unique among SSRIs in this property; implicated in sexual dysfunction profile.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: SERT blockade plus NOS inhibition; NOS inhibition contributes to nitric-oxide-mediated penile/vaginal vasodilation impairment, hence the highest rate of sexual dysfunction among SSRIs.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Strongest clinical CYP2D6 inhibitor. Phenocopies CYP2D6 PM. Tamoxifen→endoxifen reduced; codeine→morphine analgesia abolished.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs show ~3-7× higher plasma paroxetine. Paradoxically, autoinhibition of CYP2D6 makes EMs behave like PMs at steady state — major source of nonlinear PK.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Worst SSRI discontinuation syndrome — short t1/2 plus muscarinic rebound. Onset within 24 h, peak day 3-5, may persist 2-4 weeks. 'Brain zaps,' dizziness, vivid dreams, irritability classic.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Sexual dysfunction (impaired NO-mediated arousal/erection).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: plasma levels ↑ 50-100%.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Severe renal/hepatic impairment: Cmax ↑ 2-7×; start at 10 mg/day.

notes: Pregnancy category D for first-trimester cardiac malformation risk — only SSRI with this designation.

name: PCP

binding.notes: Roth 2013. Range across literature 59-250 nM; PCP is reference parent compound
Ki >10,000 nM in Roth 2013
Ki >10,000 nM in direct binding; functional DA-releasing effects may involve allosteric sites

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Strong NMDA channel block + indirect dopaminergic effects via σ-receptor-mediated DA release modulation in NAc (Nishikawa 1999, doi:10.1016/S0014-2999(99)00769-4).

neuroimaging.finding: PCP produces robust prefrontal hyperactivation + thalamic disinhibition pattern used as model of schizophrenia

routes.notes: Cook 1982; t½ 1-3 days, mean ~21 h. Vd highly variable due to lipophilicity.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Tolerance develops to subjective effects within days of repeated use
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Heavy chronic users: anxiety, depression, craving, weight loss, sleep disturbance; psychotic symptoms may persist weeks

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Contributes to atypical EEG/cardiovascular profile

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Highly lipophilic → enterohepatic recycling; gastric lavage useful in overdose

notes: Originally Parke-Davis Sernyl (1956); withdrawn from human use 1965 due to emergence delirium. Schedule II in US. Roth 2013 found PCP highly selective NMDA+σ2 with weak DAT/σ1. Two binding poses at PCP site (Zhang 2021 Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03769-9) explain SAR discrepancies across the class.

name: Pemoline

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Mechanism distinct from amphetamines — primarily dopamine reuptake inhibition with mild releasing component, NO significant noradrenergic effect (PMID 9708845). Lack of peripheral sympathomimetic side effects but produces dopamine-mediated alerting.

routes.notes: t1/2 7–12 h (7 h children, 11–12 h adults); enables once-daily dosing

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Idiosyncratic fatal hepatic failure — 21+ documented cases, 13 deaths/transplants — withdrawn from US market 2005 (FDA black box 1999)

notes: Withdrawn in US 2005 due to fatal idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity. Mechanism is selective DA release/reuptake inhibition without NE component.

name: Pentazocine

binding.notes: (-)-pentazocine is the KOR analgesic; provides analgesia + dysphoria.
(+)-pentazocine is the canonical σ1 radioligand.
Weak partial MOR agonist; can precipitate withdrawal in MOR-tolerant patients.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: KOR Gαi (analgesia + dysphoria/dysphoric hallucinations); σ1 modulation (psychotomimesis); MOR partial agonism.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Atypical — opioid + dysphoria; can precipitate acute withdrawal in MOR-dependent patients.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Dysphoria, hallucinations, anxiety at higher doses — partly σ1-mediated.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: ↓ clearance.

data_gaps_remaining: quantitative Ki values from a single paper
notes: Classic mixed agonist-antagonist; will precipitate withdrawal in MOR-tolerant patients.

name: Pentedrone

binding.notes: Simmler 2014 — pentedrone IC50 ~0.5 μM at DAT; α-propyl extension converts cathinone scaffold from substrate (releaser) to a hybrid/blocker — same SAR rule as MEC vs MC
Essentially inactive at SERT; very DAT-selective

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: DAT/NET blocker with negligible SERT activity. α-Propyl extension (vs α-methyl in methcathinone) is sufficient to switch from substrate to blocker — same SAR rule as 4-MEC/butylone/pentylone.

notes: Pentedrone is the non-pyrrolidine analogue of α-PVP — same α-propyl chain, but secondary amine instead of pyrrolidine. Same DAT blocker mechanism; lower potency than α-PVP because of the loss of the rigid pyrrolidine.

name: Pentobarbital

primary_targets: GABA-A (β-subunit barbiturate pocket; direct agonist at high conc.)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Steinbach lab: pentobarbital ~50-100 μM PAM; ~500 μM direct agonist (channel opening without GABA). Plasma anaesthetic conc 20-50 μg/mL (~80-200 μM) — overlap with both modes.
binding.notes: The direct agonist mode (channel opens with no GABA) is the property that makes barbiturates more lethal than benzos — overdose produces sustained chloride conductance independent of endogenous GABA tone, → flat-line EEG, respiratory arrest.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Same site as phenobarbital but with higher direct-activation efficacy → anaesthesia. Used for euthanasia in veterinary/MAID contexts because of predictable, rapid, deep anaesthesia followed by respiratory arrest.

routes.notes: t1/2 15-50 h. Hepatic oxidation (CYP3A4, CYP2C19) → inactive metabolites. <1% renal unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Similar pan-inducer profile to phenobarbital, less studied.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Severe — seizures, delirium; treated with substitution and taper.

notes: Higher direct-channel-opening efficacy than phenobarbital explains its preferential use for anaesthesia and euthanasia.

name: Pentylone

binding.notes: Saha 2018 — pentylone is ~5× more potent than butylone at DAT; pure blocker
Partial SERT releaser (~48% efficacy); hybrid mechanism like butylone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hybrid DAT-blocker / partial-SERT-substrate. More DAT-selective than butylone — drives stimulant rather than entactogen experience.

notes: α-Propyl extension (vs methyl in methylone, ethyl in butylone) further DAT-shifts the profile; pentylone behaves more like a cocaine analogue than an MDMA analogue.

name: PEPA

functional.readout: potentiation of glutamate-evoked currents in Xenopus oocytes
functional.notes: 100 µM PEPA produces 7-fold increase in glutamate affinity at GluA3-flop. Striking selectivity: no activity at kainate (GluR6) or NMDA receptors. Preferential modulation of flop variants is opposite to cyclothiazide (flip-selective).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Sulfonamide-class AMPAkine; suppresses desensitization. Flop-selectivity is mechanistically important — flop is enriched in adult forebrain, flip in developing brain and cerebellum.

notes: Sekiguchi/Wada 1997 — third major chemical line of AMPA PAMs (after benzothiadiazines and benzamides). Research tool; never advanced clinically. The flop selectivity is a distinguishing feature exploited in some pharmacological dissection studies.

name: Pfbt

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Lacks the C2 carbomethoxy of cocaine — much weaker DAT inhibitor (~30% potency of cocaine) but retains local anaesthetic activity at sodium channels.

data_gaps_remaining: No quantitative human Ki; no human PK.
notes: Designer cocaine analog detected by EMCDDA in 2008 'bath salt' products. Primarily a sodium-channel blocker.

name: Phenazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Soviet-developed (1970s) 1,4-benzodiazepine; reported in Russian literature as 5–10× more potent than diazepam. Both phenazepam and 3-OH-phenazepam are pharmacologically active.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~60 h in healthy adults; 15–60 h range. Tmax ~4 h. Effects last up to 5 days; some case reports describe symptoms up to 3 weeks post-ingestion.

metabolism.notes: 3-OH-phenazepam is active but in humans plasma levels are very low (<3 ng/mL) — minimal contribution. Subsequently glucuronidated.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Protracted due to very long t1/2 (60+ h). Severe in chronic users — comparable to long-acting benzos but with potency that allows easy overdose.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: marked accumulation.

data_gaps_remaining: Specific subunit Ki not published; assumed non-selective like other 1,4-benzos
notes: Originally developed in USSR 1970s as an anxiolytic/anticonvulsant; emerged as a major NPS in Europe 2007 onward. Among the longest-t1/2 benzodiazepines and a notable post-mortem-finding NPS.

name: Phenazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Vendor name for clobromazolam — see that record.

notes: Duplicate of clobromazolam — recommend deduplication.

name: Phendimetrazine

binding.notes: Phendimetrazine itself blocks basal DAT current (uptake inhibitor profile); metabolite phenmetrazine induces inward current (substrate/releaser). Dissociable mechanisms.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acts as prodrug — slow CYP N-demethylation to phenmetrazine. Resulting steady phenmetrazine plasma levels avoid the peak-trough abuse-amplifying pattern of phenmetrazine itself.

notes: Slow N-demethylation provides flatter PK profile of active metabolite phenmetrazine — reduces abuse liability vs phenmetrazine alone.

name: phenelzine

binding.notes: Irreversible non-selective hydrazine MAO inhibitor; phenelzine is both substrate AND inhibitor — unusual.
Inhibition via the active metabolite β-phenylethylidenehydrazine (PEH). Raises brain GABA levels — contributes to anxiolytic effect distinct from monoamine actions.
Active metabolite raises brain alanine.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triple action: (1) irreversible MAO inhibition → 5-HT/NE/DA accumulation; (2) GABA-T inhibition → GABA accumulation (anxiolytic); (3) hydrazine moiety scavenges reactive aldehydes (acrolein, 4-HNE) — neuroprotective.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults; phenelzine PK poorly characterised in humans because of its rapid clearance and the dominance of the irreversible PD effect.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Hypertensive crisis — classic 'cheese reaction'.
Contraindicated; 2-5 week washout required.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Slow N-acetylators (NAT2 PMs) may show altered phenelzine disposition; clinical significance uncertain.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: MAO resynthesis ~2-3 weeks
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Possible delirium, psychosis, rebound depression on abrupt discontinuation.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Hydrazine moiety chelates pyridoxal phosphate; peripheral neuropathy if B6 depleted. Supplementation often recommended.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: avoid if possible.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatotoxicity reported (hydrazine compounds historically liver-toxic); contraindicated in liver impairment.

data_gaps_remaining: quantitative human PK Cmax/Vd/AUC due to rapid metabolism and self-inactivation
notes: Unique among MAOIs in possessing GABAergic and aldehyde-scavenging activity via its active metabolite PEH. The 'no-human-data' tag in source is incorrect — phenelzine has 60+ years of human clinical use (Nardil).

name: Phenethylamine

functional.notes: Bunzow/Borowsky 2001 — PEA is the prototypical TAAR1 endogenous agonist

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine; equipotent to amphetamine at DAT in vitro but orally inactive in humans up to 1.6 g (Sabelli 1986) due to rapid first-pass MAO metabolism.

routes.notes: Endogenous PEA t1/2 ~30 s in DA neurons; oral PEA t1/2 5–10 min (intestinal + hepatic MAO). Effectively orally inactive.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Markedly potentiates PEA activity

notes: The endogenous trace amine prototype. α-methylation (→ amphetamine) protects from MAO and gives oral activity.

name: Phenibut

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Zvejniece et al. 2015 — R-phenibut Ki 23 μM; S-phenibut 39 μM; baclofen 156 μM; gabapentin 50 nM. R-phenibut is the active enantiomer for α2δ binding (~7000x weaker than gabapentin but pharmacologically relevant at high mg doses).
binding.notes: Key paper. R-phenibut also produces gabapentin-like anti-nociceptive effects in mice.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Lapin 2001 review of Soviet/post-Soviet work. R-phenibut is the active enantiomer; S-phenibut shows little GABA-B activity. EC50 in μM range, Emax ~30-50% of baclofen at GABA-B.
binding.notes: Original characterization by Khaunina & Lapin 1976 (Soviet literature, untranslated).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Dual mechanism: GABA-B partial agonism (anxiolysis, sedation, prolactin/GH release) + α2δ-1 binding (anti-nociceptive, sleep). The combination produces a phenibut phenotype distinct from either pure GABA-B agonist (baclofen) or pure α2δ ligand (gabapentin). Severe withdrawal is attributed to GABA-B receptor downregulation analogous to GHB.

routes.subject_demographics: Limited Soviet PK data (single study cited in WHO 2021 pre-review). 65% excreted unchanged in urine.
routes.notes: t1/2 ~5.3 h. Reportedly only ~0.1% reaches brain. Crosses placenta and BBB. Limited modern PK literature.

metabolism.notes: ~65% urinary unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic synergy at GABA-B and respiratory centres
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Major respiratory depression / sedation risk.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-B receptor downregulation occurs within weeks of daily use (rodent and clinical inference); recovery may take weeks to months — explains the protracted withdrawal seen clinically.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12-48 h after last dose. Severe: anxiety, agitation, psychomotor activation, insomnia, hallucinations, psychosis, autonomic instability, occasionally seizures. Duration 2-4 weeks with protracted PAWS up to months. Closely resembles GHB and severe BZ withdrawal. Treatment: baclofen tapers ± benzodiazepines; multiple Baltic/Russian case reports document the syndrome (Ahuja 2018, Hardman 2019, Magsalin 2018, Joshi 2017).

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: increased CNS sensitivity; reduce dose.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal impairment likely prolongs t1/2 (predominantly renal excretion).

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative human PK; clinical brain conc-effect relationships
notes: The withdrawal syndrome described by Magsalin & Khan 2014, Hardman 2019, Ahuja 2018 in English-language case series and earlier in untranslated Baltic/Russian literature is mechanistically explained by GABA-B receptor downregulation — analogous to GHB protracted withdrawal. Phenibut is the only dual GABA-B + α2δ ligand in widespread non-medical use.

name: Phenmetrazine

binding.notes: Rothman et al. 2002 — phenmetrazine is a substrate-type releaser at DAT and NET.
Negligible serotonergic releasing activity.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Classic NE/DA releasing agent — substrate-type (enters via DAT/NET, displaces vesicular monoamines via VMAT2 inhibition or weak base trapping).

notes: Historical anorectic (Preludin); high abuse liability led to withdrawal. Prototype phenylmorpholine releaser scaffold.

name: Phenobarbital

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 or Xenopus oocytes expressing human α1β2γ2
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Phenobarbital potentiates GABA-A in 50-500 μM range; at >1 mM activates the channel directly (without GABA). Therapeutic plasma 10-40 μg/mL (43-170 μM) — overlap with potentiation range. Lower direct activation than pentobarbital (less anaesthesia, more anticonvulsant utility).
binding.notes: Reduced propensity to directly activate vs pentobarbital — explains lower anaesthetic potency but acceptable safety margin for chronic anti-epileptic use.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Binds intersubunit β+/α- pocket in GABA-A TM domain (distinct from BZ site at α/γ interface). Effects on channel: at low conc prolongs mean open time; at high conc directly opens channel without GABA (chloride conductance increase) → this direct gating mode underlies the higher lethality of barbiturates vs benzodiazepines.

routes.notes: Extraordinarily long t1/2 (~4 days) — allows once-daily dosing for epilepsy. ~25-50% renal unchanged; balance hepatic CYP2C9, CYP2C19 oxidation.

metabolism.notes: Also CYP2C19, CYP2E1 minor.

drug_interactions_pk.with: warfarin, oral contraceptives, theophylline, many AEDs
drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: Strong pan-CYP induction (CAR/PXR activation) — CYP2B6, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 induced 2-5x
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Markedly reduced exposure of CYP3A/2C substrates; classic inducer.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2C9 poor metabolisers (~5% Caucasians) have reduced clearance — risk of accumulation.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: GABA-A subunit composition shifts with chronic exposure (α1 → α4).
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 1-3 days (long t1/2 delays). Tremor, anxiety, insomnia, seizures, delirium tremens-like syndrome. Severe; mortality without treatment 5-10%. Phenobarbital itself is used for treating barbiturate, BZ, and alcohol withdrawal due to its long t1/2 and self-tapering kinetics.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Weak inhibition at supratherapeutic conc; contributes minimally to anticonvulsant effect.

demographic_differences.age: Neonates: very long t1/2 (~100 h); elderly: prolonged.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Dose-adjust for renal failure (25-50% renal); hepatic impairment may slow metabolism.

notes: Less direct GABA-A channel activation than pentobarbital → better therapeutic index for chronic epilepsy use. Classic CAR/PXR-mediated CYP inducer (predates the cloning of nuclear receptors — 'phenobarbital induction' was the prototype).

name: Phentermine

binding.notes: Critically, phentermine is INACTIVE as a ligand or agonist of 5-HT2 receptors — this is why phen-only had no valvulopathy/PPH signal while fenfluramine did

functional.notes: Rothman/Baumann 2003 — phentermine is NE-selective releaser
Weak SERT releaser — clinically negligible

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: NE/DA release without significant SERT engagement; α,α-dimethyl substitution protects from MAO and CYP and gives long half-life (~20 h).

routes.notes: FDA label / DrugBank — Cmax ~200 ng/mL at 15 mg steady state, Tmax 6 h, t1/2 20–25 h (pH-dependent; 7–8 h in acidic urine). Only ~6% metabolised; mostly excreted unchanged renally.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Hypertensive crisis — contraindicated

notes: Currently FDA-approved as Adipex-P (15/37.5 mg) and Qsymia (phentermine + topiramate). The α,α-dimethyl gives long t1/2 and pure NE-DA release without 5-HT2B activity → no valvulopathy.

name: Phentermine+Fenfluramine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Combination: phentermine provides NE/DA stimulation + anorexia; fenfluramine provides SERT release / satiety. Synergistic weight loss but fenfluramine's norfenfluramine metabolite caused valvulopathy in ~30% of long-term users; combination withdrawn 1997. Phentermine alone has no valvulopathic signal because it has no 5-HT2B activity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Valvulopathy 30%, PPH 23-fold relative risk — basis for 1997 withdrawal

notes: Historic combination, withdrawn 1997. See individual Phentermine and Fenfluramine records.

name: phenylephrine

binding.notes: Selective α1 full agonist; minimal β activity

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Direct α1 agonist (Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG → vasoconstriction). The meta-hydroxyl positions it for α1 selectivity unlike para (synephrine) which is weak.

routes.notes: Hatton 2007 meta-analysis — oral F is essentially zero (massive first-pass MAO-A); explains FDA 2023 finding that oral phenylephrine is ineffective as decongestant
IV phenylephrine is the standard pressor for spinal anaesthesia hypotension

notes: FDA advisory panel September 2023 found oral phenylephrine ineffective as nasal decongestant — massive first-pass metabolism leaves no systemic drug. IV is potent and effective.

name: phenylethanolaminium

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cation form of phenylethanolamine; miscategorised — sympathomimetic phenethylamine.

notes: Miscategorised.

name: Phenylpiracetam

binding.notes: (R)-isomer is selective DAT inhibitor

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Stimulant nootropic, DAT/NET inhibition.

routes.notes: Not extensively metabolised; ~60% biliary excretion of parent

notes: Class-misfit — stimulant nootropic, not a psychedelic.

name: Phenylpiracetam hydrazide

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Hydrazide analog of phenylpiracetam, first reported by a Russian group in 1980 as part of an anticonvulsant series. Crosses BBB well per radiolabeled biodistribution in mice. Mechanism is largely speculative; original characterization framed it as an anticonvulsant rather than a stimulant.

notes: Almost entirely a grey-market research chemical — vendor literature claims a 'longer-acting phenylpiracetam' but no peer-reviewed PK or pharmacology supports that. Original Russian work characterizes it as anticonvulsant, not stimulant. Be skeptical of any claimed potency advantage over phenylpiracetam.

name: Picamilon

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Soviet-era prodrug: GABA + niacin conjugate. Designed to cross BBB and dissociate centrally to GABA + nicotinic acid. Niacin causes cerebral vasodilation. Modest anxiolytic/cognitive effects in Russian literature; little Western validation.

routes.notes: Limited Western PK. FDA banned as supplement 2015.

notes: Soviet nootropic; mostly Russian-language data.

name: Pinazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug to nordazepam.

demographic_differences.age: longer t1/2 in elderly

notes: Class-misfit — N-propargyl-nordazepam prodrug.

name: Pipradrol

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Diphenylmethylpiperidine NDRI — STIMULANT, miscategorised here. See stimulants-DAT-inhibitors enrichment file. Pharmacology similar to methylphenidate skeleton (but without ester); duration considerably longer.

notes: Miscategorised. See stimulants file.

name: Piracetam

functional.cell_system: hippocampal slice; reported only at mM concentrations
functional.notes: Direct AMPA potentiation in vitro requires millimolar piracetam — likely irrelevant at therapeutic exposures. Proposed mechanism is enhanced AMPA receptor 'density' or membrane fluidity rather than allosteric binding.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: After 60+ years, no consensus mechanism. Proposed: (1) membrane fluidity modulation via interaction with polar phospholipid head groups, (2) increased AMPA receptor density in aged brain, (3) facilitation of cholinergic neurotransmission, (4) improved erythrocyte deformability (relevant to cerebrovascular indications). None of these has been quantified to a Ki or EC50 at therapeutic concentrations.

neuroimaging.finding: Modest increases in interhemispheric EEG coherence in elderly subjects; small fMRI BOLD increases in language regions after acute dosing. Effect sizes generally small and inconsistent across studies.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: None — excreted unchanged renally

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: no characterized somatic withdrawal; rare reports of psychological rebound

demographic_differences.age: modestly prolonged t½ in elderly secondary to declining renal CL
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: renal impairment: dose-adjust (per CrCl)

data_gaps_remaining: Direct molecular target at therapeutic concentrations — genuinely unknown after decades
notes: Approved in much of Europe (cognitive disorders, cortical myoclonus) and ex-Soviet states; never approved in US. CSF concentrations reach ~30-40% of plasma; t½ in CSF (~8 h) is longer than plasma (~5-6 h). The remarkable feature of piracetam pharmacology is the durability of the mechanistic gap: 60 years, hundreds of papers, no consensus target. Doses are gram-scale precisely because intrinsic activity at any candidate target is low.

name: Placdyl

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ethchlorvynol — tertiary alcohol hypnotic. GABA-A PAM at a site overlapping the alcohol/anaesthetic pocket. Severe overdose has prolonged coma (5-15 days). Withdrawn 1999.

routes.notes: Biphasic, two-compartment; lipid sequestration explains prolonged coma.

notes: Withdrawn.

name: Pma

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Para-Methoxyamphetamine record.

notes: Duplicate of Para-Methoxyamphetamine.

name: Podocarpamide

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Diterpenoid amide from Podocarpus. Not a known psychoactive.

notes: MISCLASSIFIED — plant natural product.

name: Polygala tenuifolia

functional.notes: Tenuigenin (senegenin), tenuifolin, polygalasaponins, onjisaponin B all act on overlapping mechanisms: ACh enhancement (AChE inhibition), BDNF upregulation, anti-Aβ effects, antioxidant.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Herbal mixture; active components are oleanane-type pentacyclic triterpenoid saponins (tenuigenin, polygalasaponins XXXII, tenuifolin, onjisaponin B). Multimodal anti-AD effects in rodent models.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Nausea, vomiting at high doses (saponin emetic effect — historically used as an expectorant for this reason).

notes: Traditional Chinese Medicine herb (yuan zhi). Multiple saponin actives with overlapping anti-AD mechanisms in rodent models. Standardization varies wildly between preparations; human evidence is preliminary.

name: Pramiracetam

functional.readout: increased synaptosomal HACU after acute and chronic dosing
functional.notes: Pramiracetam is among the most potent racetams at enhancing HACU; the diisopropylethylamine side chain confers high lipophilicity and brain penetration.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cholinergic activation via HACU enhancement; no direct receptor binding. The basic amine side chain is the distinguishing structural feature — likely responsible for higher brain penetration than piracetam/oxiracetam.

notes: Originally Parke-Davis (CI-879); marketed in Italy (Pramistar) for cognitive disorders. ~15x more potent than piracetam in animal cognition models — attributed to better brain penetration rather than higher intrinsic activity at any specific target.

name: Prazepam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug — N-dealkylated by CYP3A4 to nordazepam. Smoother onset than diazepam.

routes.notes: Effect via nordazepam; t1/2 50–100 h.

notes: Prodrug for nordazepam, like clorazepate.

name: Pregabalin

primary_targets: α2δ-1 subunit of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

binding.tissue_or_cell: recombinant human α2δ-1 in baculovirus-infected Sf9 cells
binding.assay_buffer_notes: Belliotti et al. 2005, Bian et al. 2006 — pregabalin Ki 32 nM at α2δ-1 (~6x higher affinity than gabapentin Ki ~140 nM). Kd 6.0 nM in direct binding.
binding.notes: (S)-enantiomer is active; (R) is inactive.

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Pregabalin nearly equipotent at α2δ-1 vs α2δ-2 (Kd 6 vs 7 nM); gabapentin shows ~3x α2δ-1 preference.

functional.notes: Reduces stimulated transmitter release ~30-50% (Dooley et al. 2007).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Same mechanism as gabapentin (Cav α2δ binding → reduced trafficking → reduced presynaptic Ca2+ entry → reduced glutamate/NA/Sub-P release at hyperexcitable terminals). Pregabalin's ~6x higher α2δ-1 affinity translates to lower mg doses and a more rapid onset of clinical effect than gabapentin.

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults; PK linear up to clinical doses (LAT1 not saturated at standard 150-600 mg/d).
routes.notes: Bioavailability ~90% (higher than gabapentin because pregabalin uses multiple transporters in addition to LAT1). PK linear, predictable. t1/2 6.3 h. Renal excretion ~98% unchanged. No food effect on AUC.

concentration_effect.notes: Approximate; clinical response is dose-rather-than-conc guided.

metabolism.notes: <2% metabolised. ~98% renally excreted unchanged.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Coronial data show pregabalin involved in ~10-25% of opioid overdose deaths in regions with high prescription; UK reclassified as Schedule 3 controlled drug in 2019.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: None clinically relevant.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Onset 12-72 h. Anxiety, insomnia, autonomic activation, occasionally seizures and psychosis. More severe than gabapentin withdrawal due to higher α2δ affinity and shorter t1/2. Particularly difficult in patients with co-existing BZ/AUD dependence.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: dose-adjust by CrCl.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Strictly renal dosing required. CrCl 30-60: half dose; CrCl <30: quarter dose.

notes: Higher α2δ affinity (~6x) and predictable linear PK distinguish pregabalin from gabapentin. Higher abuse and overdose liability than gabapentin in surveillance data.

name: Promethazine

binding.notes: Sub-nM (0.33 nM) reported in some assays; 1-2 nM is the most commonly cited consensus. Behaves as inverse agonist (stabilises inactive H1 conformation) as for all first-gen H1 antagonists.

binding.reference: pmid:2884340 (Yasuda et al., Antimuscarinic effects of antihistamines; Mol Pharmacol)
binding.notes: Promethazine is the most potent muscarinic antagonist among the common first-gen antihistamines — comparable to atropine at M1 (~1 nM).

D2 affinity is moderate but clinically meaningful — explains the antiemetic action via chemoreceptor trigger zone and the rare extrapyramidal symptoms (dystonia, akathisia) reported with parenteral promethazine.
5-HT2C antagonism may contribute to anxiolytic and orexigenic properties.
α1 blockade explains the orthostatic hypotension seen with parenteral promethazine.

functional.cell_system: HEK293 stably expressing hERG, 36°C, +20 mV step protocol
functional.reference: doi:10.1016/j.phrs.2009.05.008 (Jo SH et al. — Promethazine directly blocks hERG K+ channel; Pharmacol Res 2009)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Inverse agonist at H1 (Gαq → PLCβ → IP3/DAG); silent antagonist at M1-M5 (Gq for M1/M3/M5; Gi for M2/M4). At 5-HT3 promethazine acts as a non-competitive channel blocker contributing to its antiemetic effect (separately from D2 antagonism). The phenothiazine ring is responsible for the broad off-target polypharmacology.

routes.reference: medscape:406904 (Pharmacokinetics of promethazine HCl, Strenkoski-Nix et al. 2000); Wikipedia/StatPearls compendium
routes.notes: Although >80% of an oral dose is absorbed, first-pass hepatic glucuronidation and sulfoxidation reduce absolute bioavailability to ~25%. Cmax from 25-50 mg oral 11-23 ng/mL; Tmax 2-3 h.
Mean t1/2 9.8 ± 3.4 h IM. Higher Cmax than oral due to bypass of first-pass.
IV t1/2 9-16 h. IV promethazine carries FDA black-box warning for severe tissue injury including gangrene if extravasation occurs.

metabolism.reference: pmid:8946477 (Nakamura K et al. — CYP2D6 is the principal cytochrome P450 responsible for metabolism of the histamine H1 antagonist promethazine in human liver microsomes; J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1996)

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Reduced clearance, prolonged sedation, increased anticholinergic burden

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: additive CNS/respiratory depression; CYP2D6 substrate competition (codeine→morphine activation may be impaired)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Synergistic respiratory depression; the 'purple drank' / 'lean' (promethazine-codeine syrup) culture is associated with multiple fatalities largely from respiratory arrest.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have markedly reduced clearance of ring-hydroxylation and N-demethylation pathways; expected to have 2-3× higher AUC and steady-state concentrations than EMs. UMs may have subtherapeutic plasma concentrations but are rarely characterised because promethazine is not titrated to a target.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Sedation tolerance develops over 1-2 weeks of chronic use; no formal receptor occupancy/downregulation studies for promethazine specifically.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Not formally characterised. Chronic high-dose recreational users (e.g. 'lean' culture) may report rebound insomnia, anxiety, and dystonia/restless legs (D2 receptor upregulation) on cessation.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: IC50 1.46 µM (HEK293, 36°C, +20 mV); APD90 prolongation in guinea pig ventricular myocytes IC50 0.73 µM. Clinical exposure at therapeutic doses (peak free conc ~1-2 nM) is well below this, but supratherapeutic / 'lean' culture doses (often 240-480 mL syrup = 240-480 mg promethazine) drive plasma concentrations into the µM range. Multiple reports of QT prolongation and torsades; FDA labelling carries QT warning. Notably, despite hERG block, transmural dispersion of repolarisation is preserved → clinical torsades risk lower than expected from in vitro data.

Phenothiazines have well-documented sodium channel block contributing to QRS widening in overdose; promethazine specifically less quantitatively characterised than chlorpromazine but shares the structural feature.
Non-competitive channel block at 5-HT3 contributes to antiemetic effect (in addition to D2 antagonism).

demographic_differences.age: Children — particularly under 2 years — have a black-box warning for fatal respiratory depression after promethazine. Elderly have prolonged clearance and increased delirium risk (Beers criteria — avoid).
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment substantially prolongs clearance; renal impairment has modest effect (renal excretion is minor pathway).

data_gaps_remaining: Quantitative Nav1.5 IC50 for promethazine specifically
Fraction of clearance per CYP isoform not quantified
No PET H1 occupancy data published for promethazine
notes: Promethazine is a phenothiazine — chemically related to chlorpromazine and other antipsychotics — and inherits the polypharmacology: potent H1 (~1 nM), potent muscarinic (1-12 nM at all subtypes — among the most potent anticholinergic antihistamines), moderate D2 (260 nM), 5-HT2A/2C (6-19 nM), α1 (~25 nM). This breadth explains its multi-modal clinical use (sedative, antiemetic, anti-vertigo, allergy) and its risks: anticholinergic delirium, EPS, hERG-mediated QT prolongation, orthostatic hypotension. The 'lean' recreational use (promethazine-codeine cough syrup) exploits the synergistic sedation; deaths are typically from opioid respiratory depression but promethazine contributes via additive CNS depression and arrhythmogenesis.

name: Propofol

primary_targets: GABA-A (β-subunit intersubunit transmembrane pocket; β3 critical)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Olsen 2018 review and Cohen 2014 (PMC3951778) — labels β-M286 at the β+/α- intersubunit transmembrane site. β3-N265M mutation abolishes anaesthesia in mice (Jurd 2003).
binding.notes: Photolabelling identifies multiple binding sites; β+/α- pocket dominant for anaesthetic effect.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: GABA-A PAM at the etomidate-/methaqualone-overlap β+/α- site. At anaesthetic conc directly opens the channel without GABA. Other minor targets: glycine PAM, nAChR inhibition, Na+ channel inhibition, sphingosine-1-phosphate-like signalling reported.

neuroimaging.finding: Frontal alpha (8-12 Hz) coherence increase and slow-delta dominance characteristic of propofol unconsciousness — Purdon spectrogram signature.

routes.notes: Three-compartment model. Rapid distribution t1/2α 2-4 min, redistribution t1/2β 30-70 min, terminal t1/2γ 4-12 h. Context-sensitive half-life ~25 min even after 8-h infusion — major advantage over thiopental. Hepatic + extrahepatic CL exceeds liver blood flow (extra-hepatic clearance, ~30% of total).

metabolism.notes: Major pathway.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2B6*6 reduces propofol metabolism modestly; not routinely actioned.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Withdrawal not described in normal use; abuse-related dependence reported in anaesthesia providers (occupational risk).

off_targets.target: PRIS — propofol infusion syndrome (mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation impairment)
off_targets.clinical_consequence: Lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac failure with prolonged high-dose (>4 mg/kg/h >48 h) infusion.

demographic_differences.sex: Women: ~30% faster recovery; pharmacokinetic differences modest.
demographic_differences.age: Elderly: 30-50% dose reduction (slower CL + increased CNS sensitivity).
demographic_differences.weight: Lean body mass for dosing in obesity.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment has surprisingly little PK impact (extrahepatic CL); renal failure does not require dose adjustment.

notes: The β3-N265M knock-in mouse experiments (Jurd 2003) genetically prove β3-containing GABA-A as the anaesthetic target. Distinct β3 vs β2 selectivity from etomidate.

binding.notes: Generic 'propoxyphene' = racemate; analgesia resides in the dextro-isomer.

name: Propranolol

primary_targets: β1 / β2 adrenergic (non-selective antagonist; S-(–)-enantiomer ~100x more potent)

binding.assay_buffer_notes: S-(–)-propranolol is the cardioactive enantiomer; R-(+) has membrane-stabilising effect.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-selective β-blocker; lipophilic, crosses BBB → useful for performance anxiety (peripheral somatic symptom suppression — tremor, tachycardia, sweating). Membrane-stabilising (Na+ channel) action at high conc explains overdose cardiotoxicity (similar to TCAs/cocaine).

routes.notes: Massive first-pass (~75%). t1/2 3-6 h IR. Hepatic CYP2D6 + CYP1A2 + CYP2C19. CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibitor (autoinhibition).

metabolism.notes: Mechanism-based inhibitor of CYP2D6 — autoinhibition contributes to dose-dependent nonlinear PK.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 30-50% lower exposure in smokers.
Reduced metabolism of co-administered CYP2D6 substrates.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs: higher exposure but offset by autoinhibition; PMs less common in clinical practice for dosing.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Chronic β-blockade upregulates β-adrenergic receptors → rebound HTN/tachycardia on abrupt discontinuation.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Rebound HTN/angina/MI risk on abrupt cessation; taper required.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Overdose: QRS widening, bradyarrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, seizures.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: 40% reduced CL.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: marked accumulation.

notes: Off-label use for performance anxiety leverages peripheral β-blockade rather than central anxiolysis.

notes: OTC Benzedrex inhaler. Widely abused via oral/IV ingestion despite intended inhalational use (cardiotoxicity risk).

name: Pst

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Aqueous extract of poppy seeds (Papaver somniferum) — pharmacology is morphine + codeine + thebaine eluted from seed-coat residue. Highly variable: morphine 1-2788 mg/kg of seed, codeine <1-248 mg/kg, thebaine <1-124 mg/kg (Powers 2018).

routes.notes: Pharmacokinetics dominated by morphine; same first-pass UGT2B7.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Same as morphine + codeine.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Morphine-type; can be severe with chronic use because daily morphine dose from PST can reach 100-500 mg.

demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Renal failure exaggerates M6G accumulation.

notes: The dose hazard is extreme variability — a single washed-seed batch can be inert; the next can deliver lethal morphine.

name: Pterostilbene

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methylated resveratrol analog. Two methoxy groups dramatically improve oral bioavailability and BBB penetration. Activates AMPK and SIRT1 indirectly (likely via mitochondrial signaling rather than direct enzyme binding). Activates PPAR-α (lipid lowering) which resveratrol does not.

routes.notes: Bioavailability ~80% vs ~20% for resveratrol; t½ ~105 min vs ~14 min for resveratrol. Better BBB penetration.

notes: Naturally occurring in blueberries. Pharmacologically superior absorption/distribution profile vs resveratrol but human cognitive data are sparse.

name: Pyrazolam

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Triazolobenzodiazepine with 2-pyridyl (like bromazepam) replacing 2-chlorophenyl of alprazolam. Some literature suggests α2/α3 selectivity but data are sparse. Distinct in that it does NOT undergo Phase I metabolism — directly glucuronidated.

routes.notes: t1/2 ~17 h. Unique among designer benzos in being directly glucuronidated (no Phase I).

metabolism.notes: Unusual — pyrazolam is excreted largely as parent + glucuronide; no hydroxy metabolites detected.

notes: First designer benzo to enter the NPS market (~2012). Unique: no Phase I metabolism — direct glucuronidation makes it CYP-interaction-resistant.

name: Pyritinol

primary_targets: ACh / GABA / NMDA modulation (described, not quantified)
pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Two vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) molecules joined by disulfide bridge — vitamin-derived semisynthetic. Crosses BBB; enhances glucose uptake/utilization in brain. Cleavage products include pyridoxal/pyridoxine (active B6 forms).

routes.notes: t½ ~2.5 h; 72-74% of dose excreted in urine within 24 h as conjugates.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Hepatotoxicity and cutaneous reactions (pemphigus, lichenoid) reported — particularly in elderly. Withdrawn or restricted in several markets for this reason.

name: Quetiapine

binding.assay_buffer_notes: Goldstein 2005 — H1 affinity drives the dominant sedative effect at low doses (25-100 mg), explaining the widespread off-label sleep use.
Low D2 affinity + fast dissociation explain antipsychotic efficacy at 300+ mg but minimal EPS.

binding.notes: Drives orthostatic hypotension.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Low-dose pharmacology (25-200 mg) is dominated by H1 and α1 antagonism → sedation, hypotension. Antipsychotic effect requires ≥300 mg for sufficient D2 occupancy. Norquetiapine (active metabolite, CYP3A4-generated) is a potent NET inhibitor (Ki ~12 nM) and 5-HT1A partial agonist — contributes to antidepressant/anxiolytic effects at higher doses.

neuroimaging.finding: D2 occupancy 12-44% at 150-750 mg; 5-HT2A occupancy >80% at 300+ mg.

routes.subject_demographics: Adults; t1/2 6-7 h IR, 7-13 h XR.
routes.notes: Extensive hepatic CYP3A4. F% well-absorbed; food has minor effect.

metabolism.notes: Norquetiapine is the pharmacologically interesting active metabolite — NET inhibitor + 5-HT1A partial agonist.

drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: 5-6x AUC increase — markedly higher sedation, hypotension, QT.
Major reduction in quetiapine exposure.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Histaminergic rebound: insomnia, anxiety, nausea on discontinuation, especially at sleep-aid doses.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Moderate QT prolongation, particularly in overdose.

demographic_differences.age: Elderly: 40% slower CL.
demographic_differences.weight: Weight gain via H1 + 5-HT2C.
demographic_differences.renal_or_hepatic: Hepatic impairment: 30% slower CL.

notes: Off-label sleep aid usage exploits H1/α1 dominance at low doses — separate phenomenon from antipsychotic efficacy.

name: R-(-)-MDMA

binding.notes: Higher specific 5-HT2A binding affinity than S-MDMA but NEGLIGIBLE functional activity — a binding/function dissociation. So 'psychedelic-like' marketing claims need scepticism — in humans, R-MDMA did NOT produce more psychedelic effects than S-MDMA at the doses tested.
Retains SERT-releasing activity (less than S-enantiomer).
Much less DA release than S-MDMA — proposed safety advantage (less reinforcing, less hyperthermic, less neurotoxic in animals).

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Preferential SERT-driven 5-HT release with minimal DA release. Animal data: lower locomotor stimulation, lower neurotoxicity signal, lower hyperthermia. Hypothesised as a 'safer' therapeutic enantiomer but the 2024 human trial showed comparable subjective intensity at equipotent doses (300 mg R ≈ 125 mg racemic).

routes.notes: R-MDMA half-life ~12 h (3× longer than S). Slower CYP2D6 metabolism.
Dose-doubled R-MDMA — exposure roughly doubles linearly (less nonlinear than racemic).

metabolism.notes: Slower than S-enantiomer.

data_gaps_remaining: Whether R-MDMA's preclinical safety advantages survive at therapeutically equivalent doses
notes: R-(−)-MDMA is being explored as a potentially safer therapeutic alternative to racemic MDMA. MindMed and others have programs. The human data (Holze 2024) tempers preclinical enthusiasm — at equipotent doses (~300 mg R ≈ 125 mg racemic), overall subjective intensity, MEQ30, and 5D-ASC are similar; the hoped-for 'more psychedelic, less stimulant' dissociation did not emerge in humans.

name: Remifentanil

binding.notes: Slightly more potent than fentanyl at binding. Methyl-ester structure designed to be hydrolysed by nonspecific tissue/plasma esterases.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Full MOR agonist. Ester hydrolysis by nonspecific esterases (not CES1) gives inactive metabolite — terminates effect.

routes.notes: Context-sensitive t½ ~3 min — independent of infusion duration. Cleared by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases; not affected by hepatic/renal failure.

metabolism.notes: Carboxylic acid metabolite — ~1/4000th remifentanil potency.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: BChE genotype does NOT affect clearance — different esterases.

tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: Rapid-onset withdrawal after infusion cessation; opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is well-documented and clinically problematic.

demographic_differences.age: Reduced infusion rate required in elderly.

name: Salvinorin A

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 transiently expressing human cloned KOR (cloned receptor)
binding.radioligand_or_probe: [3H]-bremazocine (competition); 48 secondary targets in PDSP screen showed no significant displacement

biased_agonism.bias_reference_compound: Salvinorin A is used as the unbiased reference (bias factor = 1) in White/Roth 2015
biased_agonism.interpretation: Salvinorin A recruits both G-protein and β-arrestin pathways with roughly balanced potency; β-arrestin recruitment is implicated in the dysphoric/aversive component shared by all unbiased KOR agonists.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: KOR Gαi/o coupling → adenylyl cyclase inhibition (decreased cAMP) and Gβγ-mediated GIRK channel activation and N/P/Q-type calcium channel inhibition. Salvinorin A also robustly activates β-arrestin-2 recruitment with subsequent JNK activation and KOR desensitisation/internalisation — these pathways underlie the rapid tachyphylaxis and dysphoric/aversive component characteristic of unbiased KOR agonism.

neuroimaging.finding: Baboon brain uptake peaked at ~40 s after IV bolus reaching 3.3% of injected dose; brain clearance half-life ~8 min — matches the <10-min behavioural duration after smoking in humans.

neuroimaging.modality: fMRI BOLD (12 healthy men, 15 µg/kg inhaled vapor)
neuroimaging.finding: Decreased within-network static functional connectivity, increased between-network connectivity, reduced dynamic FC, increased FC entropy. Most prominent effect: attenuation of default mode network (DMN) during first half of 20-min scan (F(1,11) = 9.40, p = 0.011; every subject showed DMN reduction, d = 1.50). Effect tracks the 1–10 min peak subjective intensity.
Reduced resting EEG spectral power across most bands (Ranganathan/Krystal, Yale).

routes.subject_demographics: Healthy adults, mean age 25, 4× received 21 µg/kg and 2× received 18 µg/kg vaporised via glass pipe
routes._note: Johnson/Reissig — Cmax mean 18.8 ng/mL at 2 min; subjective intensity correlated with plasma level r ≈ 0.93 across subjects; prolactin rose from 5 min peaking at 15 min, cortisol inconsistent. Effects essentially gone by 20 min, plasma near baseline by 90 min.

Up to 4 mg sublingual produced no psychoactive effects — very low bioavailability via the DMSO/PEG-400 sublingual vehicle (review citing Ranganathan).  Buccal absorption of leaf-extract juice held >10 min in mouth is the traditional Mazatec route.
Effectively zero oral bioavailability — rapid GI hydrolysis of C2 acetate to inactive salvinorin B; P-gp efflux at BBB.

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 contributes ~15% of in-vitro metabolism — theoretically PMs could see slightly higher exposure but the dominant clearance pathway is plasma esterase hydrolysis (independent of CYP), so PM/UM status is unlikely to change clinical PK meaningfully.

tolerance_and_dependence.receptor_downregulation_half_time: Acute desensitisation of KOR within minutes of salvinorin A exposure in HEK293 (β-arrestin-dependent); rapid tachyphylaxis to subjective effects when redosing within tens of minutes is reported anecdotally but not formally quantified in humans.
tolerance_and_dependence.withdrawal_syndrome: No physical withdrawal syndrome described; KOR agonists produce dysphoria/anhedonia acutely rather than dependence on cessation.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: A 2008 report suggested partial agonism at D2 (Ki 5-10 nM, 40-60% intrinsic activity); subsequent work has not consistently replicated this and the contribution to in-vivo effects is unclear.
No appreciable binding (PDSP screen, Roth 2002) — mechanistically distinguishes Sal A from classical psychedelics.
